units.la: MDXCVIII.
KAROLO VTENHOVIO NIEVLANDIÆ &c. Dn. VIRO nobilissimo, doctissimo, IANVS GRVTERVS
units.tr: To Karel Utenhove of Nieuwland, &c., most noble and most learned sir, JANUS GRUTERUS

units.la: Imocati isthac quae vides, inscripserat nomini tuo Kimedoncius noster, Colonia Agrippina redux: partim testandae gratitudini; quod dum isthic apud vos ageret, nullo non benevolentiae ac prothymiae genere cum prosecutus sueras: partim quoniam & Graecas literas, & aetatem cius, quae pueros vix exibat, optime nouisses: ideoque & errantem corrigere humaniter, & erratis committer veniam dare possis. At enim ut Menandrino versui fidem adstraxit:
units.tr: Kimedoncius, our friend, dedicated these works, which you see here, to your name when he returned from Cologne. He did so partly to express his gratitude, since you had treated him with every kind of goodwill and kindness while he was staying with you there. He also did so because you knew Greek literature and his age very well, since he was then scarcely past boyhood, and so you could both kindly correct his mistakes and pardon them.

units.la: Ὃν οἱ θεοὶ φιλᾶσιν ἀποθνῄσκει νέος,[?]
units.tr: Whom the gods love dies young [Ὃν οἱ θεοὶ φιλᾶσιν ἀποθνῄσκει νέος].

units.la: fatusque ac Deo visum, eripere ipsum rebus humanis, quū solummodo vixisset annos septemdecim, menses IX. dies VIII. quod ipsemet praepropero abitu impeditus praestare nequiit, idego nunc praesto: opus, spero & tibi pariter & defuncto gratum acceptumque. ideoq; simile quid mox facturus circa utriusq;, Philostrati Imagines, Heroica, Epistolas, &c. nec non Descriptiones Callistrati, Alciphronisque Epistolas, quae omnia vertit Latine. si minus accurate, quid mirum? imo quid tum? fatis est aestimationi hominum subiecisse, quantos qualesque fructus haec arbuscula latura fuisset, paulo maturior, quae iam tunc praecocis ingenii luxuriabat flosculis & colore simul & odore commendabilibus quo parū aetatis
units.tr: Since fate and God decided to take him from human affairs after he had lived only seventeen years, nine months and eight days, he could not finish what he had intended, because his hurried departure prevented him. I now take up that task. I hope the work will be pleasing and welcome to you and to the dead man alike. So I am about to do something similar with the Imagines, Heroica and Letters of Philostratus, the Descriptions of Callistratus and the Letters of Alciphron, all of which he translated into Latin. If the translation is not very accurate, what of it? What then? It is enough to submit to people's judgement how great and what kind of fruit this little tree would have borne had it grown to maturity, since even then it was flourishing with the early blossoms of a precocious talent, commendable both for their colour and their fragrance, though he had so little time.

units.la: vix digitali assurgant frutice, nedum inoculentur decore aliquo gemmeo. Tu sane, Utenhoui, istud quicquid est, libens excipies, scio, & fovebis; tam Kimedontii nomine, quam meo, cui tam multiplici, & patriæ, & propinquitatis, & communium literarum, aliarumque necessitudinum vinculo coniungeris.
units.tr: Scarcely does it rise above a finger-high shrub, let alone get grafted with some gem-like beauty. You, Utenhovius, will no doubt gladly receive whatever this is, I know, and will cherish it, both for Kimedoncius's sake and for mine, since you are joined to us by so many bonds: of country, of kinship, of shared learning and of other close ties.

units.la: DE THEOPHYLACTO, ET eius scriptis.
units.tr: CONCERNING THEOPHYLACTUS AND HIS WRITINGS

units.la: THeophylactus hic genus quidem ab Ægyptiis duxit, ut ait Photius, sed natus fuit in Græcia, ut ipse de se testatur, in præfatione dialogi. Præfectura alibi functus est, & munere quod vocant scripturarii. Ita enim interpretor ἀντυπηρεσίας[?] ex Lucilio lib. XXVI. Publicarum rerum assuefiam, ut scripturarius. vide Nonium. Christianum fuisse apparet tum ex aliis, tum quod secundæ dialogi partis præfat. Bacchum vocat fabulosum Deum. Extat hodie eius hic dialogus, & politissimus, & argutissimus. Epistolæ etiam quibus tersiores aut doctiores esse vix possunt. Historiæ eius superesse dicuntur in Vaticana Romæ. Nam hæc quæ interpretamur, ἐκλογαί sunt, siue Excerpta. E legationibus omnia verba sunt Simocati, si modo particulam ἐπ[?] abiicias, quam nos a reliquis, quia excerptoris est, secernimus.
units.tr: This Theophylactus, as Photius says, traced his descent from the Egyptians, but he was born in Greece, as he himself testifies in the preface to his dialogue. He held a public office elsewhere, and a post which they call scripturarius. For so I interpret the Greek word ἀντυπηρεσίας [antyperesias], from Lucilius, book XXVI: I was accustomed to public affairs, as a scribe. See Nonius. That he was a Christian appears both from other evidence and because in the preface to the second part of the dialogue he calls Bacchus a fabulous god. His dialogue survives today, and it is very polished and very subtle. His letters also survive, and they could hardly be more elegant or learned. His histories are said to survive in the Vatican in Rome. The works we are translating are Eklogai [ἐκλογαί], that is, Excerpts. All the words from the Embassies are those of Simocatta, provided one removes the particle ἐπ [ep], which we separate from the rest because it belongs to the excerptor.

units.la: THEOPHYLACTI SIMOCATTI DIALOGVS, de diversis aliquot quæstionibus physicis, earundemque solutionibus. PRÆFATIO DIALOGI.
units.tr: The Dialogue of Theophylact Simocatta, on Various Physical Questions and Their Solutions. Preface to the Dialogue.

units.la: Hirundines maternos cantus fecundum modulos musicos edoceri percepi a matribus. non enim indoctæ prolis audire mater sustinet hirundo. Docent eæ igitur suos fœtus vrbes inhabitare, & apud homines canere, ac circum superiores ædium partes carmine perstrepere concinno. Agite ergo, agite canendi vos peritissimum collegium, date puero facundiam ac theatro accinere me docete, & oden Atticam perstrepere, discentem iam primum musicum ascendere pulpitum. quod si vero nonnihil aberrauero a rhythmis, liberaliter vos ea supplete quæ deficiunt: quemadmodum illa in Locrensi Eunomo melodiæ socia cicada. Visum est & Teucro militare, & amare tropæa, ac in acie collocari. Quare proiectu clypei defensus ab Aiace; sagittas quidem Teuctas emittebat dextertime[?]: Aiax tamen suppeditabat strenuitatem. Ita vos, viri doctores, tanquam clypeum adhibete vestram beneuolentiam, & applausus hodie mihi sit pro armis, victoriamque scio reportabo, etiamsi non barbaram terram calcauero. quod si maternam artem nondum sum adeptus, at est tamen idem mihi vobiscum genus, & sermonem servo patrium, nostraque sunt, vel saltem Græca.
units.tr: I have heard that swallows are taught their mothers' songs in musical measures, since the mother swallow cannot bear to hear an untaught offspring. So they teach their young to dwell in cities and to sing among men, chattering in a tuneful song around the upper parts of the houses. Come then, come, you most skilled company of singers: give this boy eloquence, teach me to sing before the theatre and to chant an Attic ode, I who am now for the first time climbing onto the musician's platform. But if I stray somewhat from the rhythms, generously supply what is lacking, just as that cicada was a companion to the melody in the Locrian Eunomus. It seemed fitting for Teucer too to serve as a soldier, to love trophies and to take his place in the battle line. So, protected by the shield Ajax held out before him, he shot Teucrian arrows with great skill, while Ajax supplied the courage. So you, learned gentlemen, use your goodwill as a shield for me, and let today's applause be my arms; I know I shall win the victory, even though I have not trodden a barbarian land. And if I have not yet attained my mother's art, still I am of the same kind as you, and I keep my native speech, and it is ours, or at least Greek.

units.la: DIALOGI PERSONÆ, ANTISTHENES ET POLYCRATES.
units.tr: The Persons of the Dialogue: Antisthenes and Polycrates.

units.la: Cur adamas non comburatur, ac naturam ignis nequaquam sentiat. I.
units.tr: Why the diamond is not burned, and does not feel the nature of fire at all. I.

units.la: ANTIST.[?] Ariftagoram Timoclis filium diu iam Polycrates in Lyceo non vidi, numquid forte, numquidin Siciliam abiit, crateras igniuomos visum, aut Indicum sinum circumnauigat, ut aliquam sapientiæ sibi comparet scientiam? POLYCRAT. Reuera ut dicis Antigenes, siquidem Athenis cum abfuerit Apollogenes Corinthius heri forte obuiam nobis, circa variam porticum Ariftagoram dixit vidisse. Ariftonem vero Physicum & Sofipatrum Hermogenis filium, circa Leocorium eodem die redeuntes vidisse significauit. ANT. Vnde tandem, Polycrates? POL. Postquam Euxinum perlustrarunt sinum, multis nimis & maximis exerciti laboribus, mercis nobis loco quasi aureum quoddam vellus iactatas istas visarum rerum cognitiones aduexerunt. Amor enim eos scientiæ cum cepisset, irritauit quasi ambos, & ad inspectionem lustrationemque rerum exterarum incussit thyrsum. Instimulauit namque, instimulauit eos, ut Mœotim paludem lustrarent, anne curua esset, quod ad litum, nouem vero millia stadiorum eam terminat, ac definiunt, ut prædicant geographi, fide digna ad eam rem usi demonstratione. Dicunt etiam physi-cas aliquot rationes fuisse propositas a Pericle Corinthio, quem obuiam habuerint prope Bosporū. Inde sermones ac speculationes in urbe ortæ sunt, & unusquisq; in id incumbit, quo pacto magnum aliquid fit dicturus, ac elegantia doctrinæ alius alium antecellat. Peripatus cum stoa certamen habet, stoa cum Pythagoreis committitur, & Academici Epicureorum dissertationibus non sunt contenti, bellumque quoddam sine ferro per Græciam est motum. Ant. Age igitur sis optime, rem nobis narra hanc, vt namque vides, ad cognoscendum mentem arrigo, & venas scientiæ vt inueniam scritor, sicut metallarii, quando preciosissimæ cuiusdā materiæ venas viderint.
units.tr: ANTIST. Polycrates, I have not seen Aristagoras, son of Timoclis, for a long time now. Has he perhaps gone off to Sicily to see the fire-spouting craters, or is he sailing round the Indian sea to gain some knowledge of wisdom? POLYCRAT. Indeed, as you say, Antigenes: Apollogenes of Corinth, who was away from Athens, happened to meet us yesterday, and he said he had seen Aristagoras near the Painted Portico. He reported that Ariston the physicist and Sosipatrus, son of Hermogenes, had been seen on the same day, on their way back, near the Leocorium. ANT. Where have they come from at last, Polycrates? POL. After they had explored the Euxine Sea, worn out by many very great labours, they have brought us, in place of merchandise, as it were a golden fleece, these cargoes of observed facts. For love of learning had seized them, and it drove them on, as if both had been struck by a thyrsus, to inspect and explore foreign things. It urged them, I say, to survey the Lake Maeotis, to find out whether it is curved at the shore, which, as the geographers proclaim, bounds it at nine thousand stades, using demonstrations trustworthy for that purpose. They also say that some physical arguments were put forward by Pericles of Corinth, whom they met near the Bosporus. From this, discussions and speculations have arisen in the city, and each man sets himself to the task of saying something great, and to surpass the others in the elegance of his learning. The Peripatetics contend with the Stoa, the Stoa is pitted against the Pythagoreans, and the Academics are not content with the disputations of the Epicureans, and a kind of war without iron has been stirred up through Greece. Ant. Come then, my good fellow, tell us this matter; for, as you see, I prick up my mind to understand it, and I shall search out the veins of learning, as miners do when they have seen veins of some most precious material.

units.la: Pol. Non de paruo aliquo linguæ, sermones & contemplationes inter se digladiantur. Adamantinum enim quoddam institutum est bellum, ac naturæ euoluunt mysteria. Dicunt enim Periclem dicere, quod e natura, sit adamantis, ne comburatur, quodque resistere possit omniuoro igni. Hoc o amice, Philosophorum perturbat turbam, & ad indagationem tanti secreti excitauit. Nam talibus iste Corinthius nos capiens vinculis, quasi in Scythico quodam a quo exiri non potest, cognitionis Labyrintho reclusos, coegit & arctauit.
units.tr: Pol. Their talks and contemplations are not fighting among themselves over some trivial matter of words. For a kind of adamantine war has been set in motion, and they are unrolling the mysteries of nature. For they say Pericles claimed that it is by nature of adamant that it is not burned, and that it can resist all-devouring fire. This, my friend, has thrown the crowd of philosophers into confusion and roused them to investigate so great a secret. For that Corinthian, catching us in such bonds, has shut us up, cramped and constrained, as it were in a Scythian labyrinth of knowledge from which there is no way out.

units.la: Ant. Expónam tibi naturæ aliquod opus Polycrates, quoniam re elegantem hominem, sermonumque doctorum studiosum video. Etenim amico bonum vllum pulchrumque neutiquam cælauero, secundum Cyrenæum.
units.tr: Ant. I shall explain to you some work of nature, Polycrates, since I see you are an elegant man and keen on learned discourse. For I shall by no means conceal any good or beautiful thing from a friend, according to the Cyrenaic.

units.la: Pol. Age sis igitur Antisthenes, sermo ducatur de ca re, de qua solemus internos consilia cómutare.
units.tr: Pol. Come then, Antisthenes, let the discussion be led to that matter about which we are accustomed to exchange our thoughts.

units.la: Ant. Subtilissimi pori ppter nimiam soliditatem sunt in adamante, quas pter & ferrũ nihil in eum potest, Neq; enim scalpitur, neq; frangitur ob nimiã densitatẽ. inde flãmam non sentit, quasi prohibentibus poris, ac omnino ebsistentibus, ne lapidem ignis natura penetret. cumque ita nulla sit commixtio, dissociantur. dissociatorum vero dissunctorumque[?] nullus ad se vicem est habitus. Adamas igitur cum igne coniungi nequit, quare neque aduritur, & ignis naturae hostilis aduersatur. ferrum contra & aurum ignis naturam recipiunt, unde illa aut liquefiunt aut molliuntur.. equidem sane propter maiorem ariditatem, combustioni non est obnoxius adamas. Nam omne quod liquescit[?], plurimum necessario habet humoris. Por. Euge hunc sermonem! adamantinis quasi verbis de adamante expositionem hanc variasti. per sane ipsum adamantem, aut si quid adamante est infractius. Fortior autem nobis est adamante veritas. Sed age sane, & famosum illud & insigne Corinthii istius inspiciamus problema. Ant. Quodcunque volueris, consule.
units.tr: ANT. The most subtle pores in the diamond, because of its great solidity, are such that iron can do nothing against it. For it is neither scraped nor broken, because of its extreme density. Hence it does not feel the flame, as if its pores were closed and altogether opposed, so that the nature of fire cannot penetrate the stone. And since there is thus no mixture, they are dissociated. Of things dissociated and disjoined there is no mutual relation. The diamond therefore cannot be joined with fire, and so it is neither burned, and it opposes fire's hostile nature. Iron and gold, on the contrary, receive the nature of fire, whence they either melt or soften. Indeed the diamond is not liable to combustion because of its greater dryness, for everything that melts necessarily contains a great deal of moisture. POL. Well said! You have varied this exposition with adamantine words about the diamond; surely by the diamond itself, or by whatever is less breakable than diamond. But truth is stronger for us than diamond. Come, let us examine that famous and notable problem of that Corinthian. ANT. Consult whatever you wish.

units.la: Cur aquilarum penna aliarum auium pennis addite, corrumpant eas. II.
units.tr: Why the feathers of the eagle, when added to the feathers of other birds, spoil them. II.

units.la: Por. Corrumpere dixit aquilarum pennas additas forte & coniunctas iis aliarum auium pennas, quasi & hac in parte tyrannidé sibi vindicaret aquila, & solis pennis, cum eis est exuta, nihilominus regiam obtinere vellet potestatem. quae ratio est, Antisthenes? opera naturae mihi interpretare. An. O Corinthium, ut mystica quadam scientia hic sapiens est refertus. Ceterum dicam tibi quid Polycrates, tu vero attentam praebe aurem, & Sireneam vocem audies, quemadmodum aliquis Ithacesius ad has accedens, quae cygneum quoque melos exsuperent, cantilenas. Por. Dic igitur, o optime; An. Gravissimi odoris ales est aquila, unde tum fit ut cum prædam illa ceperit, non posthac præ fœtore eius reliquias aliquando accesseris, neque si heri modo, aimice, venata fuerit, sed nec reliquæ volucres vescuntur. Eodem enim die adhuc putrefcūt, quasi vel Phinei cuiufdam, vel Harpyiæ conuiuii forent reliquiæ. quare similiter etiam corrumpuntur quilarum pennæ: quia naturæ sunt putredinofæ. ac ideo nequaquam seruari poterunt aliarum auium pennæ, ficum aquilinis fuerint cópofitæ. Nam statim absumuntur.
units.tr: POL. He said that the eagle's feathers are spoiled when the feathers of other birds are added and joined to them, as if the eagle claimed tyranny even in this respect, and even when stripped of its own feathers, wished still to keep royal power. What is the reason, Antisthenes? Explain nature's work to me. ANT. O Corinthian, how full of some mystical wisdom he is! But I will tell you, Polycrates; lend me your attentive ear, and you will hear a Sirenic voice, as an Ithacan does when he approaches songs that surpass even the swan's melody. POL. Tell me, then, my good fellow. ANT. The eagle is a bird of very heavy smell, so that once it has caught its prey, one does not afterwards approach its remains because of the stench, nor if it was hunted only yesterday, my friend; and the other birds do not feed on them either. For on the same day they already rot, as if they were the leftovers of some Phineus or of a Harpy's banquet. Therefore the eagle's feathers likewise decay, because they are of a putrefying nature. And so the feathers of other birds cannot be preserved if they are joined to eagle feathers, since they are consumed at once.

units.la: Cur elephanti non prius bibant, quam aquam contarba- verint.
units.tr: Why elephants do not drink before they have stirred up the water.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Pot. Nimis sapienter, oamice. Sed intuere mihi Apellis, Antisthenes, tabulas, admiratus sum pictura, mihi homo, ornatum. spectamihi Indicum hocanimal, quomodo qui picturam fecit, optime illud expresserit. Elephantum fertur non prius bibere, quam aquam proboscide, collutu lauerit.
units.tr: Pol. Very wise, friend. But look at Apelles' paintings, Antisthenes. I admired the picture; the ornament pleased me. Observe this Indian animal, how well the painter has portrayed it. The elephant is said not to drink until it has first stirred the water with its trunk and washed it.

units.la: Ant. Non fictum est, quod fertur, exhorrer vmbram sui in aqua visam elephas. quapropter & Indos observare illunem noctem dicunt, quando transfretare volunt hocanimal. Narcisso isti, quem fabulæ celebrant, exemplo est elephas, vt fuaipfius vmbra declinata, amores auersetur a natura alienos.
units.tr: Ant. What is said is no fiction: the elephant shrinks from its own shadow when it sees it in the water. For this reason, they say, the Indians watch for a moonless night when they want to cross a river with this animal. The elephant is an example to that Narcissus whom the fables celebrate: having turned away from its own shadow, it shuns loves that are foreign to its nature.

units.la: Qua ratione torpedo piscis per lignum quod inter me- dium retis est & manus faciat morbum sui cognomi- nem, & piscatorum manus reddat torpidas.
units.tr: By what means the torpedo fish, through the wood that lies between the net and the hand, causes a malady named after itself and makes the fishermen's hands numb.

units.la: IIII.
units.tr: IIII.

units.la: Amo contemplationis vim, quam gnarus admodum tu es interpretandi rationem naturæ. Sed agedum sane de torpedine sermonem mihi expone.
units.tr: I love the power of contemplation, and you are very skilled in explaining the reason of nature. But come, explain the matter of the torpedo to me.

units.la: torpeatque superba Corinthii lingua, problemata de torpedine iactitans. Marinos aiût piscatores, fi quando torpedo reti capta fit, manus afflici,nisi (tatim rete deuinciant a pertica. Quomodo vero,o amice, per lignum piscatores lædit hoc animal? ANT. In mare miraculorum linguam, quemadmodum Pericles, mouisti. intra cognitionis terminos mentem tuam cohibe, qui quasi Atlanticum contemplationum pelagus tibi vis narrari. Ego autem tuo Polycrates in hoc amori breuiter obsequar. POL. Dicas igitur, o generosé. Urbani enim videntur mihi & unles hi sermones, qui proponantur. Non a te recedam hodie, non per optimum hunc meum ambrem. ANT. Iucundissima forte aeris est natura, resona, suda, odorata. quæ omnia in aere diuinæ quædam curæ optime procurarunt, ut illius ita opera recrearetur ac reficeretur isthæc terræ regio. multarum igitur passionum effectuumq; causator hic est. Quod enim qui laborant ex oculis, in eos qui in se intuentur, morbi sæpe partem transfundunt, per aerem certe fit circumstantem interstitii infar, unde valetudo nobis & inualetudo. Itaque per medium aerem torpedo quoque vitium potest inferre nō procul abstientib. etiamsi non tangatur. Dabo vero tibi etiam huius exemplum. Magnes, quem Heracleum quoque lapidem vocant, a ferro distat, nihilominus per medium aerem videmus operari lapidem in ferrum. Jam vero communis illa affectio, in palma arbore, cuius mentem non percellat? cuius auditum non obstupuit? Diuersus primo sexus est, discretaque femina. deinde vicinis inter se masculo existentibus & femina videas utiq; feminam mittentem ramos, tanquam comam amatoriam, ad masculum : consentientemque incoitum,ac turgentem. postquam vero non pertingunt huius quandoque ad matrem rami, argute huic amori subueniunt insitores. Perticis enim ipsam aut viminibus circumligant masculo, & sic percepta voluptate femina curuationem exit, & ad morem veterem ramos reuocat, vtquæ masculi per perticas illas habuerit copiam. absurdum ergo neutiquam, si torpedo quoque piscatores per medium, quod intercedit, lignum, afficiat.
units.tr: Pol. The Corinthian tongue, boasting of its problems about the torpedo, grows numb. Sailors say that when a torpedo is caught in the net, the fishermen's hands are afflicted unless they at once untie the net from the pole. But how, friend, does this animal injure the fishermen through wood? Ant. You have stirred up the tongue of wonders on the sea, as Pericles did. Restrain your mind within the limits of knowledge; you wish to be told about the Atlantic sea of contemplations, as it were. I, however, will briefly yield to your love, Polycrates. Pol. Speak then, noble friend. What you propose seems to me both urbane and pleasant. I shall not leave you today, not even for this best perfume of mine. Ant. The nature of air is perhaps most pleasant: it is sonorous, sweating, scented. In the air divine providence has most carefully arranged all these things, so that this region of the earth might be refreshed and restored by them. This air, then, is the cause of many affections and effects. For those who suffer from the eyes often transfer the disease to those who look at them; so through the intervening air there is certainly a kind of influence, whence come our health and our sickness. Thus the torpedo too can transmit its harm through the middle air to those standing not far off, even if they are not touched. I will give you an example of this as well. The magnet, which they also call the Heraclean stone, is distant from iron, yet we see the stone working upon the iron through the middle air. And indeed, who is not struck by that common phenomenon in the palm tree? Whose hearing is not astonished by it? First the sexes are distinct, and the female is separate. Then, when male and female stand close to one another, you may see the female sending out her branches, like an amorous lock of hair, toward the male, consenting to union and swelling. But when her branches sometimes do not reach the mother, the grafters skilfully come to the aid of this love. For they tie the female to the male with poles or osiers, and so, once she has received the pleasure, she straightens her bent frond and returns her branches to their old posture, since she has had access to the male through those poles. It is by no means absurd, then, if the torpedo too affects the fishermen through the wood that lies between them.

units.la: Cur cerui, cum cornua deiecerint, consueta loca fugi- ant. V.
units.tr: Why stags, when they have shed their horns, flee their accustomed places. V.

units.la: Pol. Doctum sermonem frater in primis naturæ mihi videris esse, Antisthenes. Sed e mari in terram transire amat sermo,ac in continentem auctor deriuare contemplationem. Ceruos Corinthius iactauit cum cornua abiecerint consueta loca fugere,quasi pudeat illos huius inornatus, quatisperadest. Aur. Putauerit equidem aliquis ludere forsitan Periclem Polycrates, aut quodammodo corybantiare, vel insanire, qui nugacem hanc quæstionem adferat. ego autem virum admiratus sum, studiumque in eo contemplationis veneror. Sed an videtur ad hanc platanum paulo defidere. cum præsertim densa sit platanus, & quod ad trunci longitudinem vmbramque, perpulchra. Pol. Atqui perge. Aur. Igiturne fili Sofiæ putas, putasne inquam cornu abiicere ceruum? Pol. Dico sane.infinities hoc vidi, quando quidem ætate puer eram, ingenio vero rudior, rebus venatoriis addictus magis, cum speluncas & colles mirarer, ac in vinbrotis montium verticibus stabulacer. ANT. Ceterum igitur dicam & ego, cur tandem stationes consuetas fugiant, cum cornu iis quasi est abstonsum. Sensus est in brutis animantibus, Polycrates, quo dirigente se suamque salutem tueri norunt. Novit sepia atramenti sui dolum, quo se piscatoribus facit invisibilem. sciunt animalia quae cuiuis unguibus sunt, suas vires. Scit lepus cursu pedumque velocitate, venatoris insidias cuitare. Scit etiam ceruus detonsus cornua, quod ii qui vim faciunt, invadant naturam se imbecilliore. quocirca abscoditur veluti miles aliquis exarmatus aciem veritus, ac pocul alibi a pugna abesse cupiens. grauissimo praeterea capitis dolore animal hoc affligitur. Atque haec natura scit, quibus philosophia est initiata.
units.tr: Pol. You seem to me, brother Antisthenes, most learned above all in nature. But your discourse loves to pass from the sea to the land, and to draw your contemplation inland. The Corinthian has put forward that stags, when they have cast off their horns, flee their accustomed places, as if they were ashamed of their unadorned state, since it is at hand. ANT. Surely someone would think that Polycrates is perhaps joking, or rather playing the Corybant, or going mad, who brings forward this trifling question. I, however, admire the man, and I venerate his zeal for contemplation. But does it seem right to sit down a little beside this plane tree, since the plane is thick and very fine, both for the length of its trunk and for its shade? Pol. Then go on. Ant. Do you think, then, son of Sophia, do you think, I say, that a stag casts off its horn? Pol. I certainly say so. I have seen this countless times, when I was a boy, and cruder in mind, more given to hunting, while I was admiring caves and hills and lingering on the mountain peaks among the brambles. ANT. Then I too shall say why they at last flee their customary haunts, since their horn has been cut off from them, as it were. There is a sense in brute animals, Polycrates, by which they know how to direct themselves and guard their safety. The cuttlefish knows the trick of its ink, by which it makes itself invisible to fishermen. Animals that are armed with claws know their own strength. The hare knows how to avoid the snares of the hunter by its speed of running and the swiftness of its feet. The stag too, once its horns are shorn, knows that those who attack it will assault a nature weaker than before. Therefore it hides itself, like some soldier disarmed who fears the battle line and wishes to be far away from the fight. Besides, this animal is afflicted by a very grievous pain in the head. And nature knows these things, into which philosophy is initiated.

units.la: Ruta cum serpentibus sit contraria. VI.
units.tr: Rue is hostile to serpents. VI.

units.la: Quam dexter, amice, venatores, maximam Peripato venatus scientiam. nunc nos fonorz circumspirant aure pulchram subter platanum, unde pulchrum est haurire sermones. Age sis itaque ad Libyca me deducas hospitem miracula. Ibi enim quod hominum opinionem excedat, aitifte[?] vidisse Corinthius, aufugere serpentes a ruta, tanquam virtutis cuiusdam repulsiuz[?]. Qua id mente fiat, responde tuo Polycrati, velut ex tripode profatus oracula. ANT. Sciscitandi nimis es studiosus Polycrates. me vero, prudentiam iuro, latuit. Sed quoniam & ad haec etiam cognoscenda peruenisti, ad hunc quoque sermonem nos non habebis imparatos. Frigida quidem, & arida neruosaque natura serpens est. Sit autem hoc tibi veritatis signum, tempore hyemali, quasi antra quædam latebras amat serpens, & ad infima terræ se penetrat profunda, quæ vtique sunt calidiora hyeme, & ad calorem idoneam habent mansionem. rursus vero æstate, serpens ipsi superficie versatur terræ, & super terram apparet. ac novit serpens temporum versiones, nō initiatus astronomicis, vel vllis Chaldæorum argutiis. Ruta igitur Libyca aridissima est, & cito, quasi crapulam quandam tenebricosamque caliginem gignens in serpentibus, eos exanimat.
units.tr: How skilled you are, friend, at hunting, the greatest science of the Peripatetics! Now the breezes breathe around us beneath the fair plane tree, where it is pleasant to draw in conversation. Come then, and lead me to the wonders of Libya, a guest to be shown what surpasses human opinion. For they say that the Corinthian himself saw serpents flee from rue, as if it had some repellent virtue. By what reasoning this happens, answer your Polycrates, as if speaking oracles from the tripod. ANT. You are far too eager to inquire, Polycrates. As I swear by wisdom, I do not know it. But since you have come to learn these things too, you will not find me unprepared for this discussion either. The serpent is indeed a cold, dry and sinewy creature. Let this be a sign of the truth for you: in winter the serpent loves hiding places, like caves, and creeps down into the deep recesses of the earth, which are certainly warmer in winter and offer a suitable dwelling for warmth. Again in summer the serpent moves over the surface of the earth and appears above ground. And the serpent knows the changes of the seasons, not being instructed in astronomy or in any Chaldean subtleties. Libyan rue, therefore, is very dry, and, producing in serpents a certain drowsiness and dark mist, as it were, it quickly kills them.

units.la: Qua ratione oleum per mare diffusum, malaciam inducat. cat. VII.
units.tr: How oil poured over the sea produces calm. Chapter VII.

units.la: Pol. Consentaneus mihi nimis hic est sermo, & veritatis simulacra referens. mihi vero iam rursus amor in mare egredi. Cum enim animus meus perspiceret telluris miracula, in mare se vult propripere. Quandocunque mare navigat, profundi ista mirabilia amat, & capitur eorum contemplatione, quæ fiunt in terra. Ant. Siquidem igitur iterum sermonibus est opus, dic certe mihi, dic qua tibi naviget contemplatio? Pol. Nautas audiui infuso oleo tranquillitatem aucupare maris, quasi placatum modo conatos reddere, quando exaestuat. Sic vero etiam piscatores in capiendis piscibus facere solent. Ad hanc me theoriam sermone, quasi lembo quodam admittere, Antisthenes. Ant. Tenuissimæ materiæ ventus est, Polycrates: oleum vero lubricum & leue. quocirca prolapsus ex hac lubricitate ventus, æstum per aquas coaceruare non potest. vnde ridet in mari tranquillitas, humano velut oleo sedata.
units.tr: Pol. This account of yours is too much in agreement with me, and it reproduces the semblance of truth. But now my love urges me to go out upon the sea again. For when my mind contemplates the wonders of the earth, it wants to hurry off to the sea. Whenever one sails the sea, one loves the marvels of the deep, and is captivated by the contemplation of those things that happen on land. Ant. Since, then, we need words again, tell me, please, where does your contemplation sail? Pol. I have heard that sailors, by pouring oil on the water, catch the calm of the sea, as if they were making it placid again when it is seething. Fishermen too are accustomed to do the same in catching fish. Antisthenes, admit me to this theory with your speech, as if in a little boat. Ant. Wind is a very thin matter, Polycrates, and oil is slippery and light. Therefore the wind, slipping away because of this slipperiness, cannot pile up the swell across the waters. Hence the sea laughs in tranquillity, calmed as if by human oil.

units.la: Cur triennium ferant vultures. VIII.
units.tr: Why vultures carry their young for three years. VIII.

units.la: Adhuc te inhibebo, & nondum remittam; Antifthenes. voluptatis enim amor concepta sturarinon patitur. Vultures esse grauidas triennale tempus Corinthius fabulatur, & alienam videtur mihi esse a naturæ legibus. nusquam enim audiui talem fabulam. AN T. Multa inter aues genera non opus habent masculorum copulatione ad coceptionem.
units.tr: I will still hold you back and not yet release you, Antisthenes, for love of pleasure does not allow a mind once captured to escape. The Corinthian tells the fable that vultures are pregnant for a period of three years, and it seems to me to be foreign to the laws of nature. For I have never heard such a tale anywhere. Ant. Many kinds of birds have no need of the mating of males for conception.

units.la: Sed alia quidem quæ ventosa sunt, non pariunt. vultures autem vt fine marium coniunctione parient, naturæ ferunt leges. vulturem itaque videre non est masculum, sed omnem sexum iis interclufit natura feminæ: quod cum sciant vultures, orbitatem veriti liberorum, in conceptionem omne genus incumbit, quemadmodum Lemniades mulieres heroum videntes appellentem classem. multiplices deinde nectunt vultures astutias. aduersus Notum ventum volitant. quod fi Notus non fit, ad affinem ei Eurum expandunt alas. postea hiantes, acita vento influente replentur: & pariunt nouâ ventosâ, sed fœtus viuos. idcirco plurimo tempore natura opus habet, vt animal perficiat, Polycrates. Difficile namque & operosum nimis est natura, animali dare essentiam, & ad animalis perfectionem producere id quod est tenuissimum.
units.tr: But indeed those which are windy do not bring forth young. Yet that vultures should bear young without the union of males is what the laws of nature allow. So one is not to see a male vulture; nature has shut off the whole male sex from them, leaving only the female. Since vultures know this, fearing the loss of their offspring, every kind of them applies itself to conception, just as the Lemnian women did when they saw the fleet of the heroes approaching. Then the vultures devise manifold cunning. They fly against the south wind; if there is no south wind, they spread their wings toward the east wind, which is related to it. Afterwards, gaping open, they are filled as the wind flows into them, and they bring forth a new windy offspring, but living young. Therefore, Polycrates, nature needs a long time to bring the animal to completion. For it is very difficult and laborious for nature to give being to an animal and to bring to the perfection of an animal that which is most tenuous.

units.la: Cur polypus mare Ponticum auersetur. IX.
units.tr: Why the polyp shuns the Pontic sea. IX.

units.la: Pol. Ego quidem putabam nugari Corinthium, Antifthenes. capti fumus, & veritatis retibus lubenter irretimur. Igiturne huc vsque saltem sapientæ differtatio? Absit sane, absit. non enim dimidiam abibo scientiam habens. circa pontum pisces omnes dicunt cōmeare, polypum vero circa finum Boreum nullum esse. Ant.[?] & valde verisimiliter, Polycrates. polypus enim in pento nullus est. Nam alii pisces refrigeratione opus habent, & potabiles aquas persequuntur: alii vero calorem sumant. & ad mare reuertuntur, quod calidius est omnibus aquis ceteris. Polypus autem mari Pontico aduersatur[?], quia frigidius est Boreum pelagus, sed etiam reliquo mari dulcius, propterea quod in id multi magnique fluuii influant. contraria vero polypo & frigus & dulcedo. ad demonstrationem, quod dicam, idoneum est. petre connexus polypus inaunl[?]fe hæret. idee dulcem fuffunduntaquam petræ periti piscatores. & hi quidem quæsito captu fruuntur, ille vero a scopulo, cuiante tam tenaciter hærebat, facile nimis auellitur.
units.tr: Pol. I, for my part, thought the Corinthian was talking nonsense, Antisthenes. We have been caught, and we gladly let ourselves be ensnared in the nets of truth. Is this discourse of the wise man to go no further than this? Far from it, far from it! For I shall not depart with only half of the knowledge. They say that all fish pass around the Pontus, but that there is no polyp around the northern gulf. Ant. Very probably so, Polycrates; for there is no polyp in the Pontus. For other fish need cooling and pursue drinkable waters, while others seek warmth and return to the sea, which is warmer than all other waters. The polyp, however, is averse to the Pontic sea, because the northern open sea is colder, yet also sweeter than the rest of the sea, since many large rivers flow into it. The polyp is opposed to both cold and sweetness. What I am going to say is suitable as a demonstration: the polyp, attached to a rock, clings fast. Thus skilled fishermen pour sweet water over the rocks, and they enjoy the catch they sought, while the polyp is very easily torn from the crag to which it clung so tenaciously.

units.la: PRÆFATIO ÆVSCVLTAT- I-onis fecunda.
units.tr: Preface, Fruitful of Listening

units.la: Semeles filium Dionysium, potius autem Iouis, (Nam dupla Dionysi ex Ioue natiuitas) Iouis igitur filium Dionysium, cum forte abortiuum deposuif-set mater, & puer femiperfectus fabulosus hic est Deus, sub femine patre absoluit prolem, ac iterūlatus est Semeles filius Dionysus. Semidiētos mihi ad finem producite sermones, viri doctores, penes quos est perfectio. non enim imperfectos orationis fertis partus. Amabat olim Pan. amabat sautem Pan seipsum, ac vocis erat refonatio, quod amabatur, etiam si Panalatuerunt fraudes insonuit, & amata sensit, abstinuit a cantu, ac disparuit quod amabat. Canam igitur & ego. resonabit enim scio collegium, & amatos ego plausus sentiam. etiamsi praeter dignitatem & meritum eorum, quae dixero, laus illa sit futura.
units.tr: Semele's son Dionysus, or rather Jupiter's, for Dionysus had a double birth from Jupiter. So when his mother had by chance cast off the premature birth, this fabled god, half-formed, was completed in his father's thigh and born again as Semele's son Dionysus. I bring my half-finished speeches to an end, learned teachers, in whose power perfection lies, for I do not offer you unfinished offspring of speech. Pan once loved, and Pan loved himself, and what was loved was the echo of his voice. Even when the deceptions rang out, the one who was loved felt it, held back from singing, and vanished, as the thing he loved. I too will sing, then. I know the assembly will resound, and I shall feel the applause I love, even though that praise will go beyond the worth and merit of what I have said.

units.la: RELIQVA DIALOGI.
units.tr: THE REMAINING PARTS OF THE DIALOGUE.

units.la: Qua rati- one sanguis hirquinus mollior adamante. X.
units.tr: By what reasoning goat's blood is softer than adamant. X.

units.la: Pol. Curiosis indagandi animis satietas non obtingit cognoscendi. Nondum igitur ad metam sermo, Antisthenes. Nam aures mihi sunt inaniores oculis. Hircino molliri sanguine adamantem dixit Corinthius, & diuina ea res, ac secreta videtur esse. Initium igitur agedum & finis huius conuentus oratio sit de adamante. Ant. Iam tibi, Polycrates, frigidam quandam, & aridam siccamque adamantis esse supposuimus naturam. Vnde contrariis verifimiliter obedit adamas. Sanguinis vero calida est & humida natura. Quapropter humiditate quidem ariditas & siccitas subigitur, frigiditas vero caloris emollitur. Pol. Et quid tandem, adamas an non quouis sanguine mollitur? Ant. Calidissimus hircinus est sanguis, vnde etiā superat adamantem. nunc autem & leonino sanguine molliunt adamantem. excellentia caloris diffringentes eiusdem duritiem. Pol. Estne ergo sanguinum quoque discriminis aliquod? Ant. omnino equidem. habet etenim suam ceruinus sanguis proprietatem, habet vero & taurinus potentiam singularem.
units.tr: Pol. Minds eager to investigate are never satisfied with knowing. So the discussion has not yet reached its goal, Antisthenes, for my ears are emptier than my eyes. The Corinthian said adamant is softened by goat's blood, and this seems to be a divine and secret matter. So let the beginning and the end of this gathering be a discourse on adamant. Ant. We have already assumed for you, Polycrates, that adamant has a cold, dry and parched nature, and so it plausibly yields to opposites. Blood, however, has a warm and moist nature. Therefore dryness and aridity are overcome by moisture, while coldness is softened by heat. Pol. And then, does adamant not soften under any blood whatever? Ant. Goat's blood is the hottest, and so it surpasses even adamant. Lion's blood also softens adamant, breaking up its hardness by the excellence of its heat. Pol. So is there some difference among bloods too? Ant. Certainly. Deer's blood has its own property, and bull's blood has a singular power.

units.la: Qua ratione seper setent lepores: XI.
units.tr: By what reasoning hares are always fertile: XI.

units.la: Pol. Veritatis introductor hic sermo, Aristhe-nes.
units.tr: Pol. This discourse introduces the truth, Antisthenes.

units.la: [illegible, ~1 letter] [illegible, ~3 letters] nes sed Ariftonis vide mihi filium, quàm dextrè adolescens equitet. ac sanè par etiam venatorum secum trahit, vt vides. Equus ei ceruicè alta, aureis quibusdam ornatus in iuba monilib. superbit quodammodo & ferocit incessu, tanquam delicias faciens. At vero puer manu dextra comprehenso freno, pedibus equum stimulat, & ad vrbem cursum dirigit. & gaudet aliquo modo adolescens. non enim sterilem habuit hanc venationem. vide mihi quantus ei lepus captus est. & ab inde nouæ contemplationis ansam sumsi. Virum audiui dicentem, qui fabulosis figmentis gloriari non est solitus, lepores alios quidem fœtuum parere, alios verò peperisse, alios verò semiperfectos gestare in vtero. ANT. Fecundissima quædam est naturaleporum, Polycrates. cui confirmando satis est, id quòd modò dictum est. Lepori improli feminæ coagulum additum, grauidam statim reddit, & facit, vt quæ sterilis ante erat, fœtum habeat subrumum. conceptio tamen in leporibus non terminatur, sed cum primi fœtus adhuc feruntur ad persectionem, superconcipiunt, vt ita dicam. sic[?] alios quidem fœtus peperit lepus, alios parit, alios in vētre circum gestat imperfectos. Ægyptum & Danaum quasi fecundissimi forent, poetæ celebrant, sed iis superior est lepus, vt inquit Abderita. Hoc autem vt credas, impune licet.
units.tr: ...nes. But look, for me, at Ariston's son, how skilfully the young man rides! And indeed he is bringing along a band of hunters, as you see. His horse, with its high neck and its mane adorned with golden necklaces, takes a proud pride and prances, as if putting on a display. But the boy, having grasped the reins in his right hand, spurs the horse with his feet and directs its course toward the city. The young man is rejoicing in some way, for this hunt has not been barren. Look, what a big hare has been caught for me! From this I have taken the occasion for a new reflection. I heard a man, one not accustomed to boast with fabulous fictions, say that some hares bear their young, others have brought them forth, and others carry half-formed young in the womb. Ant. The hare is a very fecund creature, Polycrates, and to confirm this what was just said is enough. When coagulated milk is added to an unmated female hare, it at once makes her pregnant and causes her, who was barren before, to carry a sudden litter. Conception in hares, however, is not brought to an end: while the first young are still being brought to maturity, they superconceive, as I may say. So the hare has borne some young, bears others, and carries others half-formed in the womb. The poets celebrate the Egyptians and the Danaids as most fecund, but the hare surpasses them, as the Abderite says. You may believe this without risk.

units.la: Cur astate corui non bibant.. XII.
units.tr: Why crows do not drink in summer. XII.

units.la: POL. Physicis rationibus, siue magis necessitatibus persuasisti nos, Antisthenes, firmum aliquid de leporibus interpretatus. sed ad gentem coruorum nescio quomodo, transfeat ac desiliat sermo, & in altum videat esse subleuatus, quod nimirum corui, prohibeantur, quasi æstate aquari. ANT. Patiuntur morbum aliquem æstate corui, solutionem nimirum alui, ô Polycrates. unde fit, ut fluvij, & sontes, & paludes nihil possunt æstate coruis, ne quz humore fluxus alui augeatur. Sciunt igitur artem dicetæ corui, cùm neque Hippocratem didicerint, neq; Machaonis, aut Chironis Pharmacis instructi fuerint. vident quidem Arethusam æstate corui, vident etiam Istri[?] fluenta, & sanè Nilum quoq; Ægyptum inundantem, sed simul iis non licet bibere. veram ac si Tantali essent, castigati acerbissimam hanc pœnam luunt.
units.tr: Pol. Antisthenes, you have persuaded us by physical reasons, or rather by necessities, and you have explained something firm about hares. But somehow the discourse passes on, and leaps to the race of crows, and seems to be lifted up to a height, since crows are, of course, forbidden to drink, as if in summer they were watered. Ant. In summer crows suffer from some illness, namely a loosening of the bowels, Polycrates. Hence it happens that rivers, springs and marshes are of no use to crows in summer, lest their flux be increased by moisture. So crows know the art of healing, although they have learned neither Hippocrates nor been equipped with the drugs of Machaon or Chiron. They see indeed the Arethusa in summer, they see also the streams of the Ister, and indeed the Nile flooding Egypt, but at the same time they are not allowed to drink. As if they were the very children of Tantalus, they pay this most bitter penalty, being punished.

units.la: Cur cicada femina non canat. XIII.
units.tr: Why the female cicada does not sing. XIII.

units.la: POL. Benéte, qui tanta scias. euge platanos, quam suauiter mihi fritinniunt in nouellis arbustis vocales cicadæ, & unde mihi incidit de cicadis sermo. superest ut eruam naturæ opera. veluti, cur cicada femina sit muta facta, quasi per modestiam pudeat loquacitatis. non vides compositè hanc istam cicadam insidentem ramo nimis taciturnam, tanquam si Pythagoræ instituta dogmatis? ANT. Frigida natura sunt cicadæ. ea propter circa æstiuam tropam incipiunt canere, & sole recedente suauem minuritionem iam desinunt, temporeq; meridiei sunt vocaliores.
units.tr: Pol. Well said, you who know so much! Hurrah for the plane trees! How sweetly the vocal cicadas chirp for me in the young shrubs, and how the talk of cicadas has fallen upon me. It remains to dig out the works of nature: for instance, why the female cicada has been made mute, as if from modesty she is ashamed of talkativeness. Do you not see how this cicada sitting on the branch is so very taciturn, as though it followed the precepts of Pythagoras' teaching? Ant. Cicadas are of a cold nature. For this reason they begin to sing around the summer solstice, and when the sun recedes they soon cease their sweet diminishing, and at midday they are more vocal.

units.la: Cicada igitur femina humore multum superat masculum, & natura ei silentium indixit, intendens humiditatem. ideo garrula cicada non est femina, sed veluti Theano quæpiam secreta reticens, Homero quasi, qui sermonem viris curæ esse præcipit, obedit ac obtempe-rat.
units.tr: Therefore the female cicada far surpasses the male in moisture, and nature has imposed silence on her, intending to restrain her moisture. Hence the chattering cicada is not female; rather, like some Theano keeping her secrets silent, she obeys and complies with Homer, who, as it were, enjoins that speech is a concern for men.

units.la: Cur oua ibidum, facillimè gignant, serpentes bafilifcos. XIV.
units.tr: Why ibis eggs most easily give birth to basilisk serpents. XIV.

units.la: Pol. Delectatus sum sermone, sed Desultare teiubebit[?] oratio. Primum enim venit mihi contemplatio, ab Ægypto ferens sermonem non inuenustum. Dicunt Ægyptios ibidum ouis insidiari, ne qua eorum fœtus producant aliquod malum. Animal enim horrendum quodpiam originem indetrahere, dicunt Ægyptij. sed non nugæ, autfabulæ[?] quod dicitur? ANT. Non mihi videtur, sapiens[?] enim vt verè, & Ægyptium est inuentum.
units.tr: Pol. I have been delighted by the discussion, but the conversation leaps aside. For first there has come to my mind a reflection, bringing from Egypt a not unpleasant discourse. They say the Egyptians lie in wait for ibis eggs, lest any of their offspring produce some evil. For the Egyptians say that a horrible animal derives its origin from them. But is it not nonsense, or a fable, as they say? Ant. It does not seem so to me, for it is wise, and it has truly been discovered by the Egyptians.

units.la: Quod si verò etiam sermonem audire cupis, habeo tibi, amice, quod dicam. Delectatur hic ales & vestitur maleolentibus rebus. Gaudet autem & inprimis venenatorum venationibus, maximè multiuorus. Sed & serpentibus ibis, vt basiliscus, est contraria, ideoque & pennæ ibidum sunt aduersæ serpentibus. Infercitur verò carnibus serpentium ac scorpionum, & gaudet hac venatione. Igitur ex aliquo quod illa pœperit, vt putredinofæ[?] magnum aliquod malum enascitur basiliscus. Idcirco corrumpunt Ægyptij, vbicunq; vidnrint oua ibidum quasi quæ possent aliquando sibi esse pestiferæ, præmetentes. Si igitur Ægyptios æmulatus fuisset Priamus, aut Oedipum occidisset Laius, nec capta foret Troia, nec incestus accidisset cum matre Thebis.
units.tr: But if you also wish to hear the discourse, friend, I have something to tell you. This bird delights in and is clothed with foul-smelling things. It takes great pleasure especially in hunting venomous creatures, most of all those with many feet. But the ibis is also hostile to serpents, like the basilisk, and for this reason the ibis's feathers are adverse to serpents. It is stuffed with the flesh of serpents and scorpions and delights in this hunting. Therefore from some egg which it has laid, a basilisk is born, a great evil, as if something putrid were brought forth. For this reason the Egyptians destroy, wherever they see ibis eggs, anticipating that they might someday be deadly to them. If Priam had imitated the Egyptians, or if Laius had killed Oedipus, neither would Troy have been taken, nor would the incest with his mother have happened at Thebes.

units.la: Auriginosis[?] quo pacto medeatur charactrius[?] auis. XIV.
units.tr: How the bird charadrius heals those who suffer from ear disease. XIV.

units.la: Pol. Multam habeo Periclitigratiam, Antisthenes maximæ namq; cognitionis nobis author est. Quoniam verò sermo noster Ægptium simulat Protea, ante paulo quidem de coruis subministrata contemplatione, alias adamantis,deinde ad ibidum transiens, nuncad charadriorum naturam fe insinuans: age igitur disputationem transmuta. Auriginosis aiunt mederi statim charadrium, fi in eosrefpexerit. Quare inuidus charadrius claudit oculorum pupillas, quasi salutem, ne restituatur ægro,inuideat. ANT. apageifthancabfurditatem Polycrates, apage. non enim irrationalibus incft quidquam inuidiæ. neque vexatur ab auibus Prometheus, quod hominibus bonum aliquod tradiderit, nempe ignem oculos verò claudit charadrius,quoniam morbum.cùm mutat,ipse ille morbus auem èveftigio inuadit. POL. Optimum est etiam in paruis rebus in humana natura bonum scientia.
units.tr: Pol. I am very grateful to you, Antisthenes, for you are the author of the greatest knowledge for us. But since our discourse imitates the Egyptian Proteus, having just now offered a consideration of crows, then of adamant, then passing to the ibis, and now insinuating itself into the nature of the plover, come, change the subject. They say the plover immediately heals those with ear trouble if it looks upon them. Therefore the envious plover closes the pupils of its eyes, lest it should envy the sick man his restored health. Ant. Away with such absurdity, Polycrates, away! For there is no envy in irrational creatures, nor is Prometheus harassed by birds because he gave men some good, namely fire. The plover closes its eyes because, when the disease changes, that very disease at once attacks the bird itself. Pol. It is indeed best, even in small matters, that knowledge be a good in human nature.

units.la: Quaratione amygdalus anni fertilitatem, ceterorumq; fructuum ficunditatem significet. XVI.
units.tr: How the almond signifies the fertility of the year and the fruitfulness of other crops. XVI.

units.la: POL. Euge pol ad istam amygdalum paulò commoremur, ô amice. quam suauiter sibilat, & lenes aurę circumftantillam. ANT. Specta amygdalum abundantem fructu, quam tantum non prouentus anni ad terram deprimit, & curuatam detinet. idcirco bonę fertilitatis, Polycrates signum est maximum. POL. Vndeigitur, ô optime? ANT. Mixturam aëris temperatam hæc arbor amat, & ad fertilitatem floret, quando pacifero clementiq; tempestate telluris hoc fouetur habitaculum. idco nūciat felicem anni fore prouentum amygdalus, quia neq; tepeftatis aduentum, neq; imbrium, innundationem portendit.
units.tr: POL. Well then, by Pollux, let us linger a little longer over this almond, my friend. How sweetly it whistles, and how gently the breezes play around it! ANT. Look at the almond, laden with fruit, which the year's yield almost presses down to the ground and holds bent over. That is why, Polycrates, it is a very great sign of good fertility. POL. Why so, best of men? ANT. This tree loves a temperate mixture of air, and it flourishes to fertility when the earth's dwelling-place is cherished by peaceful and mild weather. So the almond announces that the year's yield will be happy, because it portends neither the coming of a storm nor a flood of rains.

units.la: Quaratione elixeigneaqua difficilius corrumpantur, facilius ea quæ defiruntur imbribus. XVII.
units.tr: Why boiled and fire-heated waters corrupt less easily, and the waters that run down from showers more easily. XVII.

units.la: Pol. Sed si videtur, ad hanc porticum aliquanto melius accedamus. vt enim vides, substillare incipit, & imbrium aduentum ex eorum motu ventos minari sentio. Est verò & mihi, quo memoriam amicè refricem meteorologiæ. Ant. Quid igitur est quod proferas? Pol. Coctæ igneaquæ non ita cito putrefiunt ex natura sua, vt à quibus terrea materia sit separata. quare oportebat, oportebat inquam, ab imbribus delatas nobis aquas imputribiliores esse quodammodo aliis aquis: percolante sole, & attrahente quod est tenuissimum. prorsus verò contrarium videre licet: Nam corrumpuntur citius aquæ pluuiæ. Ant. Commixta maximè pluuiarum est natura, ô tu. Ex omnibus enim humidis educit Sol. Varia igitur illa & inæqualis mixtio prona est ad motum contrarium, vt vocant, & ad corruptionem magis spectat. Eorum enim quæ diuersa sunt & varia pcliuis[?] maximè est corruptio, ac sane quod magis est, grauissimum eorum quæ Sol sustulit, iterum dcfcrtur[?]: quoniam grauia moventur deorsum, ac tenuissimæ vaporis partes degeneraruntin[?] naturam ventorum.
units.tr: POL. But if you agree, let us approach this portico a little more closely. As you see, it is beginning to drizzle, and from the motion of the clouds I perceive that the winds threaten the arrival of showers. I also have something by which I can pleasantly refresh my memory of meteorology. ANT. What then is it that you wish to put forward? POL. Boiled and fire-heated waters do not putrefy so quickly by their own nature, since the earthy matter has been separated from them. Therefore it was necessary, I say it was necessary, that the waters brought down to us by rain should be somehow more resistant to putrefaction than other waters, since the sun draws up what is most fine. Quite the opposite can be seen, however: rainwater corrupts more quickly. ANT. The nature of rain is most mixed, my friend. For the sun draws up from all moist things. That varied and unequal mixture is therefore prone to a contrary motion, as they call it, and tends more towards corruption. For corruption is greatest in things that are diverse and various. And indeed, what is heaviest of the things the sun has lifted is carried down again, since heavy things move downward, while the finest parts of the vapour have degenerated into the nature of winds.

units.la: Cur Seriphiarana sint muta. XVIII.
units.tr: Why the frogs of Seriphus are mute. XVIII.

units.la: Pol. Optimè equidem. Sed me ab ignorantiæ solueris accusatione, si de natura sermones ad finem mihi vsque prosequutus fueris, Antisthenes. Seriphias ranas Lysimachus Phalaridis filius mutas ait vidisse. Ant. Quod mutæ sint eæ, in causa est aquarum natura Polycrates, ob nimiam humiditatem.unde si quis transferat hoc animal, loquax statim fecerit, & ad propriam naturam reduxerit, quasi liberatum Circæ vinculis. Cyrenæam autem ranam, quod non sit loquax; amaror aquarum efficit.
units.tr: POL. Very well indeed. But you will free me from the charge of ignorance if you follow out the discussion of nature to its end for me, Antisthenes. Lysimachus, son of Phalaris, says that he saw Seriphian frogs that were mute. ANT. That they are mute, Polycrates, is due to the nature of the waters, on account of their excessive moisture. So if someone should transfer this animal, it will at once become talkative and will have been restored to its own nature, as if freed from the chains of Circe. But the Cyrenaic frog is not talkative, because the bitterness of the waters makes it so.

units.la: Quare melli Atticonon insideat musca. XIX.
units.tr: Why a fly does not settle on Attic honey. XIX.

units.la: Pot. Nimis, ô amice, scitè. At huiusmodi quid iam patimur: in Attica confertim videor stare, quodammodo Theagenisq; refricare cōuiuium. (Excepit n. conuiuio Theagenes Salaminius, & me, & Cliniæ filium Dositheum, qui cū nobis obsonia & placentam præbuisset, ego, ut patet, valedicto conuiuio ad sermonum collationem cupidè studioseq; sum volutus.) ac ipsum ad me, Theagenem audire dicentem, Non vides Polycrates, quod non possit musca apis Atticæ corrumpere labores? & miratus sum dictum: quia nimis erat ultra captum nostrum. Ant. Thymis Polycrates Atticam abundantem est videre, quibus insident Atticæ crebrius apes. inde tum etiam grauioris est odoris. quapropter veluti visco alicui, melli Attico non insidet musca. non minus tamen circumstrepentes apis Atticæ labores carpere gestiunt. Ubi est Darius ille contra Græciam armatus? Xerxis ferociam musca doceat, quasi non fas sit Atticam potiri, aut ascendere. Pot. Magnificè me nimis procurasti Antisthenes, ad finem contemplationis quasi tragemate aliquo præbito, mellificium Atticum enarrans. sed ne à te ipso horum omnium habes scientiam? Ant. Non certè Polycrates, quippe iam antiquis multa & celebria elaborata sunt, quibus animo insidentes, sicut apes collegimus in unum opus, quod plurima comprehenderet,id ut absolutissimum quoad fieri poset redderetur oratione profequuti. Non enim Democriti mihi labores tribuo, neque Aristotelis gloriam mihi vindico, neque quid Platonicorum surripio,neq; Iamblichum sine corona reliquerim, non Proclum,non Galenum elegantissima scientia viros. non Plotinum,non Sotionem, non Alexandum , non Theophrastrum cognitionis mare, non Bolum, non Ælianum , non scientiæ plutum thesaurum (videlicet)Plutarchum,non Ambronem, non Imbrasium, non Damascium, aut silium Timagenis Hieroclem. & quid tandem tibi catalogum recenseam reliquorum, à quibus argumentis aliquot & principiis acceptis, synopsin quasi quandam tibi scrutandi cupido, pro viribus nostris dedimus. necalieno Polycrates ornari mundo sas est, quemadmodum ille fabulis dilatus graculus. nihil enim est quod ab antiquis non sit animadversum. ea vero ut omnia in promptu reperias, non prorsus est facilè. Por.[?] Ego è scientia tua fructum percepi, Antisthenes. & abeo gaudens. Hermæum enim optimum, difficilium scilicet sermonum scientiam reportaui.
units.tr: POL. Very well said, my friend, and cleverly too. But what are we suffering now? I seem to be standing in Attica and, in a way, reviving the banquet of Theagenes. (For Theagenes of Salamis received me at his banquet, and Dositheus, son of Clinias, who, after providing us with dainties and a cake, I, as is plain, having bid farewell to the feast, was eagerly and zealously drawn into the exchange of talk.) And he said to me, as I heard Theagenes saying: "Do you not see, Polycrates, that a fly cannot spoil the labours of the Attic bee?" And I marvelled at the saying, because it was too far beyond our grasp. ANT. You may see, Polycrates, how abundantly thyme grows in Attica, on which the bees settle more often in Attica, and hence it is of a stronger scent. So, as with some birdlime, a fly does not settle on Attic honey. Nevertheless the buzzing bees are eager to pluck at the labours of the Attic bee. Where is that Darius who armed himself against Greece? Let a fly teach the arrogance of Xerxes, as if it were not lawful for Attica to be seized or assailed. POL. You have served me very splendidly, Antisthenes, at the end of our contemplation, setting before me a kind of tragedy as you narrate the making of Attic honey. But do you not have knowledge of all these things from yourself? ANT. Certainly not, Polycrates. For many celebrated matters have already been elaborated by the ancients, and, dwelling on them in mind, like bees we have gathered them into one work, which would embrace very many things, and we have set it forth in speech so that it might be rendered as complete as possible. For I do not claim for myself the labours of Democritus, nor do I arrogate to myself the glory of Aristotle, nor do I filch anything from the Platonists. Nor would I leave Iamblichus without his crown, nor Proclus, nor Galen, men of most elegant learning; nor Plotinus, nor Sotion, nor Alexander, nor Theophrastus, the sea of knowledge; nor Bolus, nor Aelian, nor Plutarch, that rich treasury of learning (to be sure); nor Ammonius, nor Imbrasius, nor Damascius, nor Hierocles, son of Timagenes. And why should I recite for you the catalogue of the rest, from whose arguments and principles, having received some, we have offered you, as far as our powers allow, a kind of synopsis for your eager inquiry? Nor is it fitting, Polycrates, for the world to be adorned with another's goods, like that jackdaw puffed up with borrowed feathers in the fable. For there is nothing that has not been noticed by the ancients. But to find all of these things ready to hand is not at all easy. POL. I have gathered fruit from your learning, Antisthenes, and I go away rejoicing. For I have carried off a fine herm, that is, a knowledge of difficult discourses.

units.la: THEOPHILACTI EX. PRÆFECTI, COGNOMEN- TO SIMOCATI, Historiarum, breuis comprehensio, ex PHOTIO.
units.tr: Theophylact, Former Prefect, Surnamed Simocatta, A Brief Summary of His Histories, from Photius

units.la: E&i sunt Theophylacti Exprafecti & scripturarij historiarum libri octo. Estaüt Theophyla&us hic, Ægypto oriundꝰ. oratio qua utit,vcneris[?] equidem aliquid habét, nisi quod dictionum tropicarum, & allegoricæ interpretationis nimius vsus in frigiditatem quandam, & iuuenilem desinat inceptiam. Sed &illud, quod sententias & scita dictainterferat [?] non in tempore studij est anxij & superflui. sunt & alia prætereà quæ reprehendi possent. incipit autem ab imperio Mauricij, peruenitq; ad proclamationem vsq; Phocæ.
units.tr: There are eight books of histories by Theophylact the Ex-Prefect and historian. This Theophylact was a native of Egypt. His style has a certain charm, except that his excessive use of tropes and allegorical interpretation ends in a kind of coldness and youthful immaturity. Moreover, his inserting maxims and sayings is out of keeping with a time for serious and unhurried study. There are also other things that could be criticised. He begins with the reign of Maurice and comes down to the proclamation of Phocas.

units.la: IN PRIMO igitur libro narrat quomodo Mauricius à Tiberio rex renunciatus sit, Ioanne tum temporis Constantinopolitanorum ecclesiæ præsule, de quibusq; admonuerit Mauritium Ioannis Quæstoris in ea re vsus opera, qui & ad ipsum Mauricium & populum concionem habuit, fungens loco regis. & quomodo illi filiam desponsarit, & quomodo altero post renunciatum Mauritium die, vitam finierit. & quod priusquam moreretur visionem viderit, dicentem sibi: Hæc tibi Tiberi trifagion dicit, Tyrannica impietatis tempora sub regno tuo non orientur. quæ non nihil prædicebant tragœdiam nefariæ tyrannidis, occupatæ à cruento sceleratoque Phoca. adhæc etiam quòd cum Abaris fyrmium oppugnantibus, iam Paulo ante Mauricius inducias fecerat, eo pacto vt barbarij quotannis, per pecuniam simul & vestes, conferret auri Chiliadas Lxx. quæ cum duos circiter annos duxassent, à barbarorum inexplebili auaritia sunt diffolutæ. Viginti enim auri Chiliadum accessionem amplius adhuc postulauit barbarus, vnde solutio facta inducarium [?], & capta est à barbaris vrbs Singedon, & Augusta, & Viminaceum, obsessa verò etiam est Anchialus, & ipsa vrbs. Missiq; Elpidius & Comentiolus Romanorum legati ad barbarorum regem Chaganum, magis quàm oporteret maiestatem cius dehonestarunt, quippe cum nimisliberè ad barbarum loqueretur comentiolus. Relapso veró anno rursumElpidius ad Chaganum mittitur,ut referrct latius de viginti chiliadibus tribuendis, & accepto secum quodam ex Abaris Targetio Byzantium rediit. postquam autem Abari Romanorum plurima vastauissent, Targetius in Chalcidem Infulam extruditur exsulatum , ad menses sex. Dux verò electus Comentiolus,contra Sclauos rem fortiter gessit. Porro quomodo rursus inducias instaurauerit chagamus, deq; Bofcolobra mago, & expugnatione plurimarum urbium Romanarum per barbaros. Deinde narrat bellum Persarum & Romanorum ad Nymphium fluvium,nuptiasq; Mauricij cum Costantina Tiberij filia. Perstringit etiam incendium quod in foro factum est circa initia principatus Mauricij:Item de nece Paulini praestigiatoris,ac de miraculo quod accidit circa concham siue peluim Glyceriæ martyris.& quomodo Ioannes patriarcha, cum sententia regis lenior videretur, ipse ignibus tradendum incantatorem affirmauerit, allegatis ad id ideo verbis Apostoli, & quod Paulinus , atq; filius ciusdem impietatis conscius gladio decollati interierint. praterea de Aphnumone & Acma custodibus prasidiariis. Continetur autem hoc sermone pugna Romanorum ac Persarum, & quomodo Ioannes oppugnatus sit à barbaris. magnus adhæc ille terræmotus, qui accidit statim à principio cum salutatus esset Imperator Mauritius, de eiusdemque consulatu. quomodo item Philippicus, qui regis filiam habebat Gordiam, Orientalis exercitus fit electus imperator, eiusq; in imperio isto res bene fortiterque gestæ, & Romanorum ex Media discessus. quomodo etiam Romanus exercitus aquæ penuria laborarit, & quomodo Arzaninem regionem Romanorum dux diripiendam dederit, & fortitudo Romani militis. Et quomodo metropoli vicina quæq; Persarum exercitus dcuaftauerit. legatioq; Persarum ad Romanos, prima & fecunda. Atq; hæc quidem libro primo.
units.tr: In the first book, then, he tells how Maurice was proclaimed emperor by Tiberius, with John, at that time bishop of the Church of Constantinople, having advised Maurice in the matter. He also tells how John the Quaestor, who acted in the place of the emperor, made use of his services in this business and gave a sermon both to Maurice himself and to the people. He tells how Tiberius betrothed his daughter to Maurice, and how Tiberius died on the day after Maurice was proclaimed. Before he died he saw a vision which said to him: "The thrice-holy one says this to you, Tiberius: the tyrannical times of impiety will not arise under your reign." These words foretold to some extent the tragedy of wicked tyranny, which was seized by the bloody and criminal Phocas. He also tells how Maurice had recently made a truce with the Avars, who were attacking Sirmium, on terms that the barbarians should receive every year, in money and clothing together, seventy thousand pounds of gold. When this arrangement had lasted about two years, it was broken off by the barbarians' insatiable greed. For the barbarian then demanded a further twenty thousand pounds of gold, and since payment was not made, the barbarians captured the cities of Singidunum, Augusta and Viminacium, and besieged Anchialus itself. The Roman envoys Elpidius and Comentiolus were sent to the barbarian king Chagan, but they dishonoured his majesty more than was proper, since Comentiolus spoke too freely to the barbarian. In the following year Elpidius was sent again to Chagan, to discuss at greater length the payment of the twenty thousand pounds; and taking back with him a certain Targetius from among the Avars, he returned to Byzantium. After the Avars had laid waste very many Roman lands, Targetius was banished to the island of Chalcis for six months. Comentiolus, chosen as general, waged war vigorously against the Slavs. Next he tells how Chagan restored the truce, and about the magician Boscolobras, and about the capture of very many Roman cities by the barbarians. Then he narrates the war between the Persians and the Romans at the river Nymphius, and the marriage of Maurice to Constantina, daughter of Tiberius. He also touches on the fire that broke out in the forum near the beginning of Maurice's reign; on the death of Paulinus, the sorcerer; and on the miracle that happened near the basin or bowl of the martyr Glycerius. He tells how Patriarch John, when the emperor's sentence seemed too lenient, declared that the sorcerer should be handed over to the flames, citing for this purpose the words of the Apostle, and how Paulinus and his son, who were privy to the same impiety, perished by the sword after being beheaded. He also tells of Aphnumon and Acma, the garrison commanders. This account also contains the battle between the Romans and the Persians, and how John was attacked by the barbarians. It also contains the great earthquake that occurred immediately at the beginning, when Maurice was greeted as emperor, and about his consulship. Likewise it tells how Philippicus, who had as his wife the king's daughter Gordia, was chosen emperor of the eastern army; the successful and brave deeds done in that command; and the withdrawal of the Romans from Media. It tells also how the Roman army suffered from lack of water, how the Roman general gave the region of Arzanene to be plundered, and the courage of the Roman soldier. And how the Persian armies ravaged everything near the capital. Also the first and second embassies of the Persians to the Romans. So much for the first book.

units.la: I I.
units.tr: II.

units.la: SECVNDO vero complectitur de monte Ixala, de Insultatione contra Cardarigam Persarum ducem, & quomodo Philippici Romanorum qui pugna cum Cardariga & Persis iuxta Azarnum facta fit, & quomodo Philippus non manufactam imaginem ferens circumeundo lustrauerit exercitum, & vti tunc Romani lautissima victoria affulserit, quomodo; non manufacta imago ad Symeonem episcopum Amidenfem cum veneratione missa, spoliaque barbarorum Romani legerint, fugiente Cardariga ad vrbem Daras. hinc quomodo ipsum ab vrbe Dareni relegarint, vt omnibus viribus quantum pote debilitarctur. quomodo item Romanus miles in corpore vulnerarit. erat autem vnus ex ordine Quartopartanorum, ita dictorum, qui Berrhææ commorabantur, vrbe Syriæ dicq; expeditione Romanorum, dicq; Arzanine, & quomodo Marutha ac Iobius eius duces transfugerint ad Philippicum & Romanos. dicq; plebeiis copiis collectis à Cardariga ad circum veniendos Romanos. quomodo quoq; Heraclius Heraclij Imperatoris pater à Philippico ad hostium speculationem emissus, mirificè sit seruatus, deq; Zaberta Persa, & quomodo à Chlomarorum oppugnatione destiterint Romani. adhæc etiam de magna turpiq; fuga Philippici, turbatoq; ordinc[?] in cducendo[?] exercitu Romano. ac de morbo qui Philippicum inuaserat. & quòd Heraclius Heraclij Imperatoris pater curam ducatus in se susceperit quomodoque in Meridionalem Mediam irruptionem fecerit Romanæ militiæ subimperator. & ut verno tempore in Persarum ordines irruerint Romani. Comprehenditur quoq; libro hoc uti Comentiolus in Abaros expeditione duxerit, subimperatores habens Marinum & Captum. & quam strenuè se habuerint illi contra Abaros, postea vero vivo uterq; captus, quodq; Anfimuth duce peditum Romanorum ab Abaris capto eius postea exercitus per Thraciam excursiones secerit. & Comentioli consultatio an oporteret adriri Abaros, & habita concio super invadendis Abaris, & concioni isti concio opposita. quomodo rumor illapsus in exercitum barbarorum, irritum Comentioli fecerit contra Chaganum consilium. item de Busa milite, & quomodo dum venarctur deprehensus sit ab Abaris, & quomodo à 9. manipularibus suis per contemptum neglectus, primus ideò Abaros obsidionalia instrumenta fabricare docuerit. & quomodo abs Chagano obsessa Beroe, conatus non successerit. sic quomodo Diocletiani urbem idem ipse obsidens, & in hoc casu frustra fuerit. & quomodo Mauricius Imperator à communi Byzantiorum vulgo ludibrio habitus, propter cas quas à barbaris Europa clades acceperat, emiserit imperatorem exercitus Joannem, quem cognominabant Musto canonem, cum sub imperatore Droctone, qui etiam in obsidione Adria nopoleos ab Abaris facta commissus inter milites, urbem servavit. Continet etiam hic liber, quomodo Heraclius castellum Persicum vi capere fit aggressus, deque praesidio Beiudaës dicto, & quomodo mirabili fortitudine sapëris militis, praesidium ceperint Romani & hinc tandem aduentum Philippicii in urbem regiam.
units.tr: The second book contains the mountain of Ixala, the taunting of Cardarigas, the Persian general, and how the battle of Philippicus against Cardarigas and the Persians was fought near Azarnum; how Philippicus, carrying an image not made by hands, went around and purified the army; and how the Romans were then illumined by a most splendid victory. It tells how the image not made by hands was sent with reverence to Symeon, bishop of Amida, and how the Romans gathered the spoils of the barbarians while Cardarigas fled to the city of Daras. Next, how they banished him from the city of Daras, so that he might be weakened as much as possible by every means. It also tells how a Roman soldier wounded him in the body. He was one of the so-called Quartopartani, who were quartered at Beroea, a city of Syria. It tells of the expedition of the Romans, of Arzanene, and how Marutha and Iobius, their commanders, deserted to Philippicus and the Romans. It tells how Cardarigas gathered a mixed host of common people to surround the Romans. It also tells how Heraclius, the father of the emperor Heraclius, was sent by Philippicus to spy on the enemy and was marvellously preserved; and about the Persian Zabergan, and how the Romans desisted from the siege of the Chlomari. In addition, it tells of the great and shameful flight of Philippicus, and of the disorder in leading the Roman army out, and of the sickness that had attacked Philippicus. And how Heraclius, the father of the emperor Heraclius, took upon himself the command of the army, and how, as deputy commander of the Roman forces, he made an incursion into southern Media; and how in spring the Romans charged into the Persian ranks. This book also includes how Comentiolus led the expedition against the Avars, having as his deputies Marinus and Captus; how bravely they conducted themselves against the Avars; and how afterwards both were taken alive; and how Anastasius, the commander of the Roman infantry, after Captus was captured by the Avars, made raids through Thrace with his army. It tells of Comentiolus's deliberation whether the Avars ought to be attacked, of the assembly held concerning the attack on the Avars, and of the speech set against that assembly. How a rumour that spread through the barbarian army made Comentiolus's plan against Chagan come to nothing. Also about the soldier Busas, and how, while hunting, he was caught by the Avars, and how, being despised and neglected by his nine fellow soldiers, he was the first to teach the Avars to build siege engines. And how Beroe was besieged by Chagan without success; likewise how Chagan himself, besieging the city of Diocletianopolis, failed in this venture. And how the emperor Maurice, held in public contempt by the common people of Byzantium because of the defeats that the barbarians had inflicted on Europe, sent out as commander of the army John, whom they called Mustacon, together with the emperor Droctulft, who also, in the siege of Adrianople made by the Avars, preserved the city while serving among the soldiers. This book also contains how Heraclius undertook to take the Persian fortress by force, and about the garrison called Beudes, and how by the remarkable courage of a Roman soldier the Romans captured the garrison; and finally the arrival of Philippicus in the royal city.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Tertius autem liber disserit, quomodo electus fit Philippici loco dux orientalis militiae Priscus, & quomodo Philippicus inuidiosus Prisco, ad Heraclium scripserit, cibaria exercitui diminuta es-se, quodque Priscus cum exercitum adcedat, non ex equo descédat è more veteri, atq; ita salutet militem. quapropter cum miles, & quod cibaria sibi praecisa essent, & quod honore debito non fuisset compellatus, seditionem faceret, & Priscus accepta non manufacta imagine, per hanc exorare plebem constitueret illam quoq; lapidibus petierunt. Itaq; fuga recepit se Constantinam Priscus, & electus est ab exercitu futurus ei dux Germanus, licet inuitus. atq; hac obtinente discordia, non paucae Romanis calamitates à Persis sunt illatae. quapropter & Imperator res Priscum quidem sedat, eius vero loco remittit iterum Philippicum ducem. At miles etiam isti rebellat. & obsidetur sanè constantia à Persis, liberatur autè à periculis, auxilio Germani. praelioq; Persas inter & Romanos iuxta Martyropolin commisso, splendida Romani sunt potiti victoria, tribus Persarum millibus cum duce suo Maruzacæsis, mille captis reconciliatoq; cum Imperatore per Aristobulum exercitu, experta est ad præsidium chiligerdarum, captiuorum Romanorum fortitudo. & Gregorius Antiochiæ archiepiscopus Philippicum perslegatos ab expeditione reuocat. Capitur autem à Persis Martyropolis, fraudibus maximè Sistæ. & ab officio remouet Philippicus, suffecto Comentiolo, cui Imperator bellū Persicum eius loco crediderat. Getæ verò siue Sclaui Thraciæ vicinas regiones populabantur, Roma armabatur contra Longobardos, & Africa per Mauros infestabatur.
