Auspiciis tamen Comentioli committuntur circa sisarbanum propè inter se Persæ cum Romanis inter quos omnibus viribus vincebant Romani, Heraclio egregiè depugnante hasta. Cecidit enim & ipse Persarum dux Phrates, & spolia lecta sunt excitus. Præterea quoq; complectitur, quomodo Baram deuictus Turcis, & multis inde opibus diuitiisq; ad Hormisdam regem missis, gladium quoq; sustulerit aducersus Suaniam. Romani verò ducente Romano, cum Baram, eiusq; exercitu collatis signis opimam referunt victoriam. vnde per contemtum Hormisda & opprobrium Baramo vestè misit muliebrem. hic autem eodem contumeliæ genere vsus, literis ad eum datis, Filiæ chofroisinscripsit, nō autem filio Hormisdæ. quo etiam bello Armenij Sabbatij malignitate, ducem quidem suum Iohannem necant, & ad Persas defectionem moliuntur: Comentiolus autem à rege missus & seditionem componit,& Sabbatium ducit Byzantium:vbi tum ille ad bestias condemnatus est, nisi ab hoc mortis genere per humanitatem regiam fuisset liberatus. Hormisdas autem Saramen aduersus Baram mittit, qui Baram cum bello superior cuasisset, Saramen elephantis obiccit deuorandum,& manifesta contra Hormisdam sumsit arma. Eò verò honorum Baram venerat, priusquam deficeret, vt post regem nemo foret eo honoratior. curator enim erat palatij, quem vocant Romani, quo honore excidit. Habetur porrò hoc libro etiam repetitio eorum,quæ euenerunt temporibus hisce antiquioribus, & succincta narratio eorum, quæ facta sunt sub Imperio Iustini ac Tiberij Imperatorum. quædam item de crudelitate Hormisdæ Persarum regis, & Persicorum regum stirpis commemoratio. Et hæc ea sunt quæ liber Tertius.
units.tr: The third book sets out how Priscus was chosen in place of Philippicus as commander of the eastern army; and how Philippicus, jealous of Priscus, wrote to Heraclius that the army's rations had been reduced, and that Priscus, when he approached the army, did not dismount from his horse in the old manner and so greet the soldiers. Therefore the soldiers, because their rations had been cut off and because they had not been addressed with the honour due to them, made a mutiny; and when Priscus took up an image not made by hands and tried through it to pacify the common people, they attacked him also with stones. So Priscus withdrew in flight to Constantina, and the army chose Germanus as its commander, though he was unwilling. While this discord continued, no small disasters were inflicted on the Romans by the Persians. Therefore the emperor indeed settled the matter with Priscus, and in his place sent Philippicus back again as commander. But the soldiers rebelled against him too. Constantia was indeed besieged by the Persians, but it was freed from danger by the help of Germanus. In the battle between the Persians and the Romans fought near Martyropolis, the Romans gained a splendid victory: three thousand Persians were killed along with their commander Maruzaces, a thousand were captured; and the army was reconciled with the emperor through Aristobulus. The courage of the Roman captives was tested at the fortress of the Chiligerdi. Gregory, archbishop of Antioch, called Philippicus back from the expedition after he had been reproached. Martyropolis was captured by the Persians, chiefly through the treachery of Sista. Philippicus was removed from office, and Comentiolus was appointed in his place, to whom the emperor had entrusted the Persian war in his stead. Meanwhile the Getae, or Slavs, laid waste the regions of Thrace nearby; Rome was armed against the Lombards; and Africa was harassed by the Moors. Nevertheless, under the leadership of Comentiolus, the Persians and Romans engaged near Sisarbanum, where the Romans, with Heraclius fighting nobly with his spear, prevailed in every way. For the Persian commander Phrates himself was killed, and the spoils were gathered from the army. The book also includes how Bahram, defeated by the Turks, sent much wealth to king Hormisdas, and then took up the sword against Suania. The Romans, led by Romanus, engaged Bahram and his army with standards raised, and won a rich victory. Hence, out of contempt and reproach for Bahram, Hormisdas sent him women's clothing. Bahram, using the same kind of insult, wrote him a letter addressed to "the daughter of Chosroes," not to the son of Hormisdas. In this same war the Armenians, through the malice of Sabbatius, killed their commander John and attempted to desert to the Persians; but Comentiolus, sent by the king, quelled the sedition and led Sabbatius to Byzantium, where he was condemned to the beasts, unless he had been freed from this kind of death by the imperial clemency. Hormisdas, moreover, sent Sarames against Bahram; Bahram, having overcome him in battle, threw Sarames to the elephants to be devoured, and openly took up arms against Hormisdas. Bahram had risen to such honour before he rebelled that no one was more honoured after the king than he. For he was curator of the palace, as the Romans call it, and it was from this office that he fell. This book also contains a recollection of the events of earlier times, and a brief narrative of what was done under the empire of the emperors Justin and Tiberius; also some matters concerning the cruelty of Hormisdas, king of the Persians, and a mention of the line of Persian kings. And these are the contents of the third book.

units.la: I V.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: QVARTVS vero continet, & quomodo inter Persas ciuile bellum coaluerit,& quæcunq; acciderint sub Baramo victoriaq; & fortunæ. Pherechamis cædem. Zadestræ successum, & quomodo regno à Bindoe exutus Hormisdas è vinculis concionandi petierit veniam, quomodoq; fit concionatus, & quomodo Bindoes itē concionatus fit, iugulatusq; filius in conspectu Hormisdæ, occisaq; regina, & excæcatus ipse Hormisdas. & quomodo postea à filio quem Persæ regem constituerant, sustibus occisus. potentiam tyrannidis Barami, sugamáque chosroæ Persarum regis. quomodo item Persarum rex ad Circensium venerit ad Mauricium Imperatorem, quomodoq; ad eum miserit. de Baramo rursum, quomodo, cùm id quod moliretur, ut rex nimirum proclamaretur, non obtingeret, scipsum renuntiauerit regem. quomodo Imperator chosroen ad Hierapolim deduxerit, cum familia fatcllitioq; regio, quod ei dederat. deq; iis quæ acta sunt inter Baramum & chosroen consederatis cum cō iam Romanis. & uti cum legationem ad Imperatorem Mauricium misset Baram, repulsam tulerit, rursusq; legatione missa, chosroes quod petierat, impetrauerit. quomodo Imperator Melitenæ episcopum una cum Gregorio Antiochiæ archicpiscopo ad chosroen miserit. de Baramo Zamendæ fraudibus & Zoanambæ interfecto, ac de necce eorum qui rei huius erant conscij. de Bindoe Persa, & quomodo cum unus esset coniuratorum in mortem Parami, è Perside fugerit, quomodo Martyropolis à chosroe reddita sit Romanis, & Sittias igne exustus, solemnemq; concionem habuerit episcopus Meletinensis, nomine Domitianus, pro receptione urbis.
units.tr: The fourth book also contains how civil war broke out among the Persians and what happened under Bahram, his victory and his fortune; the slaying of Pherechamis; the success of Zadestra; and how Hormisdas, stripped of the kingdom by Bindoes and released from his chains, asked leave to address the people, and how he did so, and how Bindoes also addressed them. It tells how Hormisdas's son was butchered before his eyes, the queen was killed, and Hormisdas himself was blinded, and how he was afterwards beaten to death with clubs by the son whom the Persians had set up as king. It describes the tyrannical power of Bahram and the flight of Chosroes, king of the Persians. It also tells how the king of the Persians came to the Circus to the Emperor Maurice and what he sent to him. Concerning Bahram again: when he did not achieve what he was striving for, namely to be proclaimed king, he renounced the kingship himself. How the Emperor led Chosroes to Hierapolis with his household and the royal retinue he had given him. And what was done between Bahram and Chosroes, and the alliance then made with the Romans. How Bahram, having sent an embassy to the Emperor Maurice, was rebuffed; and when an embassy was sent again, Chosroes obtained what he had asked for. How the Emperor sent the bishop of Melitene, together with Gregory, archbishop of Antioch, to Chosroes. Concerning Bahram's treachery at Zamenda and the killing of Zoanambas, and the death of those who were privy to this business. Concerning the Persian Bindoes, and how, being one of the conspirators in the death of Parames, he fled from Persia. How Martyropolis was restored to the Romans by Chosroes, and Sittias was burned by fire. And how the bishop of Meletene, named Domitianus, delivered a solemn sermon for the recovery of the city.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: QUINTUS vero commemorat, quomodo chosroes Persarum rex, cum angustia premeretur legatos miserit ad martyrem Sergium, ad quem eundem & reliquæ gentes mittunt barbaræ, ut infortuniorum liberationem consequantur. & quomodo cruce aurea margaritis interstincta cum honorauerit. inde Tezadiphras dolosè occiditur à Rhosa, Blescharnis consilio, & alia non ingrata chosroi obuceniunt. De dato auro chosroi Persarum regi à Mauricio Imp. & quod subscripserit chosroes, accepisse. Legatio; chosrois, unde Comœtiolus[?] à ducatu remouetur,&eligitur Narses loco comentioli,confederatumq;Romanorum bellum aduersus tyrannum Baram. deq; regiis muneribus missis chosroi ab Imperatore, & quomodo claues opidi, quod vocatur Daras,chosroes per legatum Dolbā tradiderit Imperatori. Concio Domitiani Meletinensis, adhortans Romanos, vt coniunctis viribus cum chosroe Baramo se opponerent,deq; fortuna chosrois ante coniunctionem Romanorum &Persarum.& quomodo regij thesauri, Perficaq; regalia restituta chosroi per Bindoem. coniunctio copiarum Romanarum, Armeniaq; & Orientis. pugnaque commissa cum Baramo, & victoria Romanorum illustrissima. in qua pugna ductore Narse, cacapti sunt etiā Turcæ, illi qui in fronte gestitabantformam crucis,ea de causa vt reminiscerentur liberationem à pestilenti illo morbo, qui cos olim inuaserat. De iis quæ Galinduch in Perside martirieuenerunt,&quam variis illa casibus subiectam vitam egerit.reditusq; chosrois in pristina regalia.acde muneribus missis à chosroe sergio martyri,eiusdemdemq; ad eundem sanctum legatio,& quomodo abHirem quæ erat Christiana, institutus sit, atque eaquæ postulabat consequuutus, dona dapsilia multamiserit ad fanum martyris. & quo modo chosroes, qui tyrannidis erant complices, ipsumq; adeo Bindoen,quasi qui regi rebellarit,interemerit.De edictis chosrois, & quam seditiosæ fuerint Romanorum res sub tyrannis. Legatioq; Probi chalcedonensis praesulis, acde Dei genetrice ad Euripæ vrbem Anchialum,deq;spectro à chosroe per infomnium viso. & quomodo in regiam suam reuerterit Imperator, legatione Persica cui Zalambas præerat, appulsa.
units.tr: The fifth book relates how Chosroes, king of the Persians, when hard pressed, sent envoys to the martyr Sergius, to whom other barbarous nations also send in order to obtain deliverance from their misfortunes; and how he honoured him with a golden cross set with pearls. Then Tezadiphras is treacherously killed by Rhosas on the counsel of Blescharnes, and other not unwelcome things befall Chosroes. Concerning the gold given by the Emperor Maurice to Chosroes, king of the Persians, and that Chosroes received what he had agreed to. The embassy of Chosroes; whence Comentiolus is removed from his command and Narses is chosen in place of Comentiolus, and the alliance of the Romans for war against the tyrant Bahram. Concerning the royal gifts sent by the Emperor to Chosroes, and how Chosroes, through his envoy Dolbas, handed over to the Emperor the keys of the town called Daras. The speech of Domitianus of Meletene, exhorting the Romans to oppose Bahram together with Chosroes with united forces; and concerning Chosroes' fortunes before the joining of the Romans and Persians. And how the royal treasures and the Persian regalia were restored to Chosroes through Bindoes. The joining of the Roman forces, of Armenia and of the East; and the battle joined with Bahram, and the most splendid Roman victory. In that battle, under the leadership of Narses, the Turks too were captured, those who bore the form of a cross on their foreheads, for this reason: that they might remember their deliverance from that pestilential disease which had once attacked them. Concerning what befell Galinduch in Persia, and through what varied chances he passed his life; the return of Chosroes to his former royal state; the gifts Chosroes sent to the martyr Sergius, and his embassy to the same saint; and how, from Hira, which was Christian, a man was appointed and obtained what he asked, and sent lavish gifts in abundance to the martyr's shrine. And how Chosroes killed those who had been accomplices in the tyranny, and Bindoes himself, as one who had rebelled against the king. Concerning the edicts of Chosroes, and how seditious the affairs of the Romans were under tyrants. The embassy of Probus, bishop of Chalcedon, and concerning the Mother of God at Anchialus, a city on the Euripus; and concerning the phantom seen by Chosroes in a dream. And how the Emperor returned to his palace when a Persian embassy, headed by Zalambas, arrived.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: SExTo libro contenta sunt hæc. quomodo cum ab vrbe discederet, Imperator, à maris tempestate fit comprehensus, quomodoque circa Heraclëam, cum ibi commoraretur Imperator, monftrofus puer natus fit, neq; manus habens, neq; oculos, neque qualis piscium est, supercilia, neque palpebras in caudam à coxis definens & quomodo monstrum fit sublatum. de tribus Sclauis, qui citharas circumgestabant, dicebanturque ex Oceani partibus ad Chaganum esse missi, qui & comparuerunt coram Mauricio Imperatore. Legatioque Francorum ad Imperatorem, stipendiaria, promittentium auxilia, & petitionis refutatio. Boffus & Bettus erant legati, miserat autem Theoderichus. De grege cerutorum, & quomodo maximus inter eos vulneratus,in Syluam fe quandam proripuerit. & quomodo docum doryphorus eum quidam prosequeretur, & alius cum illo Gepida, doryphorus, propter aurea quæ habebat forte, à Gepida fit occisus, qui longo post tempore cum deprehensus effet occidisse, ignibus fit traditus. Exercitus Abarorum contra Romanos, & obsessio Singidonis vrbis, electioque prisci ducis exercitus. & quibus calamitatibus hoc bello Europæo suos milites exposuerit, & ut Chaganus è Drexiperis fanum Alexandri martyris obsederit, & quomodo intra vrbem Trurulum confclusi Romani à Chagano obuallati sint, quomodo doq; verba barbaro dederit Mauricius, & obsidionem soluerit, Legatioque Abarorum ad Romanos, & quæcunque Ardagastus à Romanorum copiis passus fit. Porrò etiam quæ propè Tatimerum facta, fortitudoque Romanorum ducis Alexandri, & internecio Sclauorum quos adorti erant Romani. de natis monstris in vrbe regia, altero quadrupede, altero bicipite. quomodo Priscus remotus fit à bello Europæo, deque Theodoro Legato misso ad Chaganum à Prisco, eiusque prudentia & dexteritate.
units.tr: The sixth book contains these matters: how the Emperor, when leaving the city, was caught by a storm at sea; how, near Heraclea, while the Emperor was staying there, a monstrous boy was born with neither hands nor eyes, with eyebrows and eyelids like those of a fish, and ending in a tail from the hips; and how the monster was carried away. Concerning three Sclaveni who carried lyres about with them, and who were said to have been sent to the Khagan from the parts of the Ocean, and who appeared before the Emperor Maurice. The embassy of the Franks to the Emperor, tributary, promising auxiliaries, and the refusal of their request. Boso and Betto were the envoys, and Theudebert had sent them. Concerning a herd of stags, and how the largest of them, wounded, plunged into a certain wood; how a bodyguard (doryphorus) followed him, and another, a Gepid, with him; and how the bodyguard, because by chance he carried golden things, was killed by the Gepid, who long afterwards, when caught as the killer, was handed over to the flames. The army of the Avars against the Romans, the siege of the city of Singidunum, and the election of an old commander for the army. With what calamities he exposed his soldiers in this European war; how the Khagan, from Drizipera, besieged the shrine of the martyr Alexander; how the Romans shut up within the city of Trurulus were surrounded by the Khagan; how Maurice deceived the barbarian with words and loosed the siege; the embassy of the Avars to the Romans; and whatever Ardagastus suffered at the hands of the Roman troops. Moreover, what was done near Tatimerus, and the courage of the Roman commander Alexander, and the slaughter of the Sclaveni whom the Romans attacked. Concerning monstrous births in the royal city, one a quadruped, the other two-headed. How Priscus was removed from the European war, and concerning Theodore, the envoy sent by Priscus to the Khagan, and his prudence and skill.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: SEPTIMVS liber memorat de perturbatione ordinis in exercitu Romano, fortitudinemque Romanorum contra Sclauos, siue vt antiquitus vocabantur, Getas: ac ea, quæ in ignobili quadam Thraciæ vrbe Petro eiusque subditis acciderunt. & quomodo Piragastus Sclauorum militum tribunus interemptus, Romanique in aquæ quæ illos fequuta est penuria fortiter se gesserint. & quomodo cum Petrus à Sclauis oppugnaretur, Priscus iterum fit factus Imperator exercitus. mortem Ioannis Ieiunatoris Constantinopolitani; deque acceptis à Mauricio pecuniis, eidemque data accepti Syngrapha. quaque pius princeps reuerentia, & verè Imperatoria erga mortuum vsus fit, deque pannosis aliquot per archiepiscopum eiusdem viri inuentis vestimentis. De Mauris collectis contra Carthaginem ciuitatem, & quomodo Gennadij virtute bellum fit extinctum. deq; Cometa qui per multos dies apparuit. de ciuili bello inter Turcas. & narratione instituta, de republica imperioq; Turcarum. & quomodo Chaganus Ephtalitarum cæso principe, quæ gens est Turcica, ipsam quoque gentem subegerit: ac præter eam, aliam etiam Agarenorum gentem, & eorum qui vocantur Colch ad triginta myriadas interfecerit. ac etiam noua contra se moliente sublato Turum [?], ideoq; triumphali ad Mauricium Imperatorem scripta epistola, deuicerit quoque Abaros. Narrat porrò de gente Taugas, deque alia dicta Nucri, in quam deuicti Abari sunt dissecti. deque Var & Chuni gentibus, ex quibus tempore Iustiniani pars harum gentium in Europam venit, qui & Abaros scipsi nuncuparunt. & quomodo Turcarum regio nec terræmotu, nec pste soleat infestari, deque aureo monte, qui fertur, ac de Tauga vrbe, deq; vermiculis quì faciunt vestem Sericam, & quomodo multa fiat circa Chubdan, quæ dicitur metaxa, fiue sericum: & quæ ad eius opificium requirantur, deq; Indis, quorum corpus album est. Colloquium Chaganicum Prisco, vt daret sibi Singidonem, & quomodo, cum abnegaret ei Priscus, vrbem Singidonē Priscus seruauerit, quæq; per Dalmatiam seccerint, quasq; vrbes diruerint barbari. quomodo, q; Secüdus à Prisco missus in Dalmatiam contra barbaros, rē bene profpereq; gesserit. q; vndecimo anno Imperij Mauritij pdixerit monachus quidā eius, eiusq; liberorū morte, vt qui à foro stricto gladio ad vsq; vestibulum aulæ regiæ decurrens, & ipsum Mauricium, & eius liberos gladio perituros pronunciauerit: sed & Herodianus quidam regi futura pdixerit ex fame coorta in exercitu; & quomodo Chaganus admiranda humanitate quinq; dierū famescentib. inducias concesserit, ne utiq; frumentatio Romanorum à barbaris impediretur. & uti donatus à Prisco aromatib. in vicina Myfiæ loca abierit. quomodo cùm circa Myfiam Chaganus cum Comentiolo prælium committeret, proditione Comentioli Romanus miles à barbaro fit fusus, fugeritq; Comentiolus, & cum ad urbem Drexipera venisset, ab ea veluti transfuga fit relegatus, abieritq; ad eos qui vocantur longi muri. barbari verò à tergo venientes, Drexipera primum ceperint, & incenso Alexandri martyris templo, eiusque insuper sepulchro violato, reliquiisque è Sandapila protractis, diuinam ultionem violatores martyris experti sint. septem scilicet Chagani filiis ex inguinum tumore die una morientibus. Hisita turbis durantib. Constantinopolin ferecipit Comentiolus. barbari verò ad Muros longos magis magisque appropinquant, unde Byzantiorum res eo angustiarum sunt redactæ, ut Europa relicta de transitu in Asiam cogitarent. Legationem itaque simul Imperator ad Chagonem mittit, per Harmatonem, ac splendidis muneribus, auctuarioq; tributi ad auri Chiliades viginti vix persuadet eum ut pacem susciperet, dicentem etiam, Iudicia Deus Chaganum inter & Mauritium, Romanos item inter & barbaros. De monstris, quæ apparuerunt in aquis Niloticis forma humana, deq; Nili inundatione sententias diuersorum. author verò Agatarchidæ Cnidij sententiam sequitur, quotannis nimirum in Æthiopiæ locis magnos continuosq; imbres fieri à solstitio æstiuo, utqueadæquinoctium autumnale. conuenienterque itaque Nilum hyeme remissus currere, naturali scilicet è solis fontibus profluxu : æstate vero, propter eos quos ibi recipit effusos imbres, augeri. Et hæc etiam ea sunt quæ libro septimo.
units.tr: SEVENTH book relates the disorder in the Roman army, and the courage of the Romans against the Sclaveni, or, as they were called of old, the Getae; and what happened to Petrus and his subjects in a certain obscure city of Thrace. How Piragastus, tribune of the Sclavene soldiers, was killed, and how the Romans conducted themselves bravely amid the shortage of water that followed them. How, when Petrus was assailed by the Sclaveni, Priscus was made commander of the army again. The death of John the Faster, patriarch of Constantinople; the money received from Maurice and the receipt given in return; and with what pious devotion and truly imperial reverence the prince treated the dead man; and concerning certain tattered garments found by the archbishop among this man's belongings. Concerning the Moors gathered against the city of Carthage, and how, by the valour of Gennadius, the war was brought to an end. And concerning a comet that appeared for many days. Concerning civil war among the Turks, and an account of the commonwealth and empire of the Turks. How the Khagan, after killing the prince of the Ephthalites, subdued that Turkish people too; and besides them, another people, the Agareni, and those called Colchi, whom he slew to the number of about three hundred thousand. Also how, when a new plot was being devised against him, he removed Turum(?), and by a triumphal letter written to the Emperor Maurice, he also defeated the Avars. He relates also concerning the people Taugas, and another called Nucri, into which the defeated Avars were cut to pieces; and concerning the peoples Var and Chuni, from whom in the time of Justinian a part came into Europe, and who called themselves Avars. And how the land of the Turks is wont to be troubled neither by earthquake nor by plague; and concerning the golden mountain that is said to exist, and the city of Tauga; and the little worms that make silk garments, and how much is produced around Chubdan, which is called metaxa, or silk, and what is required for its working; and concerning the Indians, whose bodies are white. The conference of the Khagan with Priscus, in which he demanded that Priscus give him Singidunum; and how, when Priscus refused him, Priscus held on to the city of Singidunum; and what the barbarians did in Dalmatia, and which cities they destroyed. How Secundus, sent by Priscus into Dalmatia against the barbarians, conducted the war well and successfully. That in the eleventh year of Maurice's reign a certain monk of his foretold the death of him and of his children, for he ran from the forum with a drawn sword to the vestibule of the royal palace, declaring that Maurice himself and his children would perish by the sword. But also a certain Herodianus foretold to the king future events arising from a famine in the army. And how the Khagan, with admirable humanity, granted a truce to the Romans who had been starving for five days, so that the Roman grain supply should not be hindered by the barbarians; and how, having been presented with spices by Priscus, he withdrew to the neighbouring regions of Moesia. How, when the Khagan engaged Comentiolus in battle near Moesia, through Comentiolus's treachery the Roman soldiers were routed by the barbarian, and Comentiolus fled; and when he came to the city of Drizipera, he was expelled from it as a deserter, and went to those called the Long Walls. The barbarians, coming up from behind, first captured Drizipera; and after burning the temple of the martyr Alexander, violating his tomb besides, and dragging the relics out of the sepulchre, they experienced the divine vengeance on the violators of the martyr: seven sons of the Khagan died on a single day of a swelling in the groin. While these disturbances continued, Comentiolus recovered Constantinople. The barbarians, meanwhile, drew ever closer to the Long Walls, so that the affairs of the Byzantines were reduced to such straits that they considered abandoning Europe and crossing into Asia. The Emperor therefore sent an embassy to the Khagan at the same time, through Harmaton, and with splendid gifts and an addition to the tribute of some twenty thousand pounds of gold, he barely persuaded him to accept peace; saying also that God would judge between the Khagan and Maurice, and between the Romans and the barbarians. Concerning the monsters in human form that appeared in the waters of the Nile, and concerning the flooding of the Nile, the opinions of various writers. The author, however, follows the view of Agatharchides of Cnidus: that every year, from the summer solstice to the autumn equinox, great and continual rains fall in the regions of Ethiopia; so that the Nile, sent back in winter, runs on in its natural course from the sources of the sun, but in summer it swells because of the rains poured into it there. And these also are the contents of the seventh book.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Octavo autem ista insunt. quomodo Chosroes obincursiones qui sub Romani erant Saracenorum, fœdus dirimire voluerit; quod tamen fartum tectum manserit Georgio ad eum legatione misso, qui maiestatem regis in eo laesit[?], quod diceret, dixisse Chosroen Georgij se causa seruare fœdus non autem Imperatoris Mauricij. quomodo item proditionis condemnatus fit Comentiolus, eiusque cum Romano milite reconciliatio, Imperatoris iterum suffragiis constituti ducis. Pugna Romanorum, ac Abarorum, auspiciis Prisci & Comentioli, quorum Comentiolus quidem aberat de certis negotiis, Prisci vero supererat exercitui. Fortitudo Romanorum, atq; occidio Abarorum usq; ad nouem millia. tertia pugna, & adhuc eorundem internecio, ad quindecim millia. Quarta pugna, & iterata Romanorum splendida victoria, cæfis barbaris computato simul puerorum numero ad millia quinquaginta. Quinta pugna, & Romanorum victoria, captis fusisque Abaris. captis quidem Abarorum tribus millibus, aliorum vero quatuor millibus, & adhuc aliorum ab iis, duobus millibus & ducentis, Sclauorumq; millibus octo. vnde cum contra spem fortunam effet expertus, Chaganus ab Imperatore captos Abaros repostulauit[?]. De Comentioli pertinacia, & quomodo eius temeritate Romanorum militum non contemnenda multitudo Philippopolim versus euntis, frigore enicata fit. vti Petrus iterum dux Europæi exercitus ab Imperatore fit ordinatus,deq; nuptiis Theodosij filij Mauritij cum filia Germani. deq; anno-næ caritate in vrbe regia, deque concursu acturba populi in templo supplicante Cæsare, ciusque le-nitate, exilioque militum, Eorumque post vnum diem reditu. quomodo Mauricius Petrum miserit, vt quocunque modo militem Thracicum in alteram Iftri partem transfretaret, quomodoque vox diuina Petro fit locuta, ac tumultu in exercitu coorto Romano, tyrannis contra Imperatorem nata fit, tyranno Phoca à militibus Imperatore Salutato.quomodo fugerit Petrus tumultusq; ad regem delatus,& quomodo primum per tribunos Plebei Sergium & Cosman plebs distracta, ac inuenti sint Praefinorum M. D. Venetorum verò c c c. & quomodo inter populum æmulatio orta. Legatioque Imperatoris ad milites tumultuantes, & legationis refutatio. quomodo item vrbem custodierit regiam. ac legatio exercitus ad Theodosium Mauricij filium,aut ipsum se,aut eius socerum proclamaturos se esse regem. quomodo etiam auditis hisce suspectum Mauricius deinceps habuerit Germanum,quasi fomitem autoremque tyrannidis:idcoque minæ, minarumque regiarum indicatio per Theodosium generum, & refugium Germani ad fanum Dei genitricis à Cyro exstructum. ac Stephani semiuiri, qui præfectus erat filiis Imperatoris,ad Germanum,vt ex templo descenderet, ablegatio irrita,& quomodo fustibus fit cæsus Theodofius à patre filius,propterea quod soceri consilia videbatur
units.tr: The eighth book contains the following: how Chosroes, on account of the incursions of the Saracens who were under Roman rule, wished to break the treaty, yet the treaty remained intact because George was sent to him as envoy. George offended the king's majesty by saying that Chosroes had kept the treaty for George's sake and not for the sake of Emperor Maurice. Likewise, how Comentiolus was condemned for treason, and his reconciliation with the Roman soldiers, when by the emperor's votes he was again appointed commander. The battle of the Romans and the Avars under the auspices of Priscus and Comentiolus, of whom Comentiolus was absent on certain business, while Priscus remained with the army. The bravery of the Romans, and the slaughter of the Avars up to nine thousand. The third battle, and the further destruction of the same, to fifteen thousand. The fourth battle, and the Romans' splendid victory again, the barbarians being slain, the number of boys included, to about fifty thousand. The fifth battle, and the Roman victory, the Avars being captured and routed: of the Avars, three thousand were taken, four thousand others, and yet another two thousand two hundred from among those others, and eight thousand Slavs. Since Chaganus had found fortune contrary to his hopes, he demanded from the emperor the return of the captured Avars. Concerning the obstinacy of Comentiolus, and how, through his rashness, a not negligible multitude of Roman soldiers, marching toward Philippopolis, was killed by the cold. How Peter was again appointed by the emperor commander of the European army; and concerning the marriage of Theodosius, son of Maurice, with the daughter of Germanus; and concerning the grain shortage in the imperial city, and the crowd of the populace in the church when the Caesar was supplicating, and his gentleness, and the exile of the soldiers, and their return after one day. How Maurice sent Peter, so that by any means he might ferry the Thracian soldiers to the other side of the Danube; and how a divine voice spoke to Peter; and when a tumult arose in the Roman army, a tyrant arose against the emperor, Phocas, having been hailed as emperor by the soldiers. How Peter fled, and how the tumult was reported to the king; and how first through the tribunes of the commons, Sergius and Cosmas, the populace was divided, and how the Prasini were found to be 5,000 and the Veneti 300; and how rivalry arose among the people. The emperor's embassy to the mutinying soldiers, and the rejection of the embassy. Likewise, how he guarded the imperial city; and the embassy of the army to Theodosius, son of Maurice, that they would proclaim either himself or his father-in-law as king. How also, when these things were heard, Maurice thereafter held Germanus under suspicion, as the spark and author of the tyranny; hence the threats, and the royal threats disclosed through Theodosius, the son-in-law, and Germanus' flight to the shrine of the Mother of God built by Cyrus; and the futile dispatch of Stephen, a half-man who was prefect of the emperor's sons, to Germanus, to make him come down from the church; and how Theodosius was beaten with clubs by his father, the son, because he seemed to be helping his father-in-law's plans; and Germanus' transfer from the church of the Virgin Mother of God to Holy Sophia, and the renewed summons to the Hippodrome, and the mistrust, because a certain Andreas kept walking about there, who by his entreaties cut off hope from that quarter.

units.la: [notes in the right margin are cut off at the scan edge; only fragments such as "Ab", "De", "pro", "An" remain, mostly illegible] debatur adiuuare, transfitusque Germani è templo Deiparæ virginis ad sanctam Sophiam & rursum provocatio ad cundū, diffidentiaq;, ppterea quod Andreas quidam ibi continuo obambularet, qui supplicationibus inde spem intercluderet. Tumultus &incendium in urbe domus Constantini patricii, qui Lartes à vulgo cognominabatur, & desperatio fugaque Mauricij: quomodo cum æstus esset maris, iter fugæ sit præcisum: missioq; Theodosij ad Chosroen, ciusq; iterum Nicæa reditus cum annulum ci ostendisset, quem filio tesseræ signíuc loco pater dederat: & quomodo ad tyrannum cives, inter quos erat etiam Septimi quod vocabatur loci præfectus, exiuerit, quomodoque Germanus in affectando regno successu exciderit, pra-finis ideo prorsus reclamantibus, quia, vt dicebant, factionis erat Venetæ. Ceterum, renunciatio in sancti Iohannis templo, quod erat in Septimo, Phocæ, adhibitis riteque factis regni ceremoniis à Cyriaco, introitusq; Phocæ, & salutatio Leontiæ uxoris Phocæ, ac tribunorum de locis contentio & expulsio Cosmæ tribuni plebis Venetæ per Alexandrum, contentioq; cum Alexandro, in eaq; forte mentio facta, quod nondum esset mortuus Mauricius: & propterea festinatio tyranni furorq; in cæde Imperatoris; adhæc occidio, filiórū regis in cóspectu patris, in portu qui vocatur Eutropij: modestia itē & regis feria pietatis cófessio: ipsiusq; illius cædes manu Lilij ac Mauricij Imp. testaménti, in quo scriptus hæres rex Heraclius erat, inuenti prælectio: quomodoq; corpora regia marino fluctui exposita: funebris item oratio super Mauricio, & quomodo ultio-
units.tr: A tumult and a fire in the city at the house of Constantine the patrician, who was called Lardes by the common people; and the despair and flight of Maurice: how, when the sea was at ebb, the route of flight was cut off; and Theodosius' dispatch to Chosroes, and his return to Nicaea when he had shown him the ring which the father had given the son as a token and sign. And how citizens, among whom was also the so-called prefect of the Septimum, went out to the tyrant; and how Germanus, in aspiring to the kingship, fell from success, the Prasini objecting absolutely for this reason, that, as they said, he belonged to the Venetan faction. Moreover, the proclamation in the church of St John, which was in the Septimum, of Phocas, the royal ceremonies being duly performed by Cyriacus; and Phocas' entrance, and the greeting of Leontia, Phocas' wife; and the dispute over places among the tribunes, and the expulsion of Cosmas, tribune of the Venetan commons, by Alexander, and the dispute with Alexander, in which by chance mention was made that Maurice was not yet dead; and therefore the tyrant's haste and fury in the slaughter of the emperor; besides, the killing of the king's sons in their father's sight, in the port called Eutropius'; likewise the modesty and the king's pious confession of faith; and the reading of the will of Lilius and of Emperor Maurice, in which King Heraclius was written as heir; and the discovery of the bodies of the royals, which were exposed to the sea's waves; likewise the funeral oration over Maurice; and how the Roman army, by divine providence, experienced the vengeance for those things which it had impiously committed against Maurice, so that in a short time none of those who had been privy to that tyranny survived from so great a number: some perished by plague, others by fire sent down from heaven, others by the sword. And when Emperor Heraclius had undertaken war against Raxates the Persian, after holding a levy of soldiers, he found only two survivors from that multitude which had favored the tyrant; and then Roman affairs began to prevail against the Persians; whereas, as long as those men had been present, victory had been on the Persians' side. The murder plotted by the tyrant through Alexander against Theodosius, the king's son, and against Peter and Comentiolus and Constantine Lardes; and the error concerning Theodosius, so that he was not killed. And how the images which stood in the so-called Tychaeum were torn from their places and foretold what had been done, to a certain calligrapher returning home from dinner. How Maurice is said to have remitted a third part of the tribute payments to his subjects, and to have given three hundred talents to the Byzantines for repairing and restoring the aqueducts; and how munificent he was toward those devoted to the mathematical sciences; and concerning the miracles in the outflow of blood from the martyr Euphemia; and how Maurice, having tested the matter by experience, afterwards held the greater belief in it because of his earlier unbelief. And how the tyrant shut up Constantia, Emperor Maurice's wife, together with her daughters, within a plebeian house. The tyrant's embassy to Chosroes, king of the Persians, came to nothing, and the dissolution of the treaty, Chosroes pretending that he would sacrifice the offerings to Maurice; and so Lilius, who was the envoy, returned without having accomplished the matter. The slaying of Alexander, one of Phocas' tent-companions, on the suspicion that he had spared Theodosius, son of Maurice, whom he ought to have killed; with which the whole end of the history is reached.

Cædes à tyranno per Alexandrum machinata Theodosij regis imperatoris filij, Petriqúe & Comentioli, & Constantini Lartis, errorq; circa Theodosium ita ut non sit occisus. & quomodo Alexandriæ imagines quæ stabant in Tychæo sic dictoloco, è sede sua divulsæ, prædixerint ea quæ facta fuerant calligrapho cuidam, à cœna redcundi domum. quomodo Mauricius dicatur tertiam partem pensionum vectigalium remisisse subditis, ac trecenta dediffe talenta Byzantinis, ad reficiendos instaurandosque aquæductus, & quomodo munificentissimus fuerit erga rerum mathematicarum studiosos, deque miraculis in effluxu sanguinis Euphemiæ martyris, & quomodo Mauricius rei facto periculo ex incredulitate maiorem ei postea fidem habuerit. & quo modo tyrannus Constantiam Imper. Mauritij coniugem una cum filiabus intra domum plebeiam concluserit. Legatio tyranni ad Chosroen Persarum regem irrita, fœderisque difsolutio, prætexente Chosroe inferias mactaturum se Mauricio. & sic Lilius, qui legatus erat, re non perfecta rediit. Cædes Alexandri, vnius ex contubernalibus Phocæ, propter suspicionem quasi Theodosio Mauricij filio, quem occidere debuisset, pepercerit in quibus totius historiæ finis est.
units.tr: ...the vengeance which the Roman army had impiously perpetrated against Maurice it experienced from divine providence, so that in a short time none of those who had been privy to that tyranny survived out of so great a number. Some perished by pestilence, others by fire sent down from heaven, others by the sword. And when Emperor Heraclius had undertaken war against Raxates the Persian, after holding a levy of soldiers, he found only two survivors from that multitude which had favored the tyrant; and then Roman affairs began to prevail against the Persians, whereas, for as long as those men had been present, victory had been on the Persians' side. The murder plotted by the tyrant through Alexander against Theodosius, the king's son, and against Peter and Comentiolus and Constantine Lardes; and the error concerning Theodosius, so that he was not killed. And how the images which stood in the so-called Tychaeum were torn from their places and foretold what had been done, to a certain calligrapher returning home from dinner. How Maurice is said to have remitted a third part of the tribute payments to his subjects, and to have given three hundred talents to the Byzantines for repairing and restoring the aqueducts; and how munificent he was toward those devoted to the mathematical sciences; and concerning the miracles in the outflow of blood from the martyr Euphemia; and how Maurice, having tested the matter by experience, afterwards held the greater belief in it because of his earlier unbelief. And how the tyrant shut up Constantia, Emperor Maurice's wife, together with her daughters, within a plebeian house. The tyrant's embassy to Chosroes, king of the Persians, came to nothing, and the dissolution of the treaty, Chosroes pretending that he would sacrifice the offerings to Maurice; and so Lilius, who was the envoy, returned without having accomplished the matter.
