units.la: DE LEGATIS ROMANO- RUM AD GENTES.
units.tr: On the Roman Envoys to the Nations.

units.la: Ex Historia THEOPHYLACTI EXPRÆFE- CTI ET SCRIPTURARII.
units.tr: From the History of Theophylact, Former Prefect and Scribe.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: QVOD Imperante Mauricio Legatos miserunt Romani ad Chaganum, & bellum deprecaturi, Elpidium mittunt virum Senatorium, Siciliæque præfectum tunc, & Prætoris tribunal ascendentem, quod officij genus apud Romanos non inhonoratum est, & Comentiolum, qui illo tum, munere fungebatur quod inter corporis custodes, à Latinis nuncupatur Scribæ. Iverunt igitur ambo ad Chaganum ad urbem Anchialum, ac de induciis tractaverunt, ut erant iussi. Hoc vero non mediocriter irato propter damna sibi illata, sed insolentiora quoque multo minitante, Muros longos sic dictam urbem disiecturum: Elpidio autem lenioribus utente verbis, quam ut ita retunderet inflatum Cagani fastum, Comentiolus cordatè & liberè linguæ ingenuitatem ostendit, & Romana libertate, in modum castæ alicuius dominæ intaminatè seruata, nec adulterius corrupta adulationibus, coram præcipuis barbarorum, atq; ipso adeò Chagano dixit. quoniam verò magna hæc modum in verbis egrediebatur reprehensio, ex feruore sanguinis, impotente sui animo, per totam faciem ita præ ira erubuit, vt, cum omnino facies eius præferret, nec legatis quidem se parsurum, maximum ex oratione ista Comentiolo immineret periculum. Violata enim barbarus legatorum religione, Comentiolum in vincula coniecit, cumque detineretur in carcere pedes eius in robur conclusit, tabernaculumq; legatorum destruxit. ac inde pro more istis regionibus consueto pro pœna mortem est minatus. posteriori autem die cum sedatior iam esset, idoneis ad eam rem sermonibus adhortati Chaganum, barbarorum potentissimi, persuaserunt, ne quid sibi proponeret de morte Comentioli, neue vltra vincula quid amplius contra legatos tentaretur. Consentiens ita Chaganus legatos, largitus iisdem non exspectatam salutem, violatos ad Imperatorem remittit.
units.tr: In the reign of Maurice the Romans sent envoys to Chagan to seek peace. They sent Elpidius, a senator and at that time prefect of Sicily, who had climbed the praetor's tribunal, a kind of office not dishonourable among the Romans, and Comentiolus, who at that time held the post that among the Latins is called "scribe" among the bodyguards. Both went to Chagan at the city of Anchialus and negotiated a truce, as they had been ordered. Chagan, not moderately angry over the losses that had been inflicted on him, threatened far more insolent things: that he would tear down the Long Walls, as the city is called. Elpidius used milder words, too gentle to beat down the Khan's swollen arrogance, but Comentiolus showed a frank and bold spirit of free speech. Keeping Roman liberty untainted, like that of a chaste lady, and not corrupted by flattery, he spoke in front of the chief men of the barbarians and Chagan himself. But since this speech went beyond measure in its rebuke, the blood boiled in him, and he lost control of himself. His whole face flushed with rage, so that, since his face showed everything, it seemed he would spare the envoys no more, and the greatest danger hung over Comentiolus because of that speech. The barbarian violated the sanctity of the envoys: he threw Comentiolus into chains, fixed his feet in the stocks while he was held in prison, and tore down the envoys' tent. Then, according to the custom of those regions, he threatened him with death as punishment. But on the following day, when he had grown calmer, certain men urged Chagan, the most powerful of the barbarians, with suitable arguments, to propose nothing about Comentiolus's death, and to attempt nothing further against the envoys beyond the chains. Chagan agreed, and he sent the envoys, who had been mistreated, back to the Emperor, granting them a safety they had not expected.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Quod relapso anno iterum Elpidius ad eandem legationem omnium suffragiis electus, missus est. Is cum esset apud Chaganum legatum postulavit, qui vna secum ad Imperatorem proficisceretur, vt sic induciis restauratis, viginti aliæ auri Chiliades adiicerentur plus, quam ante pactum erat. Chagamus autem admissis hisce, Targium illustrem apud populum Abarorum virum, ad Cæsarem cum Elpidio misit. Cur igitur Abari inducias non multò post confuderint, & bellum aperte refumferint, causam equidem dicam, nec detracto. Vir erat natione Scytha, Bolocalabra nomine. hic tum temporis periculosum perpetrauit facinus: siquidem cum vna ex concubinis Chagani rem habuit, & breui voluptate inescatus, in magnas mortis retes se coniecit. veritus autem ne aliquando sacinus hoc deprehensum ingentes poenas parturiret, persuasis exsubditis hominibus septem profugit ad antiquam à qua orti erant gentem. Hunni ca sunt. habitantes orientem, vbi vicinus est Persis, quos Turcas etiam nominari pluribus iam costat. Itaq; transmisso Istro cum tenderet ad Libidinum vrbem, interceptus à Romano quodam duce, eorū quibus est demandata Istri custodia, & gentem suam professus est, & quomodo vixisset, quamq; inde voluptatem percepisset. quoniam verò idoneus visus est ad exponendos casus suos ad Imperatorem mittitur. & hac occasione inducia Romanæ videntur esse distractæ: exortumq; bellum iam tum cum Targitas adhuc in vrbe legati esset nomine, & anniuersarios reditus à Romanis deposceret, quos Chagano quotannis ferebant inducia. Vnde non sine causa iratus Imperator, cum non minimum videret se circumuentum à barbaris, hoc equidem exigente diuitias annuas, & pacales reditus, hoc autem non quiescente, sed Europam infestante, vrbesque vastante, citatur Targitas in insulam Chalcitidem, deportatus ad menses sex, interim regis animus deferbuit, qui morte quoque in legatum se animaduersurum fuerat minatus. Miles verò Chagani & Scythiæ finitimos omnes perdiderunt, ceperuntque plurimas vrbes, Terateridam,Bononiam, Acus, Dorostolum, Salpada, Panasa, Martianopolim, ac Tropæum. in quibus omnibus non minimis opus fuit laboribus,nec, licet magna aceruatifucceffus fortuna adiuuante, qui etiamnum incuitabile malum adfert lentioribus absque sudore & molestiis ad deditionem compelli potuere hæc oppida.
units.tr: The following year Elpidius was again chosen by the vote of all to undertake the same embassy and was sent. When he was with Chagan as envoy, he asked that a man be allowed to go with him to the Emperor, so that, with the truce restored, twenty thousand more pounds of gold might be added beyond what had been agreed. Chagan granted this, and he sent Targitas, an illustrious man among the Avars, with Elpidius to Caesar. Why the Avars soon afterwards broke the truce and openly renewed the war, I will state, and I will not conceal it. There was a Scythian man named Bolocalabras. At that time he committed a dangerous crime: he had intercourse with one of Chagan's concubines, and, lured by a brief pleasure, he cast himself into the great nets of death. Fearing that, if this deed were discovered, it would bring him terrible punishment, he persuaded seven men of his people and fled to the ancient nation from which they had sprung. These are the Huns, who dwell in the east, where they are neighbours to the Persians, and whom it is now well established are also called Turks. So, having crossed the Danube and heading for the city of Libidinum, he was intercepted by a Roman commander, one of those entrusted with guarding the Danube. He confessed his nation, how he had lived, and what pleasure he had got from it. Since he seemed fit to explain his misfortunes, he was sent to the Emperor. On this occasion the truce between the Romans and the Avars seems to have been broken. The war broke out while Targitas was still in the city in the capacity of envoy, and he demanded from the Romans the yearly payments which the truce brought to Chagan each year. The Emperor, therefore, was not without reason angry, since he saw that he had been not a little outwitted by the barbarians: the truce demanded these yearly riches and peace payments, yet Chagan did not keep quiet but was attacking Europe and laying waste its cities. So Targitas was summoned and banished to the island of Chalcitis for six months. Meanwhile the king's anger cooled, for he had threatened to punish the envoy with death as well. But the army of Chagan destroyed all the neighbours of Scythia, and took very many cities: Teratorida, Bononia, Acus, Dorostolum, Salpada, Panasa, Martianopolis, and Tropaeum. In all these operations great labours were needed, and even with great success aided by fortune, which still brings an unavoidable evil, these towns could not be forced to surrender without sweat and trouble to the more sluggish.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Quod Tiberius per nuncium cum Hormisda egit, ut utrinque bellum componeretur. At verò ille superbior hac legatione factum voluit aperte sibi tributum reddi à Romanis, Armenios & Iberos sibi subiici, consentientibus in hoc Romanis, neue amplius oppidum Daras à Cæsare tentaretur. quamuis pater Chosroes utrinque inter se & Cæsarem inducias esse voluerit, neque Daras sub Imperium Cæsaris reddere detrectauerit. Postea verò quam Hormisdæ factum Tibetius audivisset, adveniente æstate, coactis rursum Copiis Persidem ingreditur Mauricius, ipse traiecto Tigride, reliquis, ut ad interiora magis Perfidis promouerent, missis.
units.tr: Tiberius sent a messenger to negotiate with Hormisdas, so that the war might be settled on both sides. But Hormisdas, prouder after this embassy, wanted it openly declared that tribute be paid to him by the Romans, that the Armenians and Iberians be made subject to him, and that the Romans agree to this and not attack the town of Daras again. Although his father Chosroes had wished there to be a truce between the two sides and Caesar, and had not refused to return Daras under the rule of Caesar. But after Tiberius had heard of Hormisdas's action, with summer coming Maurice gathered his forces again and entered Persia himself, having crossed the Tigris, and sent the rest forward to push further into the interior of Persia.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Quod cum grauiter ægreq; ferret Chaganus, Romanorum militem etiam in tenebris inclaruisse, selectissimi quiqué admonuerunt barbarum de bello deponendo. Dixerunt enim non iustam eius iram esse contra Romanos. Confidenter itaque Priscus legatū misit ad Chaganum, nomine Theodorum, à natura factum hominem elegantem, & prudentissimum. professione medicum, lingua libera & ingenua. Eo autem ad Chaganum admisso, barbarus quidem elatus animo propter ea quæ cuenerant sibi felicia, nimis quam superbus factus est, quippe qui se regem esse diceret omnium gentium, necaliquem esse quacunq; Sol videt, quiaut prodire, aut sibi se possetobsistere. Legatus verò, vt qui doctissimus esset historiarum, barbaricam exemplis contucit ferociam.ac vt historiam proseramus non erit inconsequens. Dixitigitur: Audi Chaganeantiquam nimis & vtilē historiam. quod cum attentum fecisset ad audiendum Chaganum exordium, non est præcisa reliqua historiæ narratio. Sefostrin aiunt fuisse regem felicem perquam, & omnium Ægyptiorum regum illustrissimum. Hunc gloriari solitum de diuitiis suis antiquus est sermo, potentia verò viribusq; fuisse tantis, vt expugnari non posset: eoq; ideo luxus peruenisse, vt curru fabricato ex auro, preciosisq; gemmis exornato veheretur: ac equis quidem relictis, & mulis, deuictorum colla regum eius iugo subiiceret, atq; ita in forum currum huius infelices reges protraherent. Hic igitur Sefostris cum non solum non moderaretur fortunis suis, sed superbè quoq; sæpe, numero exprobraret de victis regibus calamitatem, vnum aliquem dicunt ex regibus, qui subiecti erantiugo currus, cum magna forte & festiua celebritate magnus confluxus esset populi lentius protrahentem currum, & crebrò retrospicientem intuitum esse volutationem rotæ. Cumq; ita protractio currus esset vitiata, quia nō omnes vno æquoq; studio, qui ad rem hanc ordinati, laborarent, Æ-gyptiorum rex ad eum inquit, qui tam sæpe respiceret, Quid homo tam sæpe retrospicis? quid rotas intueris? quorsum transire hiscis? hunc tum cum multa grauitate Sesostri respondisse: Rotarum admiror volubilitatem tam varios efficere motus, easque partes quæ in altum sunt elatæ, deferri rursus in terram, & vicissim eas quæ terram radunt, postea euchi[?], quæ cum audiuisset, Sesostris didicissetque, ne nimis altum saperet, iussit se resumtis eorum loco mulis à iugo collaregum solui. Hæc te doceant, Chagane, felicitate nihil esse instabilius. quapropter admiratus prudentiam hominis Chaganus fastum comprimit, sistit confidentiam, resque componit ad statum pacis, ac ita cum per horas aliquot siluisset, ad Theodorum, Noui, inquit) animo meo moderari, quando exuberat, noui etiam iram vincere, sed habita ratione temporis. Abstineo amplius à Prisco, Theodore, sit & ille mihi æquus bonusq; amicus, ex parte prædæ ne excludatur Chaganus, in meam terram descendit, in meos subditos vim exercuit. Commune esto, si quid inde est fortunarum. Hac sic humanitate profequutus Theodorum, ad Priscum remisit. cum vero Prisco retulisset ea Theodorus quæ sibi barbarus loquutus erat, exhortatus est Romanos Priscus, vt in partem quoque spoliorum admitterent barbarum. Romani licet abnegarent primò, duciqué rebellarent, dux tamen multis, & variis vsque adeò prudentibusque verbis affatus, exercitum persuasit, vt prædam quoque diriperent inter barbarum. Reddit is itaq; Romani Chagano quos ceperant barbaris, reliqua praeda sibi retenta, discordiam omnem composucrunt. Chaganus quoq; cum lubens recepisset barbaros, per regionem suam concessit transitum. Et ita quidem Romani, quinque millibus barbarorum Chagano datis, Drizipera veniunt; dux exercitus, Byzantium. Mauricius autem eum, eiusq; lenitatem qui tam stultè barbaro de spoliis cesserit, reprehendit, & ab officio remotus est Prifcus.
units.tr: Chagan took it very badly and with difficulty that the Roman soldiers had shone even in the dark, and the most select men urged the barbarian to lay down the war. For they said that his anger against the Romans was not just. So Priscus confidently sent to Chagan an envoy named Theodorus, a man elegant by nature and very prudent, a physician by profession, with a free and open tongue. When Theodorus was admitted to Chagan, the barbarian, elated by the good fortune that had come to him, became far too proud. He said that he was king of all peoples, and that there was no one whom the sun sees who could either come forth against him or resist him. The envoy, being very learned in histories, confronted the barbarian's ferocity with examples. And to bring out the story it will not be out of place. So he said: "Hear, Chagan, an ancient and very useful story." When he had made the Khan attentive to listen, the narrative of the history was not cut short. They say Sesostris was a most fortunate king, and the most illustrious of all the kings of Egypt. It is an old saying that he used to boast of his riches, and that his power and strength were so great that he could not be conquered. And he came to such luxury that he rode in a chariot made of gold and adorned with precious gems, and, leaving horses and mules aside, he put the necks of his conquered kings under the yoke, and so dragged the chariot into the marketplace, with these unhappy kings pulling it. Now Sesostris, not only did not moderate his fortune, but often proudly reproached the defeated kings for their calamity. They say that one of the kings who were subjected to the chariot yoke, while a great crowd had assembled for a splendid and festive occasion, was pulling the chariot more slowly and often looking back, and was gazing at the turning of the wheel. Since the drawing of the chariot was thus spoiled, because not all those who had been arranged to labour at this task worked with equal zeal, the king of Egypt said to him who looked back so often: "Why do you look back so often, man? Why do you stare at the wheels? Where are you trying to go?" He, with great gravity, is said to have answered Sesostris: "I admire the wheel's turning, which makes such varied motions, so that the parts that have been raised on high are brought back down to earth, and in turn those that graze the ground are raised up afterwards." When Sesostris heard this and understood it, so that he might not think too highly of himself, he ordered that he himself, with mules taking the place of the kings, be unyoked from the collar. "Let these things teach you, Chagan, that nothing is more unstable than good fortune." Therefore Chagan, admiring the man's prudence, restrained his arrogance, checked his confidence, and settled the business toward a state of peace. And so, after he had been silent for some hours, he said to Theodorus: "I know how to govern my mind when it overflows, and I also know how to conquer anger, but only with due regard to the time. I will no longer hold back from Priscus, Theodorus, and let him be a fair and good friend to me, so that Chagan is not excluded from a share of the booty. He has come down into my land and inflicted violence on my subjects. Let whatever fortune has come from it be shared." Having treated Theodorus with such kindness, he sent him back to Priscus. When Theodorus had reported to Priscus what the barbarian had said to him, Priscus urged the Romans to admit the barbarian to a share of the spoils as well. The Romans, though at first they refused and rebelled against their commander, were nevertheless addressed by the commander with many varied and so very prudent words that he persuaded the army to share even the plunder with the barbarian. So the Romans returned to Chagan the captives they had taken from the barbarians, kept the rest of the booty for themselves, and settled all the discord. Chagan, too, gladly received the barbarians and granted them passage through his region. And so the Romans, having given five thousand barbarians to Chagan, came to Drizipara, and the commander of the army came to Byzantium. But Maurice rebuked him, and the leniency of a man who had so foolishly yielded to the barbarian over the spoils, and Priscus was removed from his office.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Quod cum Abari in Thraciam facerent incursiones, Senatus monuit Mauricium de legatione mittenda ad Chaganum. quare vocatum ad se rex Harmatonem legatum creat, & ad Chaganum mittit. Itaque Harmaton Drizipera venit, munera multa secum ferens, ubi cum Chaganus praesentes tum fortunas lugens, defleret ultra modum mortem filiorum, & in exercitu suo grassantem pestem, decem prius commoratus est dies, quam ad Chaganum admitteretur, quia fletus acerbus erat, & calamitas varia. hinc die duodecima intromittitur in tabernaculum barbari legatus, qui blandis verbis adulatus barbaro, quoniam gravabatur nimium accipere dona regia tantum non consentiens in istud tragicum, Hostium dona non dona. plurimisque usus ceremoniis, persuadet ut muneribus istis honorari se pateretur barbarus. postea vero dici, cum de pace convenisset inter barbarum, domum redire cogitavit, haec autem verba addidit Chaganus, ludica Deus inter Mauritium & Chaganum, inter Abaros & inter Romanos. Insimulauit enim ruptæ pacis Romanos, nec sine causa. Etenim reuera pacis adulteri cum fuerint, autoresq; belli in ea quæ diximus mala inciderunt. Dirimit Romanos Ifter ab Abaris, veluti sequester; vltra verò, si quis fluuium transmittat, Sclauorum ditio est. sed & adiectæ funtauri Chiliades viginti ad inducias, vnde bellum inter Abaros & Romanos finitum.
units.tr: When the Avars were making raids into Thrace, the Senate advised Maurice to send an embassy to the Khagan. So the king summoned Harmaton, appointed him envoy, and sent him to Chaganus. Harmaton came to Drizipera bringing many gifts. There Chaganus, lamenting his present fortunes and the death of his sons, and the plague raging through his army, wept beyond measure. Harmaton waited ten days before he was admitted to Chaganus, because the weeping was bitter and the calamities many. On the twelfth day the envoy was brought into the barbarian's tent. He flattered the barbarian with smooth words, since Chaganus was reluctant to accept royal gifts and did not fully agree with that tragic saying, "the gifts of enemies are not gifts." Using many ceremonies, he persuaded the barbarian to allow himself to be honoured with those gifts. Afterwards, when peace had been agreed between the barbarian and the Romans, Chaganus thought of going home, and he added these words: "May God judge between Maurice and Chaganus, between the Avars and the Romans." For he accused the Romans of breaking the peace, and not without cause. Indeed, having been truly adulterers of the peace and authors of the war, they fell into the evils we have described. The Ister separates the Romans from the Avars, like a mediator; beyond it, if anyone crosses the river, it is the territory of the Slavs. Twenty thousand more were also added as a truce, and so the war between the Avars and the Romans was brought to an end.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Quod eodem circiter tempore Chosroes molitus est pacem frangere, ista de causa. Saracenorum quidam militabant in auxiliis Romanis,& eorum vnus sponte sua Perfiam inuadens pacis tempore, excursione ista partes aliquot Babyloniæ infeftauerat. qua de re quo ea animo fieret aut in quâ partem accipienda essent, cum dubitaret Chosroes, Mauritius in Perfida mittit Legatum Georgium, qui vrbium Orientalium tributis præfectus erat, vel vt Romani vocant præfectus Prætorio. Atgrauiter ferens iniuriam illatam sibi Chosroes, relictum legatum dies in barbara regione distinuit. Itaque Georgius per multos dies detinetur, introitu in regiam nondum potitus, postea turbidis Chosroæ rebus, bonum visum est barbaro, ne tum bellum contra Romanos ingereret: sic Georgius in regiam receptus à rege Babylonio, cum præsentis tum temporis statum fauentem haberet, persuadet barbarum ne pacis pacta transiliret. eo igitur modo Chosroes volens nolens pacem amplectitur. Legatus autem omnia quæ & quomodo acciderant ple-nè sunè fuseque ad Imperatorem retulit, fine tamen rei non bono. Dixit enim Georgius Chosroen hæc regi dicere, Rex Persarum ad subditos proloquutus est, ob legati virtutem bellum non moueo.quæ cum Imperator audiisset, irascitur legato, & Georgio admodum periculosè legatio illa successit.
units.tr: About the same time Chosroes planned to break the peace, for the following reason. Some Saracens were serving as auxiliaries in the Roman army, and one of them, on his own initiative, invaded Persia in a time of peace and by this raid had laid waste several parts of Babylonia. Chosroes did not know with what intention this had been done, or how the matter was to be taken, and while he was in doubt, Maurice sent to Persia an envoy, Georgius, who was in charge of the tributes of the eastern cities, or, as the Romans call him, the praetorian prefect. Chosroes, taking the injury done to him gravely, kept the envoy waiting for many days in the barbarian's territory. So Georgius was detained for many days, not yet having gained access to the royal court. Afterwards, with Chosroes's affairs in turmoil, the barbarian thought it best not to stir up war against the Romans at that time. Thus Georgius was received into the palace by the Babylonian king, and since he found the situation at that time favourable, he persuaded the barbarian not to break the terms of the peace. In this way Chosroes, willing or unwilling, embraced the peace. The envoy then reported to the Emperor, fully and at length, everything that had happened and how it had happened, though not without some ill effect on the matter. For Georgius said that Chosroes had spoken these words to the king: "The King of the Persians has addressed his subjects: I am not making war because of the envoy's merit." When the Emperor heard this, he became angry with the envoy, and that embassy turned out very dangerously for Georgius.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: QUOD Phocas Lilium electum tyrannicæ proclamationis nuncium, cum muneribus regiis ad Chosroen ablegauit. unde Chosroes à tyrannide præsumpto belli argumento mundi illam universalem pernicem clanxit tubam, quæ utrinq; fregit & Romanorum & Persarum fortunas. ita quidem, prætexente Chosroe se Mauricij memoriæ asserturum exsequias & iusta, Persicum bellum est exortum. Lilius verò satis asperè tractatus apud Persas remansit.
units.tr: Phocas sent Lilius, who had been chosen as the announcer of his tyrannical proclamation, to Chosroes with royal gifts. From this, Chosroes, taking the tyranny as an occasion for war, sounded that trumpet of universal destruction of the world, which broke the fortunes of both the Romans and the Persians. Thus the Persian war arose, Chosroes pretending that he would avenge the memory of Maurice and see to his funeral rites. Lilius, however, was treated quite harshly and remained among the Persians.

units.la: DE LEGATIS GENTIVM AD ROMANOS.
units.tr: ON THE ENVOYS OF THE NATIONS TO THE ROMANS.

units.la: Ex Historia. THEOPHYLACTI EX PRÆFE- CTI ET SCRIPTURARII
units.tr: From the History. THEOPHYLACT, FORMER PREFECT AND SCRIPTURARIUS

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: QUOD Philippici generi Mauricij ductu ex regia urbe protectus Amidam venit. Legatione mittunt Persæ ut certis quippe conditionibus deponeretur bellum: petierunt namque à Romanis, ut pecunia pacem emerent, Mcbode[?] satrapa ad ducem ablegato. Venit ergò ad Romanos Mebodes, Persa, ac Imperator exercitus concione coacta, ad ipsum audiendum, ordinem ductores, ac tribunos, & auxiliares, reliquosque inter milites illustriores convocat, qua colleƈta concione, Persa in hæc verba orsus est:
units.tr: Philippicus, the son-in-law of Maurice, led his army out from the royal city and came to Amida. The Persians sent an embassy, since they wished the war to be laid down on certain terms: they asked the Romans to buy peace with money, and sent the satrap Mebodes to the general. So Mebodes the Persian came to the Romans, and the emperor called an assembly of the army to hear him. He summoned the commanders, the tribunes, the auxiliaries and the other more distinguished soldiers. When the assembly had gathered, the Persian began with these words:

units.la: CONCIO.
units.tr: SPEECH.

units.la: Viri bellicosi, ne vero vos percutiat audientes hoc Legati procemium. Si enim sententias mutaveritis, mutabo & ego denunciationem: Excolite pacem deposito bello, hastæque & gladius ut antiquata valeant, & pro militia capite sistulam lene simul & pastorale canentem melos; Persarum rex amans pacis est, cultu ornatur aptiore, non ornamentis bellicis. Regia enim est pacis placiditas, sicuti tyrannorum propria Discordia. Viri qui estis eodem modo nobiscum affecti, relinquatur bellum solum omnibus rebus inexplebile. Sanguine terram polluimus, sæpè mortem vidimus, mortem cuius pictor est bellum, ego vero dico etiam archetypum, & humanorum malorum autor & magister per se & naturâ suâ. Pecuniam amat aliquis, sed opibus & paupertate ludimur, aliquando victi, vincentes aliquando, & iaƈtati simul cum belli fortuna ancipiti, perpetuam quasi volutationem patimur. Superbit alius auro principum, cum voluptate possidet perfidiam, quid enim in bello magis est perfidum pecunia? absq; discrimine defertur ab illo ad alium, & ab alio rursus ad alium, quasi si evigilans somnium, quod somnia veris, videas, aut die crastino crapulæ memineris hesternæ. Vos olim, ô Romani libertatem fecistis bello, vos etiam pacis, estote discipuli, annunciantibus vobis Persis, vt lachrymosum bellum excutiatis. Qui enim primò peccant, illos etiam correctionis decet pœnitentia. Ne putetis confidentiam esse hanc meam tam humanam orationem. Cum enim nullius indigeat Persarum rex, heri forte vel nudius tertius, quando suam terram ausus est calcare Romanus exercitus, prælio congredi renuit. Auro enim multo, donisque lautis emere Romanos pacem iubet, nec sane pro pœna bellum imponere peccantibus fas est: quia multa pecuniaria & Persi-cum animum placare, & ferociâ Romanorum bellica expletam tuba, non nequit comprimere. Cùm orationem adhuc extenderet legatus adversa om-nium contra cum exsibilantium tollebantur sufragia, clamore insuper ingenti, quasi graviter serentium orationem barbari. Elatis enim videbantur esse animis, propter illas quas primum experti fuerant res prosperas, quum & Persarum disturbarunt ordines, & prædis spoliisq; potiti Cardarigam circumuenerunt. Dimissâ verò ab Imperatore concione, Persa dicendi finem fecit: nec multis post diebus Nisibidis antistes honore sacerdotali præfulgens, ad ducem abiit, eademque Metodis verba in medium proponit: quæ cum dux per tabellarium ad regem scripsisset, agnito Imperatoris sigillo ducis edicto, statim facto, Philippicum iussit impurissimas has inducias thissum facere, tanquam obstante Romana magnanimitate. Duxigitur Imperatoris tabellis conuolutis, propè Mambrathona tendit, & sic quidem bellum inualuit.
units.tr: Warlike men, let not this envoy's preamble strike you as you listen. If you change your opinions, I too will change my announcement. Cultivate peace, lay down war, and let spears and swords be discarded as obsolete; take up instead the soft and pastoral tune of the pipe. The king of the Persians loves peace and is adorned with a more fitting dress, not with the trappings of war. For the calm of peace is royal, while discord is the proper mark of tyrants. You men, who are affected in the same way as we are, let war alone be left behind, a thing that can never be satisfied by anything. We have polluted the earth with blood, and have often seen death, a death of which war is the painter. I call war the archetype itself, the author and teacher of human evils, by its very nature. Someone loves money, but we are mocked by both wealth and poverty, sometimes conquered, sometimes conquering, and tossed about together with the uncertain fortune of war, we suffer a kind of endless rolling. Another is puffed up with the gold of princes, and rejoices to possess treachery. For what in war is more treacherous than money? Without any risk it is passed from one man to another, and from that man again to another, like a dream one sees on waking, or like the drunkenness of yesterday one remembers on the following day. You Romans once won your liberty by war; now, too, win peace. Be disciples, while we Persians announce it to you, so that you may shake off this tearful war. For those who first sinned ought also to repent when corrected. Do not think that this speech of mine is a confidence so humane in tone. Since the king of the Persians needs nothing from anyone, he refused to join battle the day before yesterday, or perhaps three days ago, when the Roman army dared to tread on his land. Instead he bids the Romans buy peace with much gold and lavish gifts; indeed it is not right to impose war as a punishment on those who have sinned, since a large sum of money can both appease the Persian spirit and restrain the warlike ferocity of the Romans, which is not able to be satisfied by the trumpet. While he was still extending his speech, the legate was hissed by everyone opposed to him, and loud shouts rose up, as though the barbarians were taking the speech badly. For their spirits seemed elevated because of the prosperous successes they had first experienced, when they had broken the ranks of the Persians and, having seized plunder and spoils, had surrounded Cardariga. When the assembly was dismissed by the emperor, the Persian made an end of speaking. Not many days later the bishop of Nisibis, shining with sacerdotal honour, went to the general and set forth the same words to him. When the general had written them to the king by courier, the king, recognising the emperor's seal on the general's edict, at once ordered Philippicus to make these most filthy truces void, as though the Roman magnanimity stood in the way. So, with the emperor's letters rolled up, he made for a point near Mambrathona, and in this way the war flared up.

units.la: II.
units.tr: II.

units.la: Qvod Chosroes milite suo fuso, seditionem veritus, proposuit sibi de pace conferre cum Tiberio Cæsare, de qua re consultus Cæsar conditionem decreuit accipere. Mittit igitur, qui de pacificatione colloquerentur, viros ad eam rem idoneos, legatis lectis Ioanne & Petro summa apud Senatum dignitate, vtroque patricio, ac Theodoro Magiftri, vt vocant Latini, præfectura condecorato. Chosroes etiam Sarnachosganem virum in Perfica politia ob dignitatem spectatum, cum aliis viris dignissimis, bello per illos pausam facturus. Sed circa illud forte tempus in Armenia ingenti pugna commissa inter Parthos & Romanos, Tamchosroe ducente copias Babylonicas, Iustiniano Romanas, cum reliçti aliquanto plus fuissent à pristina illa strenuitate Romani, pacis conditiones Medi fuftulerunt, iterumque bellum iis incendentibus exarfit, cum super successu isto nupero non possent sibi moderari. Itaque Legati verbis tenus perfecto proposito, intermissaq; pace domum redire.
units.tr: When Chosroes had lost his soldiers and feared a mutiny, he resolved to confer with Tiberius Caesar about peace. The Caesar, consulted on the matter, decided to accept the terms. So he sent men fit for the business to discuss the pacification: the envoys John and Peter, both patricians of the highest dignity in the Senate, and Theodore, decorated with the office of Magister, as the Latins call it. Chosroes too sent Sarnachosganes, a man esteemed in the Persian polity for his rank, together with other most worthy men, so that through them he might bring about a pause in the war. But about that time a great battle was joined in Armenia between the Parthians and the Romans, Tamchosroes leading the Babylonian forces and Justinian the Roman. Since the Romans had fallen somewhat short of their former vigour, the Medes broke the conditions of peace, and the war flared up again, as they were inflamed by that recent success and could not restrain themselves. Thus the envoys, having achieved their proposal only in words, and peace having been dropped, returned home.

units.la: III.
units.tr: III.

units.la: Qvod Chosroes deiectus & fugatus à Baramo, regnoq; eiectus, & infra decimum lapidem à Circensio sub die in agro metatus nuncium amandauit, aduentum significans, fortunasq; recentes, & refugium ad Cæsarem commeatuque domum postulato, auxilia à Romanis expeti. Tertia vero vi-gilia filia[?] noctis nuncij ad portas aduenerunt, qui cum de quibus causis venirent, edocti effent portæ cuftodes, ad præfectum celeriter vbi mittunt, ij quorum portarum erat custodia, præfectoque tam insperatæ festinationis causam exponunt. Præsidiaris tum cohortis præfecto nomen erat Probo, quare Probus de mane intromissum in vrbem Chosroem, humaniter & beneuole excepit, in mulieribus item eius, fubrumos puerulos gestantibus nimis quam maxima humanitate vsus, defensoribus quoque & stipatoribus, quorum triginta forte erant Chosroi, bona multa fecit valdè amicè.
units.tr: When Chosroes was overthrown and put to flight by Bahram, driven from his kingdom, and had pitched camp under the open sky less than ten miles from Circesium, he sent a messenger announcing his arrival and his recent misfortunes, seeking refuge with the Caesar and asking for provisions for the journey home, and that help be sought from the Romans. In the third watch of the night the messengers came to the gates. When the guards of the gates had learned why they had come, they quickly sent word to the prefect, and those in charge of the gates explained to the prefect the reason for such unexpected haste. The commander of the garrison cohort was named Probus. So Probus, in the morning, received Chosroes into the city kindly and courteously. He showed the greatest humanity to his women, who carried small children, and to his defenders and attendants, of whom Chosroes had about thirty; he did many good things for them, very kindly.

units.la: altera die Probum quæsiuit Chosroes per litteras mittens ad Cæsarem, & cum exaraffet Sigillum regium per Probum ad Imperatorem dedit. Posteriori verò die Comentiolum ducem Hierapoli comorantem, certiorem fecit de præfentia Chosrois, missis ad eum simul, quæ Chosroes cum honore dignitatéque ad Cæsarem perscripsêrat. Comentiolus quæ sibi significata erant Hierapoli à Probo, per celeres cursorum ad Cæsarem curauit perserenda, quibus Imperator Mauricius auditis, fubrifit, & de meliori sibi spe gratulatus, detractisque signis Perficis, ea etiam quæ intus exarata erant, legere sategit & cognoscere. Dignitas verò Persæ, qua regem appellabat, in his erat maximè. Alloquij enim opponam legationem non fucatam verbis, vt ruditate orationis mentem dignitatis exhibitæ non fictam inspiciamus.
units.tr: On the next day Chosroes sought Probus, sending a letter to the Caesar. When he had written it, he gave the royal seal to the Emperor through Probus. On the following day he informed Comentiolus, who was staying at Hierapolis, of Chosroes' presence, and at the same time sent him what Chosroes had written to the Caesar with honour and dignity. Comentiolus had the information that Probus had given him at Hierapolis forwarded to the Caesar by swift couriers. When the Emperor Maurice heard it, he smiled, and rejoicing at a better hope, he removed the Persian seals and strove to read and understand also what was written inside. The dignity of the Persian, by which he called himself king, was especially evident in these words. For I shall set out the embassy, not disguised with flattering words, so that we may look at the mind of the dignity displayed, unfeigned in its rough style.

units.la: Chosroes Persarum rex, regi Romanorum illuftriffimo, Felici, pacifico, potenti, libertatis vindici, tyrannidis ofori, moderato, iusto, iniuriatorum protectori, beneficio illatorum non memori, Salutem.
units.tr: Chosroes, king of the Persians, to the most illustrious king of the Romans, the fortunate, peaceful, powerful, avenger of liberty, punisher of tyranny, moderate, just, protector of the wronged, forgetful of injuries inflicted: greetings.

units.la: Duobus quasi oculis mundum illustrari totum olim iam & à principio curauit Deus, hoc est potentissimo Romanorum Imperio, ac prudentissimè constitutis sceptris Persicæ Reipublicæ. His n. maximis Imperiis efferæ & bellicosæ gentes comprimuntur, reliquiq; homines exornantur, & prorsus gubernantur: quarum rerum cum dictis nostris est videre conuenientè consequentiam. Quoniam verò & aliqui mali in mundo circumcuntes dæmones, omnia quæ à Deo pulcherrimè ordinata sunt, auent quidem confundere, ne succedant eorum conatus, decet amatos Deo & piissimos viros restere, vt qui habeant à Deo sapientiæ thesaurum, & iustitiæ bracchium & arma. His igitur circiter temporibus nocentissimi dæmones contra Persarum surrecti Rempublicam, peffimis quibusque perpetratis, & seruos contra dominos armarunt contra regnum famulos, contra ordinem disturbationem, contra decorum indecorum, & omnia quæ contrariafunt bonis, produxerunt. Baramus enim detestandus ille seruus, à nostris maioribus prouectus, in hanc honoris lucem elatus, nec potens tantæ gloriæ magnitudinis, ad perniciem delapsus est, & regnum sibi promittens omnem turbavit Persarum Remp. & omnia facit & allaborat, vt magnum extinguat oculum potestatis, vnde capiant gentes feræ & iniquæ libertatem & potentiam grassandi aducrsus manifestissimum Persarum Imperium: nec hoc solum, sed etiam procedente posthac tempore contra vobis tributarias vires, quæ coerceri non
units.tr: God long ago, and from the beginning, arranged that the whole world should be illuminated by two eyes, that is, by the most powerful empire of the Romans and by the sceptre of the Persian commonwealth, most wisely established. For by these great empires the savage and warlike nations are restrained, the rest of mankind is adorned and altogether governed; and one can see a fitting consequence of these things with what we have said. But since some evil demons wander about the world and desire indeed to confound all that God has most beautifully ordained, lest their attempts succeed, it is fitting that God's beloved and most pious men should resist, since they have from God the treasure of wisdom, and the arm and the weapons of justice. About this time, then, the most harmful demons rose up against the commonwealth of the Persians; having carried out every wickedness, they armed slaves against masters, servants against the kingdom, disorder against order, the indecent against the decent, and produced everything that is contrary to good. For that detestable slave Bahram, promoted by our ancestors and raised to this light of honour, not equal to the magnitude of so great a glory, fell into ruin; and promising himself a kingdom, he has thrown the whole Persian commonwealth into confusion, and does and labours at everything so as to extinguish the great eye of our power. Thence wild and unjust nations may take the liberty and the power to rage against the manifest empire of the Persians; and not only this, but also, as time goes on, against forces that pay tribute to you, which cannot be restrained [illegible, ~6 letters] and will be most destructive. It is therefore fitting that you, the peaceful one, in accordance with your foresight, should apply a saving hand to a kingdom that has been attacked and violated by tyrants, and should contribute your effort to this, so that the beginning of this empire may be destroyed, and, as it were, general trophies of common safety may be raised.

units.la: [illegible, ~6 letters] non poterunt, & maximè perniciosas. Decet igitur pacificum pro vestra prouidétia, infestato regno & à tyrannis violato adhibere manum salutarem, &c. in hoc conferre vestram operam, ut Imperium incipiens destruatur, & salutis communis quasi tropaea generalia in Romanorum republica figere, &c. vos proclamare Conditores, & Scruatores, & Medicos adfliétæ Pérsarum Reipublicæ liceat. Omnia enim quæ iusta sunt, à potentissimis regibus expediri omninò conuenit, & inde sibi fortitudinis encomia, & gloriam post mortem non abolendam, comparare ac ita exemplo esse, quod non debeant armaferre ferui contra dominos. Varietatem igitur Persicarum in politia rerum ex officio véstro; est gubernare. Splendidius enim inde quoque pernos Romanorum fiet nomen. Hæc ego Chosroes, ut qui præfens adsim, per epistolam alloquor. Chosroes tuus filius & famulus. Non enim propter fortunam eorum quæ euenerunt, afpernaberis aptum hoc conditioni utriusque nostrûm nomen. Datores bonorum Angeli Dei regnum veftrum sospitent & conferuent, ne & ei aliquando, aut opprobrium, aut tyrannis illudere possit.
units.tr: ...cannot be restrained, and are most destructive. It is therefore fitting, in your foresight as a man of peace, that you lend a saving hand to a kingdom that has been attacked and violated by tyrants, etc.; that you devote your effort to this, so that the empire which has begun to rise may be destroyed, and that you set up, as it were, general trophies of common safety in the Roman commonwealth, etc.; that it may be permitted to you to be proclaimed founders, preservers and physicians of the afflicted Persian commonwealth. For it is entirely fitting that everything that is just be carried out by the most powerful kings, and that they thereby win for themselves praise for courage and a glory not to be abolished after death, and become such an example that slaves ought not to take up arms against their masters. It is therefore your duty to govern the variety of Persian affairs in their polity; for the name of the Romans will thereby become more splendid also among the nations. These things I, Chosroes, speak to you by letter, as one who is present. Chosroes, your son and servant. For you will not, on account of the fortune of what has happened, disdain this name, which suits the condition of both of us. May the Angels of God, givers of good things, keep and preserve your kingdom, lest at any time it be exposed either to reproach or to mockery by a tyrant.

units.la: IV.
units.tr: IV.

units.la: Quod Chosroes impetrata petitione per Legatos ad Mauricium missos, ad vrbem Hierapolim dictam venit: nec sanè dux Comentiolus non est. non honorariis muneribus profequutus eum, quidum carebat regno. Sic enim visum est Mauricio, & ut visum est, ita quoq; procuratum est. In regione itaq; sic dicta [?]Bedamas, obuiam factus Chosroi Comentiolus regio illum donatum apparatu, magnifico prorsus satellitio comitatuque produxit. Nona vero etiam die nuncium ad præsidia Persica Martyropolim misit Chosroes hominem dignitate Satrapam, nomine Miragdum, significans simul & recentem fortunarum statum, & Imperatoris cam magnanimitatem, quam tota urbs etiam si refertissima non possit capere, quippe quæ immunes belli, in amicitiam recepti essent Persæ. Bestamum etiam illustrem apud Persas virum Adrabiganum in Armeniam amandavit, ut & urbem, & qui ibidem commorarentur Persas Imperio Cæsarisubiiceret, & hæc quidem manifesto. Ut vero vafer factus, & nihil non dolis & fraudibus postposuit, hospitalitatis iure violato, ac infinita ista benevolentia pedibus calcata, quintum nuncium ab legavit ad Chaldæos habitantes Martyropoli, néve quid præsidiis deesset, néve iis, quæ palam egisset, apponerent animum. Occasione igitur reditus sibi facta in regnum ad Imperatorem Romanorum venire instituit. Quare Mauricius cum rescisseret huius desiderium, literis regiis ne se adiret vetuit, contemnens Imperator gloriam, & in Chosrois simul utilitate & commodo allaborans. Putavit enim non amplius illi procedendum esse ad Persarum Rempublicam, neita à Baramo occupatæ tyrannidi invalescendi subministraretur argumentum. Primo autem vere Chosroes ad Regem mittit, tertiaque die convocata ab Imperatore concione[?], cum honore ingenti adoratur à legatis. Itaque Silentio indicto Senatui, ac libertate Persis ab Imperatore facta, ea quæ haberent exponendi, primarius inter legatos profusis lacrymis, ac inde captata Imperatoris miseratione, in eiusmodi verba dixit.
units.tr: When Chosroes, having obtained his petition through envoys sent to Maurice, came to the city called Hierapolis, the general Comentiolus did not fail to honour him with gifts, though he lacked a kingdom. For so it seemed good to Maurice, and as it seemed good, so it was also carried out. Therefore, in the region called Bedamas, Comentiolus met Chosroes and escorted him with royal equipage, a truly magnificent bodyguard and retinue. But on the ninth day Chosroes sent a messenger to the Persian garrisons at Martyropolis, a man of satrapal rank named Miragdes, announcing at the same time both the recent change in his fortunes and the emperor's magnanimity, which the whole city could not hold even if it were very crowded, since the Persians, freed from war, had been received into friendship. He also sent Bestamus, a Persian man of distinction, and Adrabiganus into Armenia, so that they might subject both the city and the Persians dwelling there to the empire of Caesar; and these things he did openly. But, growing crafty and putting nothing ahead of tricks and frauds, he violated the right of hospitality and trampled underfoot that boundless goodwill. He sent a fifth messenger to the Chaldeans living in Martyropolis, lest the garrisons lack anything, and lest they should pay heed to what he had done openly. Therefore, the opportunity of returning to his kingdom having been given to him, he resolved to come to the Roman emperor. When Maurice learned of this desire, he forbade him by royal letter to approach, the emperor disregarding glory and working for the advantage and convenience of Chosroes at the same time. For he thought that Chosroes should no longer proceed into the Persian commonwealth, lest an argument be supplied for strengthening the tyranny seized by Bahram. But at the first spring Chosroes sent to the king, and on the third day, after an assembly was called by the emperor, he was greeted with great honour by the envoys. Thus, silence having been ordered for the Senate, and freedom to speak granted by the emperor, the chief of the envoys, pouring forth tears and thereby winning the emperor's pity, spoke in words of this kind.

units.la: Quære in de Concione.
units.tr: Look for this in the speech.

units.la: Collatis utrinque vero multis, & his ita à legatis dictis, ac petitione facundia sermonis extorquente, ut quæ proponeret probarentur ac Placerent, à Senatu simul & ab Imperatore decretum est, ut Chosroi Romani opitularentur, Baramoqúe[?] ad nixo studio bellum facerent. quippe cum indignũ Latino iudicaret Imperator Imperio, si non præuaricato res contra arma sumeret, periclitaretúrque potius rei nō honestæ gratia propter promissi magnitudinem, ac Romani contracta ignominia non obliviscendis in æternum opprobriis passim diffamarentur. Decreti igitur huius adhuc eadem die per urbem regiam sententia pronunciatur & & promulgatur. Quinti vero hi legati admissi ad Cæsarem, donisq; ornati regiis, litteris inscriptam regis sententiam secum ferunt. Præterea Saramen & Chosroperozen, aliosque jam ante belli tempore ab Romanis captos ad Chosroen Imperator una cum legatis remisit. At Chosroes regiis lectis litteris, miratus istam Romanorum virtutem, relicta Hierapoli, simul cum Comentiolo ad urbem devenit Constantinam. nec multò post antistes Melitinæ Domitianus, iussu regis ad Chosroen venit, qui Domitianus cognatus erat Imperatoris, prosessione sacerdos, præstanti vitæ sanctimonia, oratione placidus, ad negotia conficienda folers, consilio sapientissimo. Adiunctus illi ibat Gregorius Antiochenæ præses Ecclesiæ. Nam & hoc volebat rex, & quemadmodum voluit, ita factum est. Cum ergo sacerdos uterq; Constantinæ effet, sermonibus ac muneribus delinientes, melioris spei desolato spem fecerunt. Quare Chosroes per Nisibin missis Legatis, Persis in memoriam vocat beneficiorum in stirpem regiam admonitis unâ concionis suæ auditoribus, quòd tyranno nec faciendum sit, nec confringendæ leges veteres, ac patriæ, quæ tot indeiam annis in Persarum sint observatæ Republica, quodque nequaquam à rerum nouarum molitionibus turpitudo abssit, & ignominia.
units.tr: After many had been brought forward on both sides, and these things had been said by the envoys, and their petition, drawing out the power of eloquence, had won approval for what they proposed, it was decreed by the Senate and the emperor together that the Romans should aid Chosroes and make war on Bahram with all zeal. For the emperor judged it unworthy of the Roman empire, if he did not take up arms in this matter without prevarication, and that it was better to run the risk, for the sake of a not honourable cause, on account of the magnitude of the promise, than for the Romans, having incurred disgrace, to be spread abroad with reproaches that would never be forgotten. Therefore the sentence of this decree was announced and published throughout the royal city that same day. Moreover, these envoys, admitted to Caesar and adorned with royal gifts, carried back with them the king's decision inscribed in letters. Besides, the emperor sent back Sarames and Chosroeperozes, and others already captured by the Romans in the war, to Chosroes together with the envoys. But Chosroes, having read the royal letters and marvelling at that Roman virtue, left Hierapolis and came with Comentiolus to the city of Constantina. Not long after, Domitian, bishop of Melitene, came to Chosroes by the king's command. Domitian was a kinsman of the emperor, a priest by profession, of outstanding sanctity of life, gentle in speech, skilful in carrying out business, and of most wise counsel. Gregory, president of the church of Antioch, went with him. For the king wished this too, and as he wished, so it was done. Therefore, when both priests were at Constantina, they soothed him with their discourses and gifts, and made hope to one who was in despair into a better hope. Wherefore Chosroes sent envoys through Nisibis, calling to the Persians' memory the benefits bestowed on the royal line, and reminding the hearers of his assembly that one must neither obey a tyrant nor break the ancient and ancestral laws, which have been observed for so many years in the Persian commonwealth; and that shame and disgrace are by no means absent from the undertaking of new revolutions.

units.la: V.
units.tr: V.

units.la: Quod ubi Baramo primum innotuit, de conseruato Chosroe, humaniterq; à Romanis excepto, legatos misit, cauens Imperatori, ne Chosroe quaquam fortunis subueniret, pactus ideò & urbem Nisibin Romanis se daturum, & loca usq; fluvium Trigidem. Sed quoniam non ille Baram erat, qui nomen regium extingueret, frustra tum fuit.
units.tr: When Bahram first learned that Chosroes had been preserved and had been received kindly by the Romans, he sent envoys, warning the emperor by no means to come to Chosroes' aid in his fortunes. He therefore promised that he would give the Romans the city of Nisibis, and the lands as far as the river Tigris. But since he was not the Bahram who would extinguish the royal name, it was in vain.

units.la: VI.
units.tr: VI.

units.la: Quod re contra Baramum bene feliciterq; gesta, Chosroes ad Mauricium principes aliquot è comitatu suo misit, & eorum quæ evenerant exposita fortuna, petiit ut auxilio misso metum sibi demeret, opitularetúrque quàm citissimè. affirmabant etiam Legati si pecuniæ copiam Imperator faceret Chosroi, refusurum eam Romanis quam primum suum recuperaret regnum. Romanorum autem rex, præterquam quòd armis coniunctis ferebat opem, maximam quoque ei pecuniæ summam est largitus, ac ita Chosroes relicta Imperatori Syngrapha, ingentem pecuniarum vim rea portauit, quam deinde diribitam Perficis suis copiis distribuit.
units.tr: When the matter had gone well and fortunately against Bahram, Chosroes sent several leading men of his retinue to Maurice, and having set out the state of his fortunes, he asked that by sending aid they might remove his fear and bring him help as quickly as possible. The envoys also affirmed that if the emperor granted Chosroes a supply of money, he would repay it to the Romans as soon as he recovered his kingdom. The Roman emperor, besides bringing help with joined arms, also gave him a very large sum of money; and so Chosroes, leaving a written bond with the emperor, carried away a great quantity of money, which he afterwards distributed among his Persian troops.

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: QVOD non longè post Saramen ad regem Mandauit Chosroes, orans Cæsarem, vt ducatu Commentiolum deponeret, vt qui contumeliosus esset, & sub prætextu auxilij afferre detrimentum. cumque Sarames fecundam quod iustus erat appulsus Byzantium, Legationem Imperatori exposuisset, Comentiolo ab officio ducis depositum aditum in Persidem ademit Imperator, Narsique, qui ducis erat armiger, ducatum dedit. Sexta vero die Mauritius cingulum variegatum gemmis, & tiaram regiam, lectulosque & mensas aureas Daras misit ad Chosroen & instructa in ipsius gratiam regia pompa ex suis doryphoris, magnificè donauit, vt ne destitutum apparatu regio Romani Persæque aspernarentur. Cinctus est igitur Chosroes vndique satellitio regio, quanto apud Romanos sceptra regia observari obtinet. ac ita videntes Medi quibus vi-ribus ab Imperatore circumdatus sit Chosroes, relicta tyrannide transiuerunt ad partes Chosroes. & Barami quidem resindies debilitatæ sunt, Chosroi vero secundum animi sententiam, accrescentibus eo modo viribus, successere. quapropter etiam decreuit aliquod Chosros Mauricio beneficium referre, literisque regiis Mauricij Imperio pro muncre obligat vrbem Daras, Delauzam quoq; Satrapam, virum spectatum Byzantium mittit, qui ferret claues opidi, & cum clauibus quod literis continebatur munus. tradidit itaque cum esset in urbe regia legatus Romanis urbem, & ad colloquium Imperatoris admissus est. Mauricius autem, cum donasset hominem regalibus munereque, eorum quoque quæante pepigerat firmauit fidem, Chosroe ad eam rem nominato Filio.
units.tr: Not long after, Chosroes sent Sarames to the emperor, begging Caesar to remove Comentiolus from his command, since he was insolent and, under the pretext of aid, was doing harm. When Sarames, having arrived at Byzantium for the second time, as was just, had set out his embassy to the emperor, the emperor removed Comentiolus from the office of general, took away his access to Persia, and gave the command to Narses, who had been the general's armour-bearer. On the sixth day Maurice sent to Daras for Chosroes a girdle variegated with gems, a royal tiara, and couches and golden tables, and generously gave him, with royal pomp arranged for his benefit, some of his own bodyguards, so that the Romans and Persians would not despise him as lacking royal equipage. Chosroes was therefore surrounded on every side by a royal bodyguard, as much as royal sceptres are kept in honour among the Romans. And so the Medes, seeing with what forces Chosroes was surrounded by the emperor, abandoned the tyranny and went over to Chosroes' side; and the forces of Bahram were indeed weakened, while Chosroes succeeded according to his mind, his strength growing in that way. Therefore Chosroes also decided to repay Maurice with a benefit, and by royal letters bound the city of Daras to the empire of Maurice as a gift. He also sent Delauzas, a satrap, a distinguished man, to Byzantium, to carry the keys of the town and, with the keys, the gift contained in the letters. Accordingly, while he was in the royal city as envoy, he handed the city over to the Romans and was admitted to an audience with the emperor. Maurice, having presented the man with royal gifts, also confirmed the faith of those agreements which he had made, naming Chosroes' son for that purpose.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Quod Veritus Chosroes, ne quis clam percussor à subditis sibi substitueretur, rogauit Mauricium, vt ad custodiam corporis mille suorum sibi militum daret. Romanus autem rex custodes corporis Chosroi misit.
units.tr: Because Chosroes feared that some assassin might be set against him secretly by his own subjects, he asked Maurice to give him a thousand of his soldiers as a bodyguard. The Roman emperor, however, sent bodyguards to Chosroes.

units.la: IX.
units.tr: IX.

units.la: Quod Mauricius ad Septimum vsque qui ita dicitur locus, peruenit, quoniam Hunnos educi audiuerat, certiórq; factus de Dalaurę Persę ad se aduentum recurrit ad urbem regiam, compositaque, vt par erat, legatione, propositum rursus abitum promouit.
units.tr: Because Maurice came as far as the place called Septimum, having heard that the Huns were being led out, and was informed of the approach of the Persian Dalaurus towards him, he turned back to the royal city. There he arranged an embassy as was fitting, and then put off again his intended departure.

units.la: X.
units.tr: X.

units.la: Quod dietertia legati ab urbe regia missi sunt, petente senatu ab Imperatore vt rediret. Cui is legationi obsecundans, cum legatis rediit.
units.tr: Because on the third day ambassadors were sent from the royal city, the senate having asked the emperor to return. He, yielding to this embassy, went back with the envoys.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Quod ad Anchialum metatus vallum, ibidemq; perquindecim dies moratus Mauricius, cum venire audiuisset à Persarum rege legatos Byzantium, in vrbem rediit regiam. Tertia verò post die Celtiberiæ eodem quoq; Legati veniunt. Legatis nomina erant Bofo ac Betto, quos princeps gentis (Franci hi recentiore lingua vocantur. at illi nomen Theodoricho) ad Imperatorem misit, promisitq;, sc,si[?] vectigalia sibi darentur, opitulaturum Romanis, ac pro muneribus cum Chagano gesturum bellum. Imperator tamen muneratus legatos, si sua auxilia subpeditarent Franci, vt id gratis facerent iussit, nequaquam emi passus à Romanis opem barbarorum. Interim Chaganus ad priora pacta additamentum ab Imperatore flagitat, in qua re barbarus non auditus, statim restaurauit bellum.
units.tr: Because Maurice, having pitched camp at the rampart near Anchialus and remained there fifteen days, heard that ambassadors from the Persian king were coming to Byzantium, and so returned to the royal city. But on the third day after, ambassadors from Celtiberia also arrived. The envoys' names were Bofo and Betto, whom the leader of their people (these are called Franks in more recent speech; his name was Theodoric) had sent to the emperor. He promised that if tribute were given to him, he would help the Romans and wage war on the Chagan in return for the gifts. The emperor, however, rewarded the envoys and ordered that, if the Franks supplied their aid, they should do so for nothing, by no means allowing the Romans to buy the help of barbarians. Meanwhile the Chagan demanded an addition to the earlier agreements from the emperor. Since the barbarian was not heard in this matter, he at once renewed the war.

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Qvod Priscus quindecim valla metatus, traiecto Istro fluuio, quarta die superiores Nobas venit. quod cum rescisceret Chaganus, ad Priscum legatos misit, causamque scire voluit aduentus Romanorum. Respondit dux, ad venationem & aequitatum esse loca idonea, & aquosa satis: cui Chaganus ostendit alienam terram calcare Romanos, citraque pactum agere Priscum, & aperte pacem ab eo conuelli. Respondet Priicus[?], Romanum quoque tu subis solum. Chaganus, armis, inquit, & iure belli. Romanos hoc amisisse. Chagano amplius rixante & disceptante de his locis, Priscum fugam ex oriente exprobrasse dicunt Chagano. Instante namque aestate Chaganus, qui laudibus, à Turcis in oriente celebratur, legatos miserat ad Mauricium Imperatorem, eaque concinnata epistola exarauit epinicia: REGI ROMANORVM CHAGANVS magnus dominus septemgentium, dominus climatum vniuersi:
units.tr: Because Priscus, having pitched fifteen camps and crossed the river Ister, came on the fourth day to the upper Nobae. When the Chagan learned this, he sent envoys to Priscus and wished to know the reason for the Romans' arrival. The commander replied that the place was suitable for hunting and sufficiently well watered. To this the Chagan pointed out that the Romans were treading foreign soil, that Priscus was acting without a treaty, and that he was openly breaking the peace. Priscus replied: "You too tread Roman soil." "By arms," said the Chagan, "and by the law of war. The Romans have lost this." As the Chagan went on quarrelling and disputing at greater length about these places, they say Priscus reproached the Chagan with flight from the east. For as summer drew near, the Chagan, who is celebrated with praises by the Turks in the east, had sent envoys to the emperor Maurice, and having composed a letter he wrote out a boastful announcement of victory: TO THE KING OF THE ROMANS, THE CHAGAN, great lord of seven hundred, lord of all the climates:

units.la: XIII.
units.tr: XIII.

units.la: Quod incipiente vere, instante maxima temporum festiuitate, qua passionem simul & resurrectionem Dei seruatoris solent celebrare, faméq; Romanos premente, insperato quodam siue casu, siue prouidentia Dei, Chaganus ad Romanos mittit fami impositurus finem, quam rei nouitatem in dubium primum traxit Priscus, nec ei confidit. Postquam vero securus factus, Romani inter se & barbari fecerunt ac susceperunt quinque dierum inducias, sublatoq; omni metu, Chaganus esurientibus Romanis ad frumentationem praebuit vehicula. Propterea tam inopinata ista barbarica humanitas ad nostra vsq; tempora est propagata. Quarta die Romanis copiis instructis ad vitam rebus necessariis, Legatos misit Chaganus, Indicas à Prisco petiturus merces, in qua re barbaro Priscus obsecundatus, & piper misit, & folium Indicum, casiamq;, & quae dicitur Costus. Hic vero acceptis Romanis muneribus, aromatibus delinitus, ad modum oblectatus est. Et sic à pugna abstinuit, donec Romanis publica illa ingens celebritas praeteriisset. Ob inuicem vero se cum[?] metati cessent, vtrinque tamen omnia erant secura. Finito deinde festo, nuncios Chaganus misit, sciungendarum à se mutuo copiarum.
units.tr: Because at the beginning of spring, with the greatest festival of the year at hand, on which they usually celebrate together the passion and resurrection of God the Saviour, and the Romans were pressed by famine, the Chagan sent to the Romans, by some unexpected chance or by the providence of God, to put an end to the famine. At first Priscus doubted this novelty and did not trust it. But after he became secure, the Romans and barbarians made and accepted a five-day truce, and with all fear removed, the Chagan provided wagons to the hungry Romans for carrying grain. Therefore this so unexpected barbarian kindness has been handed down to our own times. On the fourth day, when the Roman forces were supplied with the necessities of life, the Chagan sent envoys, about to ask Priscus for Indian wares. In this matter Priscus obliged the barbarian and sent him pepper, Indian leaf, cassia, and what is called costus. The Chagan, having received the Roman gifts, was delighted by the aromatics and gratified in like measure. And so he abstained from battle until that great public festivity of the Romans had passed. Although they ceased to encamp against each other, on both sides everything was secure. Then, when the festival was over, the Chagan sent messengers to arrange the separation of their forces from each other.

units.la: XIV.
units.tr: XIV.

units.la: Quod à quinta pugna, deuictus à Romanis Chaganus, antequam Imperatori aliquid de facto constaret, Legatos ad Mauricium misit de captiuis recipiendis: Erant ea millia septemdecim cum duducentis: Mauricius itaque minis barbari percuf-sus, orationeque circumuentus, per tabellarium Prisco mandauit, ut captiuos redderet Chagano Abaros. accita quidem a periculo liberi redduntur Chagano barbari.
units.tr: Because after the fifth battle, the Chagan, defeated by the Romans, before anything about the deed was certainly known to the emperor, sent envoys to Maurice about the recovery of the captives. There were seventeen thousand two hundred of them. Maurice, therefore, struck by the threats of the barbarian and won over by his speech, sent word by courier to Priscus that he should give back the captives to the Chagan of the Avars. Released from danger, the captives were restored free to the Chagan.

units.la: I.
units.tr: I.

units.la: Eth. Critias Plotino. I.
units.tr: Eth. Critias to Plotinus. I.

units.la: CIcada vocalis ineunte vere musicam suam auspicatur: vocalior vero canoriorque, & loquacioris naturæ auditur circa meridiem, quando expleta quasi est atque incensa radiis solaribus. Trinnit igitur hæc meloda, suggestus loca constituta arbore, agro Theatri; & viatoribus musicæ periculum proponit. Itaque & nos ad tuas virtutes canendas incendimur. Confouent enim aliquo modoex, &inflammant ad encomium: quia olim sepultos iam situ, tuis literis ad virtutem refuscitasti. ita, qui Critias eram, factus sum Plotinus, qui, vel extra corpus Philosophatur hic in terra, vel Philosophia corpus induta solidum cum hominibus, velut homo conuersatur.
units.tr: The cicada, a singing creature, begins its music at the start of spring. Its voice grows louder and clearer, and its chattering nature is heard more around midday, when it is, as it were, filled and kindled by the rays of the sun. So it trills its melody, having taken up its station on a tree in the field of the theatre, and it offers the danger of its music to travellers. So we too are kindled to sing your virtues. For they cherish and inflame us in some way to praise, since you have revived us, long buried in neglect, to virtue by your letters. Thus I, who was Critias, have become Plotinus, who either philosophises here on earth outside the body, or, clothed in philosophy as a solid body, lives among men as a man does.

units.la: Ruft. Dorcon. Moschoni. II.
units.tr: Rust. Dorcon to Moschus. II.

units.la: Ductor ouium admirandus mihi aries mortuus est; ac pastorali ducatu carent pecudes, ita malum quidem aliquod passus sum maximum: Videor enim mihi iratum esse Pana, neque eum aluearium primitiis honorauimus. quapropter ad vrbem iter facio, iratum deprecaturus, & simul ciuibus duritiem eius exponam, Propter placentam dicens,Pan gregis mci ducem fubftulit.
units.tr: The leader of my sheep, my admirable ram, is dead, and the flock lacks pastoral guidance. So I have suffered a very great misfortune. I seem to myself to have angered Pan, since we did not honour him with the first-fruits of the beehives. Therefore I am making my way to the city, to appease the angered god, and at the same time I will set out to the citizens his harshness, saying, on account of the cake: "Pan has taken away the leader of my flock."

units.tr: Love-letters. Theano to Eurydice, I–II.

units.la: Naturalis decor in te prateriit, & vicina rugis est facies. tu vero fingere veritatem niteris, suppofitis pigmentis amatores eludendo. Concede tempori anicula. neque enim speciosa stant floribus in senectute prata. memento & mortis,cui appropinquafti, & temperantiam ex necessitate instituas excolere. Eteniminiuria afficis & senectutem & iuuentam : quarum hanc dum simulas, ementita es; illam,dum habes interpolafti.
units.tr: Your natural beauty has passed away, and your face is close to wrinkles. Yet you strive to counterfeit the truth, deceiving your lovers with applied cosmetics. Give way to time, old woman. For meadows do not stand in flower in old age. Remember too the death you are approaching, and set yourself to cultivate self-control out of necessity. For you wrong both old age and youth: while you pretend to the one, you lie; the other, while you still have it, you adulterate.

units.la: Eth. EVAGORAS ANTIPATRO. IV.
units.tr: Ethical. EVAGORAS TO ANTIPATER. IV.

units.la: Terminos mundi opifex marino quoque æstuí constituit,& littoribus pelagius cohibetur fluctus: & arena quædam paruo interstitio continentem discriminat à mari. Neque enim conceflum est mari periculum aliquod inferre vicinæ terræ: sed recurritac reuoluitur in fe sua per furentia vestigia, magnam terræ minitans cluuionem. Terminos igitur & leges, ô Antipater,animo tuo pone, nec manum adbibeas ad iram. Et verò eodem modo cum manibus, modeste philosophiceque linguam instituere fummus,gradus est perfectæ virtutis.Sed fi non par fis huic moderandæ, quantiuis contumelis animum tuum oblecta, fi can.bus[?] adsimulari volueris latrantibus. Sic enim iratum quoque mare, iram vltra spumam & agitationem non producit.
units.tr: The Maker of the world set limits to the sea as well, and the waves of the deep are held in check by the shores. A thin strip of sand separates the land it borders from the sea. The sea has never been permitted to do any harm to the neighbouring land. Instead it runs back and rolls in upon itself through its raging footprints, threatening the land with great destruction. So, Antipater, set limits and rules for your mind, and do not raise your hand in anger. Indeed, to govern the tongue as modestly and philosophically as the hands is the highest step of perfect virtue. But if you are not equal to restraining it, let your spirit be entertained by however many insults you like, provided you choose to bark back at the barking dogs. For even an angry sea does not raise its rage beyond foam and agitation.

units.la: Rust. ÆGIRVS PLATANO. V.
units.tr: Rustic. AEGIRUS TO PLATO. V.

units.la: Malas vicinas habemus, ô amice, grues. bellum perpetuum gerunt circa hunc agrum. Nam neque cum ipsis patribus nostris rem habuerunt compositam,neq; nobiscum postillos rebellare intermittunt: licet eas primitiis è messe sæpenumero donaverimus. Sed & agelli partem quandam tanquam Deo sacram ingratis istis consecrauimus: quæ dona,ut videtur, nihilominus tamen non proficiunt. quare hinc omnes abmigremus. Saxa enim nobis utilius erit colere, quam campos & colles, ubi grues habeas vicinas.
units.tr: We have bad neighbours, my friend: the cranes. They wage perpetual war around this field. They never made peace with our fathers, and they do not stop rebelling against us. We have often given them the first-fruits of the harvest, yet they do not improve. We have also consecrated a part of our little field to God, as it were, for those ungrateful birds, and these gifts, it seems, are of no use to them. So let us all emigrate from here. It will be more useful for us to farm the rocks than the plains and hills where you have cranes for neighbours.

units.la: Amat. ERATO TERPSITHEÆ. VI.
units.tr: Amatory. ERATO TO TERPSITHEA. VI.

units.la: Aureum istum Callicraten imaginem tibi pinxisse dicunt. Pictura vero non Terpsithean exprimere arbitror, sed ad quam rem non ementitas Parrhatij tabulas appello, Lacedæmoniam Helenam. Dupliciter itaque peccasti contra artem, in quam contumeliosa es reperta, & contra naturam, quam fallis. Mentiri namq; artem coegisti Parrhasij, & quæ tibi non adsunt, per tabulas nihilominus deducere: tanquam si ita velles naturæ vitia fucare, plurimam eius inertiam arguens. Ego vero etiam pictorem laudo, ut qui tuæ informitatis pictor esse noluerit, & prudentiam naturæ sum mirata, quæ pessimæ animæ corporis decorem non concrediderit.
units.tr: They say that Callicrates has painted you as a golden image. But I do not think the picture expresses Terpsithea; rather, I call it, with no lie, the Spartan Helen of the paintings of Parrhasius. You have therefore sinned twice: against the art in which you have been found so insulting, and against nature, which you deceive. For you have forced the art of Parrhasius to lie, and to portray by means of pictures things that you do not possess, as if you wished in this way to disguise the defects of nature, thereby proving how thoroughly she is idle. As for me, I even praise the painter, since he refused to be the painter of your ugliness, and I admire the prudence of nature, which did not entrust the beauty of the body to a soul so wicked.

units.la: Eth. SOSIPATER TERPANDRO. VII.
units.tr: Ethical. SOSIPATER TO TERPANDER. VII.

units.la: Mos est æquabus, & ut mihi videtur in primis ille bonus. Namq; laudo in illis quod singulari quo-dam dam in fœtus amore pollent. Sed quis eis est mos? Lactentem adhuc equum, quum nutrice destitutum viderint, & longius alicubi abesse matrem, maternum aliquid faciunt, sicuti debet ea quæ pullum peperit (nec enim suæ ipsius naturæ obliuiscuntur) & æquo per omnia faciliq; animo foucnt reliƈtum, quemadmodum foucnt veros propriosque fœtus. Et hæ quidem à natura itafunt affeƈtæ. non enim Soloniscoguntleges. Transferam sermonem ad te. nepotem tuum despicis deianua commeantem ad ianuam,miserrima tunicula vestitum. Bruta certe tibi mens est magis, quam brutis. Canes alienos & externos nutris: itá enim verius dicentur, qui tecum conuersantur adulatorcs, nam optimè tibi velle videbuntur, quousque de tuo luxuriantur, ó miser, allatrabunt autem omninò & te, crapula iam qua se nuper ingurgitauerant, eruƈtata. Ete- nim naturá secum fert adulatorum, & memoriam ad inferendum malum, & obliuionem boni. Sero tandem nepotis curam, Terpander, suscipe.quod si minus, diuinum istud numen inexpugnabilem habebis hostem, quod flentis naturæ lacrimis gladium suum acuit.
units.tr: Mares have a custom, and in my view a particularly good one. I praise them because they excel in a singular love for their offspring. But what is their custom? When they see a sucking foal left by its nurse, and its mother somewhere far off, they act as a mother should towards a foal she has borne (for they do not forget their own nature), and they cherish the abandoned foal with an easy and gentle spirit, just as they cherish their own true offspring. These creatures are so disposed by nature, for it is not Solon who compels them by laws. I will turn my words to you. You despise your grandson, who goes from door to door, clothed in a most wretched little tunic. Your mind is surely more brutish than the brutes. You feed other men's dogs, outsiders and strangers. For they would be more truly called those who keep company with you are flatterers: they will seem to wish you well for as long as they feast on your wealth, but, wretch that you are, they will bark at you altogether once the gluttony with which they recently gorged themselves has been vomited up. For flattery carries with it by nature a memory for inflicting harm and a forgetfulness of kindness. Terpander, take up your grandson's care at last, though late. But if you do not, you will have that divine power as an unconquerable enemy, which sharpens its sword with the tears of a weeping nature.

units.la: Rust. DAPHNON MYRONI, VIII.
units.tr: Rustic. DAPHNON TO MYRO. VIII.

units.la: Quousque excauas agellum deriuando? & an etiam pluuia delapsam aquam exhauries, miser? aut forte machinaris vt per hanc ariditatem liberi mei fameant?tuus enim ager circum circa inundat,nou ster vero ctiam aquæ naturá aut essentiam ignorat hactenus. Rogantor, vos nubes per Deos an Soli Daphnoni aquam demitatis[?]. Vir inuidus, magnum Daphnoni[?] ... [illegible, ~6 letters] Daphnoniaquam demitatis. Vir inuidus, magnum est malum. quod si vero & vicinus esse contigerit inevitabile infortunium, & vix cum ipsa morte desiturum.
units.tr: How long will you keep digging out your little field by diverting water to it? Will you even drain off the water that has fallen in the rain, you wretch? Or perhaps you are plotting that my children should starve through this dryness? For your field floods all around, and yet, until now, you have not known the nature or substance of water. I ask you, do the clouds pour water down on Daphnon, or on the Sun, by the gods? You envious man, it is a great evil for Daphnon ... [illegible]. Daphnon's water is being diverted. You envious man, it is a great evil. And if it should happen that you are also my neighbour, it is an unavoidable misfortune, one that will hardly end even with death itself.

units.la: Amat. EVRIPPA DEXICRATI. IX.
units.tr: Amatory. EURIPPA TO DEXICRATES. IX.

units.la: Ad IX. definentis Anthesterionis rediturum ad nos te recepisti, & fidem fregisti, Dexicrates mihi vero & renes excanduerunt in amore, & instar facis exarserunt præcordia: quotidie quoq; profudi lacrimas cum gemitu, & in somnis tuum sæpe mihi finxi reditum. forium[?] præterea quocunq; itrepitu[?] semper mihi te adesse imaginabar. tu vero, Dexicrates, in aliam amorem transfudisti, & ad peregrina noua vé[?] tibi animus est propensior. Celerrime namque satiari Solitæ sunt inertium animæ. Infida res & infamis est amores & cupido. cades & aliquando tu. Nam calamitates eorum qui iniuriam patiuntur, ad inferentis caput resiliunt.
units.tr: You promised to return to us at the end of Anthesterion, and you withdrew your pledge, Dexicrates. But my kidneys burned with love, and my heart blazed like a torch. Every day I poured out tears with groaning, and in my dreams I often imagined your return. Moreover, at every sound at the door I kept imagining that you were there with me. But you, Dexicrates, have transferred your love to another, and your spirit is more inclined to new foreign attachments. For the souls of the idle are accustomed to being satisfied very quickly. Love and desire are an unfaithful and infamous thing. You too will fall at last, for the calamities of those who suffer wrong rebound onto the head of the one who inflicts them.

units.la: Eth. HERMAGORAS SOPATRO: X.
units.tr: Eth. HERMAGORAS TO SOPATER: X.

units.la: Deiecto nimis animo paupertatem flere te audiui, diuitiis male dicere, tanquam non æquali modo euntibus inter homines, his quidem possibilem impetratu, his vero impossibilem præbendo sui possessionem, ac ita quodammodo naturam sui hominibus inuidendo.
