Si enim Solis lux in communi neque æquo modo, & ignis copia omnibus est promptissima, si amnium torrentiumque & perennium cursus omnibus sunt affluentissimi; quid igitur inquis est, quod aurum natura ita abconditum ab hominibus reposuit, propter quod maxima mala surgunt quacunque Luna ilta videt? ego vero magnum in risum effundor tuarum differtationum ergò. Nam quam hypothefin vitupcrationis pofuisti, est eadem ipsa laus naturæ, & tu idem passus es cum noctua, siquidem videntur illi cæcitatis effe causa, illustres fulgores Solis. Vtilis hæc est auri famesin humano genere,Sofipater. Indeetenim[?] & artes vitæ acceffernnt, & vrbes ædificatæ sunt, & in contractibus orta conuentio. fi verò summatim dici debeat,omni ornatu priuatus effet quacunque terrarum locusinhabitatus,fi non auri intercessione factum foret,vt homo alter alterius inuicem indigeret. Nam neque nauta nauigabat, neque viator faciebat iter, neque aratorem bouem agricolæ possidebant, non regiæ maiestatis adorabantur Sceptra,non magistratibus & iuridicis ornati erant subditi, non dux agebat exercitum. Quod fi autem secretum sermonem scire vis,virtutis &malitiæ habenas habet aurum, & probatur appetitus animæ peripfum, celticique[?] fluminis est æquale viribus. Falsæ enim virtutis & vitij verissimum est argumentum.
units.tr: I heard that you were deeply downcast and wept over poverty and spoke ill of riches, as though the gifts of fortune were not distributed equally among men. Some, you say, can easily obtain wealth, while for others it is impossible, so that riches in a way deny themselves to men and hold nature in envy. For if the light of the sun is shared by all, not unequally, if fire is most readily available to everyone, and if rivers and streams flow for all alike, then why, you ask, has nature hidden gold away from men, when it is the cause of the greatest evils wherever the moon looks down? I burst out laughing at your arguments. The thesis you have set up for blame is itself a praise of nature, and you have suffered the same fate as the owl, which is said to be blinded by the bright rays of the sun. This lust for gold is useful to the human race, Sopater. For through it the arts of life have come, cities have been built, and agreement has arisen in contracts. To put it briefly, every land on earth would be stripped of all adornment if it were not for gold's mediation, which makes one man need another in turn. No sailor would sail, no traveller would make his journey, no farmer would own an ox to plough with, no sceptres of royal majesty would be revered, no subjects would be governed by magistrates and judges, no general would lead an army. But if you want to hear the secret truth, gold holds the reins of virtue and of vice, and the desire of the soul is tested by it, and it is equal in strength to the Celtic river. For it is the truest sign of false virtue and of vice.

units.la: Ruff. CALLISTACHUS CYPARISSONI.X- I.
units.tr: Ruff. CALLISTACHUS TO CYPARISSUS: X-I.

units.la: Infructuosas & feras arbores heri forte exussit Simichidas. Eiusmodi enim sententiam tulit aduersus arbores quæ ad maturitatem non proucniunt.at natura omniuori ignis impetum habuit immoderatum, viciniq; agri subito & eximprouifo fundum perdidit: hic autem relicta pelle ligoneque ad vrbem vadit: auxilium Rhetoris assumpturus. & Simmichidæ tribunal est indictum.idem ego contrate, Cypariffio, moliar,nisi tuas apes ab alicnis alienis pratis abstinere feceris: & disces alienis vi[?]is obliquum aditum non haberi.
units.tr: Yesterday Simichidas, by chance, burned up some barren and wild trees. He passed this sentence against trees that do not come to maturity. But the fire, having no moderation, seized the whole of the neighbouring field suddenly and unexpectedly and destroyed its soil. The owner, leaving aside his hide and mattock, goes off to the city to take the help of a rhetorician, and a tribunal is summoned against Simichidas. I shall plot the same against you, Cyparissus, unless you make your bees keep away from other people's meadows. And you will learn that a crooked approach is not open to the violence of others.

units.la: Amat. MEL[?].POMENE PRAXIMILLÆ. XII.
units.tr: Amat. MELPOMENE TO PRAXIMILLA: XII.

units.la: Ad Leocorium moras traxit aulæda Chryfogone.fortè etiam oblectare se putat meos amatores, aitá; nos mercetricula factum istud ægrè ferre. ego verò id quod fecit non multi facio. Amatores enim omnes Chryfogonæ mores & habitum cum nostris conferrent. Sed sis mihi, per Deos, non falsi responsi nuncius certissimus, & Lacænæ dicas: Magnas equidem tibi gratias huius rei gratia, Chryfogona, debemus. Tua enim deformitate nostra apparebunt venustiora, quia etiam non præsente graculo & coruus decoris annumerabitur auibus.
units.tr: Chrysogone the curtain-girl has lingered at Leocorium. Perhaps she thinks she is amusing my lovers too, and says that we, mere whores, take this thing badly. But I do not care much about what she has done. For all my lovers would compare Chrysogone's manners and bearing with mine. Come on, then, for the gods' sake, be a most certain messenger of no false answer, and say to her in Laconian: "Chrysogone, we owe you great thanks for this. For by your ugliness our beauty will appear the more lovely, since even when the jackdaw is absent the raven will be counted among the beautiful birds."

units.la: Eth. ARISTO NICIÆ. XIII.
units.tr: Eth. ARISTO TO NICIAS: XIII.

units.la: Difciplinofiffimum dicunt animal esse elephantum, & dexterrimo captu ad omnia ea quæcunque ab hominibus edoceatur. ncq; enim in illo tantum molcs miranda corporis, quantum disciplinæ cultus æstimatur. & ea quidem Indorum pueri divulgant. At ego Niciam admiratus sum, irrationalibus animantibus rationem habere irrationaliorem. ut, qui, cum sis viri eloquentis filius, paternis studiis abiectis, in aleæ ludo ac palæstræ otio vitam detereras, egressus ingenuitatem generis. Quare si filius audire velis Hermagoræ, ferò aliquando ad eius vitam redij, & bonum est, si in senectute sapientia adsit & prudentia quod & Platoni videtur. Si verò molestum est ex pristinis vitiis resurgere, & seipsum Hermagoræ filium iactitas, scito te futurum furem paterni sepulchri. Nam tua malitia virtutes eius infamas, & contumelia afficis.
units.tr: They say the elephant is the most teachable of animals and most quick to grasp whatever men teach it. For the marvel of that creature lies not so much in the bulk of its body as in the value placed on its training, and the boys of the Indians spread this report abroad. But I was amazed at Nicias, that he, a creature with reason, has less reason than the unreasoning animals. You, who are the son of an eloquent man, have cast aside your father's studies and wasted your life in dice-playing and idleness in the wrestling-school, departing from the nobility of your birth. So if you wish to hear Hermagoras, return at last to his way of life. It is good if wisdom and prudence come in old age, as Plato also thinks. But if it is troublesome to rise again from your former vices, and yet you boast of being Hermagoras' son, know that you will be a thief of your father's tomb. For your wickedness disgraces his virtues and brings shame upon him.

units.la: Ruff. MYRONIDES DAMALO. XIV.
units.tr: Ruff. MYRONIDES TO DAMALUS: XIV.

units.la: Gregem totum puer tuus læsit, multralia femperlactecomplens. Ad platanos secedit furcifer, stratoq; stibadio decubare solet, & inertem vitam ample&itur. deinde fistula prehensa quasi conuivalem cantum ad securitatem adiicit, & agrestes effingit modos. pecudes vero hinc inde difparguntur, & aditui cuiuus sunt obnoxiæ. Sanè & fimum leui precio diuendidit nebulo, & Myroniden iniuria afficere nequaquam veritus est, absorpto herivino fæculento. Caricæ enim mihi & cicadæ sunt obsonio. at vero diuinus hic adolescens caricas plerafque omnes deuorauit, & cicadas nescio quomodo deglutiit. Fœcatum vero est exhaustum, & partem postquam satur esset, postulabat referendam domum. Absit in posterum ab agro meo Clinia. Optabilius enim est à malis abesse procul, quam domi alere hostem occultum.
units.tr: Your slave has harmed the whole flock, filling himself with milk many times over. The rascal retires to the plane trees, and usually lies down on a spread couch, and gives himself up to a lazy life. Then, taking up his pipe, he adds a song as though for a dinner companion, and plays rustic tunes. Meanwhile the sheep are scattered here and there, and are exposed to whoever comes upon them. Indeed, the wretch sold the dung for a small price, and he did not at all shrink from wronging Myronides, having swallowed down the thick dregs of the wine. For figs and cicadas are my relish, but this divine youth devoured nearly all the figs, and somehow gulped down the cicadas. The jar has been drained dry, and after he was full he demanded that part of it be carried home. Let Clinias keep away from my field from now on. For it is better to keep far from evils than to nurse a hidden enemy at home.

units.la: Amat. ATALANTA CORINNÆ XV.
units.tr: Love. ATALANTA TO CORINNA, XV.

units.la: In palæstra Augiam & spectauimus, Corinna, & spectaculum neque sermo edicere, neque pictoris manus imitari possent. Aderant enim adolescenti robur & vires, erectum firmumque corpus, pectus pilosum, oculi quales sunt ceruarum siue dorcadum, visus neq; rubens ex ira, neque mollicie deicctus, sed simul virilis & placidus. Color corporis neq; albicabat, vt in fœminis, neq; nimis erat niger. crinis modicè crispus præ teneritudine, & purpurantem tempore malaciæ pontum retulit, & quando vicinam terram leni allapsu circumfundit, surore fluctus & barbarie sedata. Genarum rubor non supra modum, quod fœmineum, neq; rursum carundem decorem offuscabat pallor. Nasus elaboratissimè detornatus, vt plurimum naturæ opificis artificium argueret. Oleum circumfusum Solisin modum fulgerabat, & splendore lucis palæstram quasi radiisillustrabat. animo inde, Corinna, vulnerata maiorem accutioremque dolorem sentio. Amatorios enim affectus commemorare pudet fœminas,
units.tr: In the wrestling-ground, Corinna, we have seen Augias, and no speech could describe the spectacle, nor could a painter's hand imitate it. The young man had strength and vigour, a upright and firm body, a hairy chest, and eyes like those of stags or gazelles. His look was neither flushed with anger nor cast down in softness, but at once manly and calm. His complexion was neither pale, as in women, nor too dark. His hair was slightly curled with youthful softness, and it recalled the purple sea in a calm season, when the waves, rolling gently onto the nearby shore, soften their fury and their roughness. The flush on his cheeks was not excessive, so as to be womanish, nor was their beauty dimmed by pallor. His nose was finely shaped, so that it showed the craftsmanship of nature the maker. The oil poured over him shone like the sun, and with its brightness it lit up the wrestling-ground as if with rays. So, Corinna, I, wounded here, feel a greater and sharper pain. For I am ashamed to speak of amorous passions as a woman.

units.la: Eth. GORGIAS ARISTIDI. XVI.
units.tr: Ethics. GORGIAS TO ARISTIDES. XVI.

units.la: Cùm fœnore accepisti, gaudes; exactus dolcs.& incidens in fœneratores metu percelleris, quasi feris quibusdam, incidere visus immanibus. & circum spectas triuia, & oculos coniicis ad porticus evitare[?] cupiens fœneratores: sicuti nauigantes in magna tempestate ad portum applicare desiderant. Sed & malum malo addis. Postquam enim fœnori ab aliis acce peris,aliis reddis debitum,idem aliquid faciens, quod ij qui se metu mortis præcipitant.Quoniam igitur fœnerati multiplex hominibus est malum, & fabulosa ista hydra,cui sponte renascebantur tot capita, multò est peius, caue ctjam[?] ne vel insomnis tibi fœneratione imagineris. Sic enim libere adspicies solares[?] radios, & aërem in terra leniter nimis & placide respirabis.
units.tr: When you have received money on usury, you rejoice; when you are pressed for repayment and fall in with the moneylenders, you are struck with fear, as if you had run into savage beasts. You look about on the crossroads and turn your eyes towards the colonnades, wishing to avoid the moneylenders, just as sailors in a great storm long to reach harbour. But you also add evil to evil. For after you have received money from one man, you pay a debt to another, doing something like those who throw themselves headlong from fear of death. Since therefore the usurer's debt is a manifold evil for men, and is like that fabled hydra, whose heads grew again of their own accord, it is much worse. Beware lest you even dream of being in debt in your sleep. For then you will look freely upon the sun's rays, and breathe the air on earth gently and calmly.

units.la: Rust. LOPHON PEDIADÆ. XVII.
units.tr: Rustic. LOPHON TO PEDIAS. XVII.

units.la: Ne Leucippus. Milam[?] enim nobis agellus enutriuit bestiam juxta terminum colliculi. Mihi & Softrato indictum est tribunal. Leucippus autem toto animo perditus est, ut qui auro corrumpi passus sit judicium. talis in aurum affectus abripuit hunc miserum. quod cum Softratus sciret, auro victoriam redemit, & muneribus sufferciit fauces Leucippi. Virgo Justitia vitiata est, & auro victoria appenditur hominibus. Justum enim & momentaneum judicium periit, & dona magis aestimantur, quam quod justum est.
units.tr: Not Leucippus. For a little field of ours has nourished a beast beside the boundary of a small hill. Softratus and I have been summoned before the same tribunal. Leucippus, however, is utterly ruined in mind, as one who has allowed justice to be corrupted by gold. Such an affection for gold has carried off this wretched man. When Softratus knew this, he bought victory with gold and stopped the throat of Leucippus with gifts. The Virgin Justice has been violated, and victory is weighed out to men for gold. For a just and sound judgement has perished, and gifts are valued more than what is right.

units.la: Amat. EROTYLVS HIPSIPYLÆ. XVIII.
units.tr: Amatoria. EROTYLUS HIPSIPYLAE. XVIII.

units.la: Turgent & palmæ amore naturali, & mas appetit fœminam, & incuruatur amore mas, & frondibus amatam nectit. quod si longius à mare distet fœmina, semen ex fœmina sublatum imponunt mari, atq; ea callidate solantur huius amorem. Si igitur ad vos tam cito repedare non potens pictoris opera mihi mitiges hunc amorem, & in tabulis pictura tuas cogitationes mihi exhibeat. Nam & spectatio in amore nimios fallendo solet esse par.
units.tr: Palm trees swell with natural love: the male desires the female, and the male bends towards the beloved and binds her with fronds. But if the female stands too far from the male, they take pollen from the female, place it on the male, and by this contrivance ease the longing for her. So if you, unable to return to me so quickly, would soften this love for me through a painter's work, let the picture present your thoughts to me on the panels. For sight too, in love, is wont to be an equal deceiver of the excessive.

units.la: Eth. DIOGENES CHRYSÆ. XIX.
units.tr: Ethics. Diogenes Chrysae. XIX.

units.la: Divitiarum te condum[?], non dominum opum esse perhibeo, id quod etiam tui contra te lata sententia produnt mores. Bonis enim ut participent aliquibus impiæ animæ non est fas. Refundas idcirco terram, & aurum custodi miserrime. non enim tuæ,sed penes te creduntur esse divitiæ. Nam Phrygis Midæ malignitatem æmulatus, esuriendo ditescis, veluti laqueo suspensus aureo.
units.tr: I declare that you are a keeper of riches, not their master, as your own character, pronounced against you, also reveals. For it is not right for an impious soul to share in any good things. Therefore give back the earth and guard your gold, most wretched man. For the riches are believed to be not yours but in your keeping. For, imitating the meanness of Phrygian Midas, you grow rich by starving, like a man hanged on a golden noose.

units.la: Amat. CHLOAZON MECONI. XX.
units.tr: Love poem. CHLOAZON TO MECON. XX.

units.la: Amafiz heri, Mecon, pyra misi,hæc autem repente surgens ex lanificio abiectatrama, accepta dona proftauit porcis,& hominem à me missum,ut nuncium infaultum amádauit. Ego verò fleo. terribilis enim amor iniuriam nobis facit, qui in tam feroci puella nos cogat. Cæcutiunt fortuna & amores,hi quidem dolores,hæc verò felicitatem vanam & fortuitam exhibendo.
units.tr: Yesterday, Mecon, I sent Amafiz a pear, but she suddenly rose from her wool-working, threw my gift to the pigs, and drove away the man I had sent as a messenger, as though he were an unlucky herald. I weep for it. Love is a dreadful thing and does me wrong, since it forces me to pursue such a fierce girl. Fortune and love are both blind: the one brings sorrows, the other offers a vain and chancy happiness.

units.la: Amat. PERDICCA RHODOPÆ. XXI.
units.tr: Amat. PERDICCA RHODOPÆ. XXI.

units.la: Inamænè canis,& mœrore exples amatores,non lætitia. Tragœdiam namque voce querula cantillas cantum delinientem nihil auditores. & plorant amatores tristitia affecti. temperantes enim potius docendo sunt tua carmina,quam libidinantes,non enim elaborafti cantionem, per illecebras. Parcas igitur nobis,per Deos,in posterum dolores & mœrores nostros. Nam neq; aulæda videris esse spectatoribus sed præfica, & omnes cera aures obturabimus,cum canas: audituri alias Sirenum planctum, & Musarum Næmias.
units.tr: You sing without charm, and fill your lovers with grief rather than joy. For your plaintive voice sings a tragedy, and your song, which soothes no one, leaves the listeners unmoved; and the lovers weep, overcome with sadness. Indeed, your verses ought rather to teach moderation than to inflame desire, for you have not worked out your song to win us over by enticements. So spare us, I beg you by the gods, from now on your sorrows and lamentations. For you seem to be not a curtain for the spectators but a hired mourner, and when you sing I will stop all my ears with wax, since I would rather hear the wailing of the Sirens and the dirges of the Muses.

units.la: Eth. ANTISTHENES PERICLI. XXII.
units.tr: Eth. ANTISTHENES PERICLI. XXII.

units.la: Philippi filius Alexander fecundis fortunis nequaquam intumuit. sed philosophica moderatione direxit fortunæ ventos, maximis ac summis eius fauoribus non inescari solitus. quare cecidisse videns Darium in belli ancipite fortuna, Chlamyda texit hostem, virtutis & fortunæ ostendens generofitatem. inde calumniati sunt subditi Alexandrum,regisq; pietatem peregerunt ream. Sed quidem Alexander, vt erat philosophus, reueritus est, vt videtur, fortunæ varietatem. quare missis sibi quam plurimis vna bonis, O Iuppiter dixit, intermisce aliquod bonis ctiam infortunium. Sic Alexander cauté versabatur in rebus summis fapientiffimè. Tu itaq; fi naturam vicissitudinibus obnoxiam hactenus ignorasti, eius rei non multò post videbis periculum factum, quod te condoccfaciat & cognitione antiquiora habebis documenta. quod fi sponte volensq; czcutias, difficiliori pœna exerceberis, peccatorum & ignorantiæ subiturus multam.
units.tr: Philip's son Alexander was in no way puffed up by his prosperous fortunes. Rather, by philosophical moderation he steered the winds of fortune, being accustomed not to be enticed by his greatest and highest favours. Therefore, seeing Darius fallen in the uncertain fortune of war, he covered the enemy with his own cloak, showing the nobility of his virtue and of his fortune. Then his subjects slandered Alexander and brought the king's piety to trial as a crime. But Alexander, being a philosopher, was, it seems, mindful of the variability of fortune. Accordingly, when very many good things had been sent to him all at once, he said: "O Jupiter, mix some misfortune in with the good things too." Thus Alexander conducted himself cautiously and most wisely in his highest affairs. You, then, if hitherto you have been ignorant that nature is subject to changes of fortune, will soon see the danger of this fact put to the test; it will teach you, and you will have lessons more ancient than knowledge itself. But if you resist of your own accord and willingly, you will be punished more severely, and you will undergo a fine for your sins and ignorance.

units.la: Ruf. ASTACHYO MILONI. XXIII.
units.tr: Rufus to Astachyus Milo. XXIII.

units.la: Agrum ab aconito purga, meas enim corrumpisapes. Neper Deos, homini agricolæ laborem exhibeas, ne fucum quidem vobis perdidit. quid igitur abfq; causa irasceris vicino, & nisi abstinens à malitia pessime, tuam ego proteruiam meis inscribam foribus, & iniuriam vicinis indicabo, vt ita te velut ominosum euitent.
units.tr: Purge your field of aconite, for you are destroying my bees. By the gods, do not cause trouble for a farmer; he has not even lost a drone to you. Why then are you angry with your neighbour without cause? Unless you stop your wickedness, you wretch, I will write your insolence on my doors and report your injustice to the neighbours, so that they may shun you as a bad omen.

units.la: Æmat. TELESILLA LAIDI. XXIV.
units.tr: Æmat. Telesilla to Laidi. XXIV.

units.la: Neq; metallarij, quum auri venas inuestigant, neq; fossores puteorum, secreta terræ subterranea scrutantes, cum aquas quærunt, sic enituntur in ar-te sua vt oculi eo acrius videant, quemadmodum ego totam vrbem excutio atque rimor, an Agefilaum alicubi forte peruidere possim. Potionem cnim ei præparasse audio mœnadem istam Leucippen vt impetuofum quasi fulmen desubito in nos inciderit: vnde tum infolabiles istæ mihi funtortæ lacrimæ. quapropter in peragenda tragœdia nos nostras quoq; partes habebimus. neq; posthac resurgentem Solem videbimus: atque ita Medea fiam sæuior, & Phædra.
units.tr: Neither miners, when they search for veins of gold, nor well-diggers, when they probe the hidden depths of the earth in search of water, strain at their work so hard that their eyes see more keenly than I do as I turn over and pry into the whole city, to see whether I can perhaps catch sight of Agefilas somewhere. For I hear that that maenad Leucippe has prepared a potion for him, so that he might fall upon us suddenly like a thunderbolt. This is why I have been overcome by these unbearable tears. So in playing out this tragedy we too shall have our own parts. Nor shall we see the sun rising again after this. And so I shall become more savage than Medea, and than Phaedra.

units.la: Eth. SOSIPATER AXIOCHO. XXV.
units.tr: Eth. Sosipater to Axiochus. XXV.

units.la: Fratrem nuper te sepeliisse dicunt,& nimis ægrè immoderateque ferre eius obitum.& quomodo te philosophum hominem fatis admirer,ob tale quid affectui succumbentem ? Somnus enim quidam est, quæ fertur apud nos esse mors. consueto quidem longior, ad futuram tamen diem fi conferas breuissimus. In fceffionem breuem ablegantur mortui. non longò post futura & est nostra feceffio. Perfer hanc disiunctionem ,sexspecta iterum coniunctionem. ne afficiatur ita tuus animus, vt corporis amore trahi videatur.quoniam Plotinum quoque puduit, quod effet in corpore. ita tristem habuit istum philosophum.mortalis hic circumiectus, siste hactenus mihi lacrimas, terminos pone tristitiæ, prudentia subueni affectui, medicus esto tibi ipsi. Rationem habes, istud est medicamen, Nepenthesq; & mite, malarum oblitio rerum. non ex meliore statum peiorem transfert vnquam creator suas creaturas. mortalibus mortalia relinquamus. magnis enim maculis hinc animæ ista maiestas inquinatur. ego natiuitatem , quam mortem magis plorarem. Illa namq; lacrimarum est initium; hæc aduersorum solutio. ignorantia nos vinctos habet, De morte igitur ita accipiamus, non quod malum fit, sed quod ignorctur ab hominibus. nemo enim qui cam quid fit sciat , tam temerè eam accusat. Quare ne Niobæ similis fias, ne videaris & ipse in lapidem humanam naturam transmutare.
units.tr: They say you have recently buried your brother, and that you are bearing his death too painfully and immoderately. How could I greatly admire you as a philosopher if you give way to feeling over such a thing? For death, which among us is said to be a kind of sleep, is longer than usual, yet compared with the day to come it is very brief. The dead are sent away for a short retreat, and not long after, our own withdrawal will come. Endure this separation, and look forward again to the reunion. Do not let your mind be so affected that it seems drawn by love of the body, since Plotinus too was ashamed that he was in a body; that philosopher was so sad. You who are enveloped in mortality here, for now stop your tears, put an end to your grief, come to the aid of your feelings with prudence, and be your own physician. You have the reason; that is the remedy, Nepenthes [νηπενθές] and mild, forgetfulness of evils. The Creator never transfers his creatures from a better state to a worse. Let us leave mortal things to mortals, for this majesty of the soul is stained by great blemishes from here. I would rather mourn my birth than my death, for the one is the beginning of tears, the other the release from troubles. Ignorance holds us bound. Let us therefore take death in this way: not as an evil, but as something people do not know. For no one who knows what it is would accuse it so rashly. So do not become like Niobe, and do not seem yourself to be turning human nature into stone.

units.la: Amat. Cecropis Dexicrati. XXVI.
units.tr: Love. Cecrops to Dexicrates. XXVI.

units.la: Magnetem lapidem amare ferrum dicunt & ideo viuere affirmant lapidem, donec cum amato cohæret. Quam enim primum lapis à compare dissociatur, statim emoritur, & vires suas deponit. tales affectuum consensus etiam inanimatis insunt, Dexi-crates. Ego autem quid patiar amicissime, tantopere à familiaritate tua relicta. Eloqui ea arbitror acerbius mihi esset, quam pati. Sic dolore afficiam, qui me afficiunt. & Amoribus fiam telum, scintilla, Venerea maris igni ardentior.
units.tr: They say the magnet loves iron, and for that reason they claim the stone lives for as long as it clings to what it loves. As soon as the stone is parted from its mate, it dies at once and loses its powers. Such a sympathy of feelings is present even in inanimate things, Dexicrates. But what am I to suffer, most dear friend, now that I have been so greatly cut off from your companionship? I think that to put these things into words would be more bitter to me than to endure them. So I shall afflict with grief those who afflict me, and become a dart to loves, a spark, more ardent than the Venereal fire of the sea.

units.la: Ruft. Theristro Spironi. XXVII.
units.tr: Ruft. to Theristro Spironi. XXVII.

units.la: In Ætnam Siciliæ montem transmigramus, dicentes Atticæ telluri Vale. Nunquam enim infeliciorem ad fructus ferendos terram vidimus. pro frumento, murrhinas; pro ordeo hederas nobis edidit arca verò mea panaria vacua est: & area præter famem nil nouit. Quapropter primis feminibus non enatis, fecundo non reddentem non scro[?]. Non potest agricola famem & militem sufferre hostes. neque nautæ quicunq; sint, sufficiunt contra ventum & fulmen pugnare.
units.tr: We are moving across to Mount Etna in Sicily, bidding farewell to Attic soil. For we have never seen a land less fruitful in bearing crops. Instead of wheat it has given us myrrh, and instead of barley, ivy. My granary is empty, and my threshing floor knows nothing but hunger. Therefore, since the first seeds have not sprouted, I do not sow again in a land that gives no return. A farmer cannot endure hunger, nor a soldier the enemy, and sailors, whoever they may be, cannot hold out against wind and lightning.

units.la: Eth. Heraclides Antisthen. XXVI- II.
units.tr: Eth. Heraclides Antisthenes. XXVI-II.

units.la: Nondum mihi de ira remisisti, Antisthenes, & adhuc nobis es offensus, & induéta verborum schemâ cælas offensam, vt illi qui scintillam ignis coucluduntin fauilla? expurga posthac cordis fæditatem, quod à te petunt sermones nostri, si minus maries inhumanior. Sopit enim istud feritatem, &nautis humanam faciem exhibet, quando oleo illinunt iactatum nimiis aestibus.
units.tr: You have not yet let go of your anger, Antisthenes, and you are still offended with us. Under a veil of words you hide the offence, as people cover a spark in ashes. From now on, cleanse the foulness of your heart, as our words ask you to do, unless you are more savage than a man. For that softens wildness, and it gives a human face to sailors when they smear with oil those who are tossed about by excessive storms.

units.la: Ruft. LACHANO PEGANONI, XXIX.
units.tr: Rufus. TO LACHANUS OF PEGAE, XXIX.

units.la: Veni ad me mane crastino. Ibo enim ad vrbem, & conuiuium praebebo, amicissime: quia Nymphis & Pani Deo primitias gregis dedicaui. Nam bene nobis volunt fero tandem aliquando hi Dii; piffy?bia mihi lacte sunt expleta. Oues f.liciter[?] perpererunt, adsultant caprae propter abundantiam quasi gaudentes. Desiuimus cum paupertate ceitare[?], maleuola bestia & morosa. Lappae in morem poffidentibus adhaeret. Affabile malum est, deses & iners, subtriste, ad moestitiam pronum, ad dolorem facile, insomne, curarum amans, laboriosum, malorum inuentiuum, inglorium, aspernabile, non inuidendum. neq; enim quis incidere velit in tale malum, nisi fi Orestis furorem insanire iudicetur. Abiicientes itaque ea quae paupertatis sunt cum ipsa paupertate, ad bona alia tranfcamus, commutatione facta cum animo & sapientia.
units.tr: Come to me early tomorrow. I am going to the city and will give a banquet, my dearest friend, because I have dedicated the first-fruits of the flock to the Nymphs and to the god Pan. These gods at last are favouring us well: my pails are filled with milk. The ewes have given birth happily, and the goats frisk about in their abundance as if rejoicing. We have ceased to wrestle with poverty, that malevolent and sullen beast. She clings to those who possess her like burdock. She is an affable evil, idle and sluggish, rather gloomy, prone to sadness, easily moved to grief, sleepless, fond of cares, toilsome, the inventor of troubles, inglorious, to be despised, not to be envied. For no one would wish to fall into such an evil, unless he were judged to be mad with the madness of Orestes. Therefore, casting away what belongs to poverty together with poverty itself, let us pass over to other goods, the exchange being made with spirit and wisdom.

units.la: Amat. RHODINA CALLIOPAE. XXX.
units.tr: Amat. RHODINA TO CALLIOPE. XXX.

units.la: Super amatoribus me differs, & calumniaris de partu relaxatam mihi distentionem turgiditatemque corporis esse cauillata. tu vero tuas fraudes occultas esse putas; quoniam immaturos, ô fcelerarissima[?], quos concepisti foetus occidis, & abortus praefers partionibus, per ocriora medicamenta uis in ventre conceptibus enicatis, sic quam homicida Medea immaniores committis caedes. Liberos isti suos vt cnecaret in causa fuit improbus maritus, fœminæ laudabili alias, & certaminum eius comiti.tu verò ne formam corrumperet mille strages edis, meretricula. Quare desistas inhumanitatem tuam tegere, & nostræ pietati illudere : apud quas humanius est parere, quam aboriri. Scias verè etiam terram tibi iratam fore, & quin exigat occiforum liberorum pœnas, haudquaquam neglecturam.
units.tr: You put me off about the lovers, and you slander me by claiming that the slackening and swelling of my body after childbirth is a fabrication. But you think your own frauds are hidden, since you kill the immature offspring you have conceived, and bring on miscarriages, using swifter drugs to destroy the conceptions in your womb. So you commit slaughters more savage than Medea the murderess. A wicked husband was the cause of her killing her children, though she was otherwise a praiseworthy woman and a partner in his contests. But you, so that you may not ruin your looks, commit a thousand massacres, you little harlot. Therefore stop trying to hide your inhumanity and to mock our piety, among whom it is more humane to give birth than to abort. Know truly that the earth too will be angry with you, and that it will by no means neglect to exact punishment for the children you have murdered.

units.la: Eth.[?] HEPHÆSTIO TALETI. XXXI.
units.tr: Eth.[?] HEPHÆSTIO TALETI. XXXI.

units.la: Medicæ auis pauo Medorum quoque superbiam est sortita, magnū aliquid tumidumq; de pulchritudine sua sentiens: in qua re tamen modestior vidētur esse pavo fœmina. Pennas ergo veluti comas erigit, & illustrissimam speciem exhibet spectantibus, & formam orbicularem rotundat, mundumq; coelestem exprimit & oculis caudæ astrorum ornaturam repræsentat. Atq; hic mos est avium gloriæ & elegantiæ plenus, sed enim non invident, ornatum suum, quibus exemplo sunt pictoribus. tu verò tuis insides libris, ac tuas virtutes contegis, & labores inostensos finis, tantam utilitatem nobis, qui caremus, invidens. Si igitur invidia quodammodo vos detinet, res est philosopho indigna, & à tua professione aliena. si verò pigritia editionem impedit, idem pateris cum viro aliquo rustico, qui multum sudavit in excolenda terra; & cùm viget æstas maximè, non decerpit spicas.
units.tr: The peacock, a bird of the Medes, has also received the pride of that people, feeling great and swollen self-regard about its beauty; yet in this respect the female peacock seems more modest. So it raises its feathers like a crest, displays its most splendid appearance to onlookers, rounds its form into a circle, and imitates the heavenly world, presenting to our eyes the adornment of the stars in its tail. And this habit is full of glory and elegance for birds; but they do not begrudge their ornament to those who serve as models for painters. You, however, shut yourself up in your books and hide your virtues, keeping your labours unrevealed, and begrudging such great usefulness to us who lack it. If, then, envy somehow holds you back, it is a thing unworthy of a philosopher and foreign to your profession. But if laziness hinders publication, you suffer the same as a certain countryman who has sweated much in cultivating the land, and when summer is at its height, does not gather the ears of grain.

units.la: Ruf.[?] Poas Ampelio. XXXI- I.
units.tr: Ruf.[?] Poas to Ampelio. XXXI- I.

units.la: Agedum coniuncto luctu, senecio, comploremus. Iluvius transilut, & malum nobis saltavit sal-tum tum.totum agrum inundauit, & nouellas vites li-mo obstruxit, ille durus maius autem hoc est ma-lum;non vult scelestus inde repedare. Libenter verò, & non sine voluptate agellum habitat, & ex agro nostro sibi fecit cubile.amplius etiam est videre dignum lacrymis. Pro vitibus enim pisces colimus miseri. cùm fluuio lubet, capimus: cùm lubet iterum, famemus: & magno aliquo dono donatus videor. utinam æstate nubes nequaquam euocemus,ut imbrem nobis largiantur in ariditatibus,ita enim iis, quæ possidemus, non priuabimur.fluuius verò per se satis onerosus est. quod si imbres etiam auxerint, igne est intolerabilior, & nullo modo ferociæ suæ frenos ponit.
units.tr: Come, old man, let us weep together and lament. The river has leapt its banks and jumped upon us in one great bound. It has flooded the whole field and choked our young vines with mud. That savage fellow, the greater evil, will not go back again. He gladly and with pleasure lives in our little field and has made a bed for himself out of our land. Even more, it is a sight worthy of tears. For instead of vines we wretches now farm fish. When the river pleases, we catch them; when it pleases again, we starve, and yet I seem to have been given some great gift. Would that in summer we did not summon the clouds, so that they might pour rain upon us in our droughts. In that way we would not be deprived of what we possess. But the river is burdensome enough by itself. And if the rains also swell it, it is more intolerable than fire, and in no way does it put a curb on its fierceness.

units.la: Amat. GALATEA THETIDI. XXXIII.
units.tr: Amatory. Galatea to Thetis. XXXIII.

units.la: Laudo tuam prudentiam,& experientiam tuam nimiam admiror. Velut enim ex tripode aliquo Pythico futura mihi profata es,ac Lynceo acutius, profundioresq; & immanifestas res pervidisti. Calimachus nos reliquit; avolat in altum evectus acerrimis satietatis pennis; aufugit à nobis scelestissimus, & satietatem prætulit cupiditati, tu verò multa me monuisti; juriiurando ne persvadere Galatea; juramento nihil est levius, in amantibus. Juvenes enim capti & inebriati voluptatibus amatoriis, non iam rectæ rationis dictamini obediunt, sed faciunt & loquuntur quodcunque præscripserint amores. neq; enim pro suo arbitrio velle possunt,quod volunt. Perfidia fide videtur firmior & stabilior,& ad fallendum, Juramentum magister est idoneus.
units.tr: I praise your prudence and greatly admire your experience. For you have foretold my future as if from some Pythian tripod, and you have seen into deeper and hidden matters more keenly than Lynceus. Callimachus has left us. He has flown off, lifted high on the sharpest wings of satiety. That most wicked fellow has run away from us and preferred satiety to desire. But you have warned me of many things, and told me not to persuade Galatea by an oath, for nothing is lighter than an oath among lovers. Young men who are captured and intoxicated by amorous pleasures no longer obey the dictates of right reason. They do and say whatever their loves prescribe, and they cannot will freely what they wish. Perfidy seems firmer and more stable than faith, and for deceiving, an oath is a fit teacher.

units.la: Eth. Themistocles Chrysippo. XXXIV.
units.tr: Eth. Themistocles to Chrysippus. XXXIV.

units.la: Quoniam temperantia ipsis quoque fabulis est laudata, age sane Chryfippe, narrabo tibi fabulam non indecoram. Conuenerunt olim ad Iouem aues, legatione missa ad Olympium regem. Illud namq; ægre ferebant aues, quod effent fine Imperio, quodq; summo aliquo & bono principatu carerent: ac ideo sordes & illuuiem multam sibi contraxerant. Annuit igitur Iuppiter; & in opus ex consilio res est produ&ta, donumq; datum fupplicibus admirandnm. Regia enim dignitas erat, quæ dabatur. quapropter ad fontes & lacus abire iussit aues, ablotum suas sordes & aquæ commisit inquifitionem regis. Erat autem à Ioue propositus formæ decor & elegantia, vt quæ præstaret eâ, rex diceretur. Lautæ itaq; aues omnes ad Iouem recurrunt protinus, ostenditque vna quæque suam pulchritudinem. Graculus verò metuens informitati suæ, propriæ naturæ opificium interpolauit, alieno mundo fe adornans. Sed arguit informitatem, noua, fi&titiumq; mundum prodidit. Cognitis enim inibi suis aliquot pennis, eas vt proprias abftulit, & aliis auibus exemplo fuit, vt singulæ, quod suum effet, auferrent. Sic graculus rursum factus est graculus. Fabula hæc, ô Chryfippe, veritatem quasi insonat, non exiguam temperantiam nobis interpretata. Sic enim homines qui fumus, nihil horum quæ hîc sunt possidemus proprium. Sed viui quidem ad breue tempus fi&titio ornamur cultu: exuimur verò mortui, iis quæ non sunt nostra. Despicias ea propter bonorum corporisq; curam, rei vero immortali sis intentus, nimirum animæ, hæc enim sempiterna & immortalis: illa vero mortalia & ad breue tempus nostra sunt.
units.tr: Since temperance has been praised even in fables, come now, Chrysippus, I will tell you a fable that is not unseemly. Once the birds gathered before Jupiter and sent an embassy to the Olympian king. The birds were troubled that they were without a ruler, and that they lacked some supreme and good sovereignty; for this reason they had gathered much filth and squalor on themselves. Jupiter therefore nodded assent, the matter was carried out by his counsel, and a wonderful gift was given to the suppliants. For what was granted was royal dignity. Accordingly he ordered the birds to go to the springs and lakes to wash away their filth, and he entrusted to the water the task of choosing the king. Jupiter had set the standard as beauty and elegance of form: whichever bird excelled in this would be called king. So all the birds, washed clean, hurried back to Jupiter at once, and each displayed its own beauty. But the jackdaw, fearing its own ugliness, patched up its natural appearance with another's finery, adorning itself with a foreign plumage. Yet this exposed its ugliness and revealed its new, pretended finery. For when its own few feathers were recognised there, it plucked them out as its own, and it became an example to the other birds, so that each took away what was its own. Thus the jackdaw became a jackdaw again. This fable, Chrysippus, seems almost to sound out the truth, and it sets before us a lesson in no small temperance. For so we men, who are but smoke, possess nothing here that is our own. While we live for a short time we are adorned with a borrowed finery; but when we die we are stripped of what is not ours. Therefore despise the care of goods and of the body, and be intent upon the immortal thing, namely the soul; for this is everlasting and immortal, while those others are mortal and belong to us only for a short time.

units.la: Ruft. MYRONIDES MOSCHIONI. XXXV.
units.tr: Ruft. Myronides to Moschion. XXXV.

units.la: Aratorem bouem mutuo dedi Tucaniæ: quia ei integrum jugum non erat. at vero promisit[?] itidem sui mihi quoque tauri usum se facturum Tucania: quoniam & ego uno boue sum destitutus. Mirus enim ille mihi taurus mortuus est, quando difficilis illa pestis inter pecudes est grassata. Bonus vero Tucania pactum fregit, & donec assequutus est quod voluit, visus est conditioni acquiescere; ego autem tyrannicum hoc contagium fleo, non enim habemus boues ad arandum, & arandi tempus jam propinquauit. Tribunal igitur Tucaniæ parabo, & Judices omnem hunc agrum constituam, & huius ille fraudis pœnas subibit, & ita docebimus injuriofos & proteruos abstinere malitia, unius hominis calamitatem habendo temperantiæ magistram.
units.tr: I lent Tucania my ploughing ox, since he had no complete yoke. And Tucania promised likewise that he would let me use his bulls, since I too have been left with a single ox. For that remarkable bull of mine has died, since that dreadful plague has spread among the cattle. But the good Tucania has broken his agreement, and, until he obtained what he wanted, he seemed to accept the terms; meanwhile I weep over this tyrannical contagion, for we have no oxen for ploughing, and the time for ploughing is now near. I shall therefore set up a tribunal against Tucania and appoint judges over this whole field, and he shall pay the penalty for this fraud; and so we shall teach the wrongdoers and the wanton to refrain from malice, taking the misfortune of one man as a teacher of temperance.

units.la: Amat. ERASMIVS LYSISTRATO. XXXVI.
units.tr: Amat. Erasmus to Lysistratus. XXXVI.

units.la: Ludunt hominum genus, amores, & arbitrio suo subiiciunt eos, qui sub Luna sunt, pueri, ut pictoribus etiam in aliquo adsentiamur, alati, atque etiam bellum videre liceat. Sic enim alternis amores qui feriunt feriuntur; sed in hac ipsa parte amplius peccauimus, quod & holtes[?] ignorauimus, ut natura sunt. Quam enim nullæ rationis est affectus, quo ego tencor[?]? Melanippen Diodori neptem extra modum amo, quam ne per somnium quidem ante mulierem vidi, sed audiui solum ab aliquo eam canere here mirabiliter; & in animam accepi vulnus, nequidquam læsus ab oculis, quod solitus sum pati; Lyfistrate, nunc vero mihi sunt & oculi & aures. talia natura amorum potuit. Anigitur insania quædam fit in hoc commento, ignoraui hactenus. an vero phantasia aliqua fit, quod dictum mihi esse dixi, non constat, neq; unus testis veritati sufficit. Doleo vero simul ab anima, & non visam amo. Panicoq; furori partim participare videor, & id inuisum est, quod amo, & illa sola opinio amatæ rei habuit essentiam.
units.tr: Love mocks the human race, and subjects to its will those who live under the moon; the boys, as painters too would have us agree in some measure, are winged, and one may even see them at war. For thus love wounds those who wound in turn; but in this very matter I have sinned more grievously, since I did not know even the enemy, as they are by nature. For what reasonable cause is there for the feeling by which I am held? I love Melanippe, granddaughter of Diodorus, beyond measure. I had not seen the woman even in a dream, but I only heard someone sing of her wonderfully, and I received a wound in my soul, though I was struck without any help from my eyes, which is what I am used to suffering. Lysistratus, now indeed I have eyes and ears for her. Such is the nature of love. Some madness, then, has come upon me in this affair, which I had not known until now. Whether some illusion is involved, or whether what I said I had heard was really said to me, is not clear, and no single witness is enough to establish the truth. Yet I grieve in my soul, and I love a woman I have not seen. I seem to share in the frenzy of Pan in part, and what I love is hateful, and that opinion alone has given substance to the thing loved.

units.la: Eth. Evrtades Cimonı. XXXVII.
units.tr: Eth. Eurtades to Cimon. XXXVII.

units.la: Promittis multa, & facis pauca, & linguam habes vehementiorem, quam actum. Sed si quidem ornatus verborum in admiratione apud te est, pictores lingua tua pollentiores existunt; qui talia per tabulas effingunt, quæ natura facere non potest. quod si gaudere quoq; vides promissis auditores, breui quidem oblectas, non multo vero post contristas: id quod accidit istis tum multo molestius. quoniam & quæ in somniis apparent pulcherrima, non tantum nos læ- tos reddunt dormientes, quam tristes cum expergiscimur. Spes namque cum somno auolat. congruentes vero res adfer cum lingua, ne & amicis mentiendo reddaris inimicus, & inimicis vituperandi materiam præbeas, ut veritatis expers.
units.tr: You make many promises and do little, and your tongue is more violent than your deeds. But if the adornment of words is what you admire in yourself, your tongue turns out to be more powerful than the painters, who portray by their panels things that nature cannot make. But if you see that your hearers also rejoice in your promises, you delight them for a short time, and not long afterwards you sadden them; and this happens to them then all the more painfully. For even the most beautiful things that appear in dreams make us happy only while we sleep, and sad when we wake. For hope flies away with sleep. Bring your words into agreement with the facts, so that you do not become an enemy to your friends by lying, nor give your enemies material for blame, since you are without truth.

units.la: Ruf. Tettigon Ortygoni. XXXVIII.
units.tr: Ruf. Tettigon to Ortygon. XXXVIII.

units.la: Quid igitur vestem permutasti, & perdicces dissipasti? vinum tibi malo fuit. Vino etiam Cyclopis oculo positum esse dicunt Vlyssem. quare nifi congregaueris, Tettigon, auiculas, tecum praecipitabo etiam me. Nam puerum intemperanter vivere, graue est; & ante patrem sibi sepulchrum comparare filium, nimis quam est grauissimum.
units.tr: Why then have you changed your clothes and squandered your partridges? Wine was your undoing. They say Ulysses also put out the Cyclops' eye with wine. So unless you gather in your little birds, Tettigon, I shall throw myself down the cliff with you as well. For a boy who lives intemperately is a grievous thing, and for a son to prepare a tomb for himself before his father is far more grievous than anything.

units.la: Eth. THETIS ANAXARCHO. XXXIX.
units.tr: Eth. Thetis to Anaxarchus. XXXIX.

units.la: Non amare Thetidem potes, & Galatcam. neque pugnat enim cupido, neque dividuntur Amores. Sed neque duplicatum sufferre poteris amorem. Nam sicuti terra duobus solibus foveri non potest: sic una anima, duabus amatoriis facibus non est subiecta.
units.tr: You cannot love both Thetis and Galatea. For desire does not fight, and the Loves are not divided. But you will not be able to bear a doubled love either. For just as the earth cannot be warmed by two suns, so a single soul cannot be subjected to two torches of love.

units.la: Eth. SOCRATES PLATONI. XL.
units.tr: Eth. Socrates to Plato. XL.

units.la: Iniuriam patitur vero nemo, sed omnes afficiuntiniuria, vnusquisque; eam sibi sponte inferens, ac voluntario. Virtutis enim & vitii sumus Imperatores. Agrum tibi ademit Leonides: exceptis hisce, & animae tuae nequaquam nocuit, damnum dedit Philippus, & annulum in suum commodum adsumsit, nihil iniuriarum intulit. Haec enim aliunde acquisita, & aduentitia, non sunt nostra, tuum filium rapuerunt barbari, nihil passus es mali. non enim in aeternum possedisti puerum. Nuper tibi non habenti natus est, & iterum non est, quoniam non est, sed fuit, non igitur iniuriam inferunt, non patiuntur homines. & Homericum Cyclopem admiratus sum, qui nulli ex iniuria nocere te dicebat, & erat ea pastori elocutio, quae est veritatis affirmatio.
units.tr: No one, however, suffers an injury, but everyone inflicts injury on himself, each one, bringing it upon himself willingly and of his own accord. For we are the commanders of virtue and vice. Leonides took a field from you; apart from these things, he has in no way harmed your soul. Philip caused a loss and took the ring for his own advantage; he inflicted no injury. For these things are acquired from elsewhere and are adventitious; they are not ours. Barbarians carried off your son; you suffered no evil, for you did not possess the boy forever. Recently he was born to you when you did not have him, and again he is not, since he is not but was. Therefore they do not inflict injury, and men do not suffer it. I also admired the Homeric Cyclops, who said that you harmed no one by injury; that was the shepherd's way of speaking, which is an affirmation of the truth.

units.la: Ruff.
units.tr: Ruff.

units.la: Ruft.[?] MARATHO PEGANONI. XLI.
units.tr: Ruft.[?] Marathon of Peganon. XLI.

units.la: Ciuilium molestiarum procellam fugiens, & invitabiles turbas urbis; precio conduxi hunc agrum, & animæ inde recreationem arbitrabar suturam. Sed in maiora mala coniecti sumus. Nunc enim rubiginem habeo infestam, nunc locustas: alias etiam grandinem, pruina verò corrumpit fructus, tanquam hostis inexorabilis, & sudoribus meis miser ventis gratificor. heu me infelicem! quo me vertam? quando labores rusticos conduximus, urbana appetimus: quando versamur in strepitu urbico, ea quæ in villicatione sunt, amo, & præsentibus absentia semper potiora iudico. Molestiarum una solutio mors est, siue naturalis illa fit, siue rursum manu facta, non igitur suffocationem adhibere pro medicamento reformido, Differre namq; mortem infortunatos, stultum est.
units.tr: Fleeing the storm of civic troubles and the unwelcome crowds of the city, I hired this field for a price, and I thought it would bring my soul some refreshment. But we have been thrown into greater evils. For now rust attacks me, now locusts; at other times hail, and frost ruins the fruit like an implacable enemy, and I wretchedly offer my sweat to the winds. Alas for me! Where shall I turn? When we have taken on rustic labours, we long for city life; when we live in the noise of the city, we love the concerns of farming, and we always judge absent things better than present ones. The one release from troubles is death, whether it comes naturally or is brought about by one's own hand; so I do not dread choking myself as a remedy. For to put off death is foolish for the unfortunate.

units.la: Amat. PERICLES ASPASIÆ. XL- II.
units.tr: Amat. PERICLES ASPASIÆ. XL- II.

units.la: Si dona quæris, nonamas. non enim acceptant amores munera; & eadem lege suos instruunt amantes. Si quidem igitur amas, dare potius, quàm accipere te conuenit, si vero bonaappetis, & propter diuitias amorem simulasti, animum lingua redarguit, vendens auro voluptates cuicunque cupienti.
units.tr: If you seek gifts, you do not love. For love does not accept presents, and by the same law it arms its lovers. If, then, you truly love, it becomes you to give rather than to receive; but if you desire good things and have feigned love for the sake of riches, your tongue betrays your mind, selling pleasures for gold to whoever desires them.

units.la: Eth. DIOGENES DEMONICO. XLIII.
units.tr: Ethical. Diogenes to Demonicus. XLIII.

units.la: Arteilla facta fœmina, semivir bis natus, ad naturam neutram neq; perfectus, nec utilis, contumelia afficiendus venit Lydius Eunuchus. omnia enim corporis membra linguam habere clamant non ingenuam, ego vero secundum Homericum Vlyssem eiusmodi tela non sentio. Absurdum namque foret, si mulicbris sexus herois animum percuteret. Latrare igitur & furere Eunuchis convenit, quia privati manuum vi, omnia volunt lingua agere. Nostram vero amici lenitatem accusant, quoniam contumeliosum non poenis remunerati sumus. Sic enim & asinus si calcitrarit, non ei tribunal denunciabis, quod etiam idem à Sophronisci filio Socrate pulchrè dictum est.
units.tr: Made into a woman, a half-man twice born, neither fully of either nature nor useful, the Lydian eunuch comes to be insulted. For all his limbs cry out that his tongue is not free-born, but I, following Homeric Ulysses, do not feel such weapons. It would be absurd if the feminine sex could wound the spirit of a hero. Eunuchs ought to bark and rage, since, deprived of the strength of their hands, they wish to do everything with their tongues. They accuse our friend's gentleness because we have not repaid the insult with punishment. For so, if an ass kicks, you will not summon him before a tribunal, a point Socrates, son of Sophroniscus, also made nicely.

units.la: Rust. PRAMIDES CORYDONI. XLIV.
units.tr: Rustic. Pramides to Corydon. XLIV.

units.la: Cras convivium dabimus, omnia ad nuptias mihi parata sunt, pulmentarium ex leguminibus, cicer, caricæ multæ, & mulsum, & placenta, & popana. ipse autem adfer artificem istam fistulam, mela cantaturus omnes hymnos euincentia, es enim pastoralis musicæ peritus, Corydon. Consilium enim cepi thalamum venereis voluptatibus sollicitare vocibus exhilaratum tibiæ.
units.tr: Tomorrow we will give a feast; everything is prepared for my wedding: a side dish of pulses, chickpeas, many dried figs, mead, cakes and popana. But you yourself bring that skilful pipe, to sing hymns that surpass all others, for you are skilled in pastoral music, Corydon. For I have resolved to stir the bridal chamber with the pleasures of love, delighted by the voice of the flute.

units.la: Amat. LEANDER PYLADI. XLV.
units.tr: Amatory. Leander to Pylades. XLV.

units.la: Nimis nobis adversantur amores, ego quidem amo, at amata odit. & quid agam miserrimus?Non æqualem habent amorem lancem, & inæqualiter dependunt hominibus lacrimas. Si ergo iniuriam faciunt, Dei non nominentur: si nomen non mentiuntur, recte iudicent, & dolores itaque mihi non iniquo modo dividant.
units.tr: Loves are too much against us. I indeed love, but the beloved hates. What shall I do, most wretched? They do not hold an even balance of love, and they weigh out tears to men unequally. If therefore they do wrong, let them not be named before God; if they do not lie in the name, let them judge rightly, and so divide my pains in no unfair measure.

units.la: Eth. DIOGENES ARISTARCHO. XLVI.
units.tr: Ethical. Diogenes to Aristarchus. XLVI.

units.la: Macedoniam perculit Alexander, Bucephalo inuectus equo. Eum vero equum narrant, neque freno dominari potuisse, neque mansuetis blandimentis emolliri. Intractabile enim animal fuit, & quod tantum non voluerit non esse equus, & malum quoddam inaccessum fuit, obuiisque nimis ominosum. Vndeigitur ascendit Alexander[?] immanitatem equus quasi lenitate miscuit mutata superbia in fubmiffionem, vt videre fuerit temperantem intemperantem. Neque enim fas fuit Alexandro repugnare. Esto itaque, Ariftarche, tu quoque fortunæ obtemperans. Nam non Alexandro, sed fortunæ obediuit Bucephalus.
units.tr: Alexander struck Macedonia, mounted on Bucephalus. They say that horse could be governed neither by the bridle nor softened by gentle caresses. It was an intractable animal, one that would not be a horse at all, a kind of untamable evil and too ominous to approach. Yet Alexander mounted it, and by a kind of gentleness he tempered the beast's savagery, changing its pride into submission, so that the intemperate became temperate. For it was not right for Alexander to resist. So be it, Aristarchus: you too must obey fortune. For Bucephalus obeyed not Alexander, but fortune.

units.la: Ruft. POEMNION ARNONI. XLVII.
units.tr: Rustic. Poemnion to Arnon. XLVII.

units.la: Vbera mearum ouium à lacte disrumpentur. & mulgariorum nescio vnde fimus habituri fatis. Quare da tu mihi quidem mulgaria: contra ego tibi dabo lac, magnis donis paruas relaturus gratias.
units.tr: The udders of my ewes will burst with milk, and I do not know where I shall get enough dung for the milking-pails. So give me the milking-pails, and I will give you milk in return, and I shall repay small favours with great gifts.

units.la: Amat. CHRYSOGONA TERPANDRO. XLVII- I.
units.tr: Amatory. Chrysogona to Terpander. XLVIII.

units.la: Ne reprehendas probris insectantē te amasiam, & contumeliis. Suauiter enim sæpè potiuntur voluptatibus amatores, sæpè verò etiam plagis & vibicibus insigniuntur. Si verò contumelia cæsus ægrè fers, neq; rosam carpes, qui spinam euitas.
units.tr: Do not reproach with insults and abuse the mistress who harasses you. Lovers often enjoy their pleasures sweetly, but they are often marked with blows and weals too. If, struck by insult, you take it badly, you will not pluck the rose if you shun the thorn.

units.la: Eth. LEONIDES PERIANDRO. XLIX.
units.tr: Ethical. Leonides to Periander. XLIX.

units.la: Misertus est Priamum filius Theticlis orantem, Canos, n. hoftiū reucritus est Pelides, patriq; mortuum dat filium, infelicissimo dono muneratus Priamum, & eius quidem audaciam sum miratus, huius vero humanitatem laudaui. Fias mihi tu quoq; Æacides, & cani capitis miserere lacrimas, filio mihi meo vivo reddito. Infelicitamur enim & nos, ut & Priamus. Tenamq;, qui non es hostis, de puero rogamus lacrimis, nonatramento epistolæ conscribillantes litteras. Sed si quidem humanitatem tuam obtinere amas, anteuertat petitionem donatio. quod si vero ratio tibi non moderatur, sed iraq; & tetricitas antiquiora sunt, ad breue quidem lætus eris: tristaberis vero magis, tam duri & à philosopho alieni animi magnas aliquando luiturus pœnas.
units.tr: The son of Thetis took pity on Priam when he begged, for he respected the grey head of his enemy, and he gave back the dead son to his father, rewarding Priam with the most unhappy of gifts. I admired his boldness, and I praised his humanity. Be you too, son of Aeacus, have pity on a grey head with its tears, my son being restored to me alive. For we too are unhappy, as Priam was. We ask you, who are not an enemy, about the boy with tears, not scribbling letters with ink. But if you wish to win a reputation for humanity, let the gift anticipate the request. If, however, reason does not moderate you, and anger and harshness hold sway, you will be glad for a short while but will grieve more, destined at some time to pay great penalties for a mind so hard and so alien to a philosopher.

units.la: Ruff. CALAMO SPIRONI. L.
units.tr: Rustic. Calamus to Spiron. L.

units.la: Si agricola esse constituisti, turbis urbanorum abstine. si vero Rhetoribus, curiisq; ac tribunalibus studes, remisso ligone, fumtisq; calamo & chartā, ad corvos ito, Senecio. Non enim sycophantas homines, & id Iudices crebrius iterantes, rusticorum admittit politia.
units.tr: If you have resolved to be a farmer, keep away from the crowds of townsmen. But if you are devoted to rhetoric, law courts and tribunals, put down the hoe, take up pen and paper, and go to the crows, Senecio. For the polity of countrymen does not admit sycophants, men who repeatedly haunt the judges.

units.la: Amat. RHODOPLEA HYPSIPVLÆ. LI.
units.tr: Amatory. Rhodoplea to Hypsipyle. LI.

units.la: Pirœum heri noctu forte circuivi, & amatorem tuum cum Chryfippa vidi: & adolescens prælucebat facem: & qui ex amicis honoris ergo præirent, anus erat Abrotonium. cum vero eam quæ ibat præ, alloquerer, rogavit amator tuus ne hæc paam [?] quæ in tenebris facta essent, divulgarentur. Igitur neq; iuranti, neq; blandienti credas. Linguæ enim dolus utrum libet est fallax.
units.tr: I happened to walk around the Piraeus last night, and I saw your lover with Chrysippa. A young man was carrying a torch, and those who went before them, out of friendly respect, were an old woman, Abrotonium. When I addressed the woman who was walking in front, your lover asked that what was done in the dark should not be divulged. So believe neither the one who swears nor the one who flatters, for the tongue's trickery is deceptive, whichever way it turns.

units.la: Eth. SOCRATES CLEONI. LII.
units.tr: Eth. SOCRATES TO CLEON. LII.

units.la: Quando lupi magna prœda potiti sunt, & satie-tate sibi temperant, abstinent quodam modo ab agnis, & more isto fero in humanitatem verso mirabili quadam iustitia imbuuntur à satietate. cum quibus enim una pascunt, & parcunt donec venter latrauerit. Sed tu lupis morem habes impudentiorem, & co auariori multo es intemperantia, quando aurum catuziunt tui thesauri, non secus atque ebriis accidere solet: qui cum vino saturati sunt, tamen sitiunt, & in ebrietate, ebrietatis augent vehementiam. propter enim summam copiam ad contrariam dispositionem exhilarante simul & exurente vino, ebriosi dilabuntur. apage intemperantem ebrietatem isthanc intemperans, nequandoque, si fortuna ea, quæ dedit, auferat, ad contrariam partem devoluaris; talibus enim pœnis immoderatos castigat atque temperat.
units.tr: When wolves have seized a great prey, they are sated and restrain themselves; in a manner they hold off from the lambs, and their savage nature, turned into a kind of humanity, is steeped in a remarkable justice that comes from satiety. For they graze with the lambs and spare them until their belly growls. But you have a more shameless habit than wolves, and you are far more intemperate in your greed, since your treasuries gush with gold, much as usually happens to drunkards. Although they are saturated with wine, they still thirst, and in their drunkenness they increase the violence of their drunkenness. For because of the great abundance, the wine, which both exhilarates and burns, pulls the drinkers over to the opposite condition, and they slip and fall. Away with that intemperate drunkenness, you intemperate man! Lest, if fortune takes away what it has given, you be tumbled over to the opposite side. For by such punishments it chastises and tempers the immoderate.

units.la: Ruff. MINTHES RHIZONI. LIII.
units.tr: Ruff. MINTHES RHIZONI. LIII.

units.la: Fluvius Chrysippus agelli mei partem furatus est, & agro tuo vindicauit stultum quid committens, & vecors in re aliena sibi potestatem facit. sed si quidem tribunalis onus tuis humeris ferre non es par, donis fluvij ne fruaris, si vero alienis rebus gaudes, non multo post flebis privatus & exutus tuis.
units.tr: The river Chrysippus has stolen part of my little field and claimed it for your land; in doing so you commit a foolish act, and in your madness you make yourself master of what belongs to another. But if indeed you are not equal to bearing the burden of the tribunal on your shoulders, do not enjoy the gifts of the river; and if you do rejoice in other people's goods, you will not long from now weep, stripped and deprived of your own.

units.la: eAmat. MEDEA IASONI. LIV.
units.tr: Amat. MEDEA TO JASON. LIV.

units.la: Nihil ita positum est in studio hominis, aut fastidio, quàm affectio amatoria, vbi tibi lacrimarum flumina,quæ ad pedes nostros defudisti? vbi auolas runt tibi mille ista genera sermonum illorum & verborum,aut fubmiffio,& humilitas? puto neque fœnerantes eiusmodi ad fœneratores vti verbis, neq; vulneratum,quum in hostiles deuenit manus. Continuaabiit in somnia,matutina reliquisti blandimenta, abiecisti mille preces, pactaiuramenta, quæ per adminiftorias foeminas mihi fanciuifti. adaliam de subito puellam delapsus es, quemadmodum qui dormiunt indiscriminatim ab unoin fomnio relabuntur ad alterum. Laudo pictores. eltos enim amores pingunt, & arte transformant id quod verè est,& fictionibus veritatem exprimunt.
units.tr: Nothing in a man's pursuits is so set aside, or so despised, as an amorous passion. Where are the streams of tears you poured out at my feet? Where have those thousand kinds of speeches and words flown, and your submissiveness and humility? I suppose that people who lend money do not use such words to moneylenders, nor does a wounded man use them when he falls into enemy hands. You have gone off into dreams; you have left behind your morning flatteries, and cast aside a thousand prayers and sworn oaths, which you once pledged to me through your go-between women. Suddenly you have slipped over to another girl, just as sleepers, without distinction, pass from one dream to another. I praise painters, for they paint lovers as they should be and, by their art, transform what is true, and through their fictions express the truth.

units.la: Eth. PARMENIDES CHRYSOSTHENI. LV.
units.tr: Eth. PARMENIDES TO CHRYSOSTHENES. LV.

units.la: Experrectum quidem esse per omnia, immortalis naturæ proprium est, moderatè verò dormire, est ex iis quæ nos præstare possumus, & ut videtur, humanum. sed ultra dormire quàm decet conueniens potius mortuis est, quâ vivis plurimas, Chrysosthenes, tuæ vitæ partes abstulisti. semper enim dormis, & ab hislocis te transfers, veluti quidam Vlysses extra habitatum nobis orbem exerrans, quasi in Oceani vicem vsus somno; & neque surgentem neq; cadentem Solem videns.
units.tr: To be fully awake at all times is a property of an immortal nature; to sleep in moderation is among the things we are able to manage, and, as it seems, is human. But to sleep beyond what is fitting belongs rather to the dead than to the living, Chrysosthenes, and by it you have taken away the greater part of your life. For you are always asleep, and you carry yourself from place to place, like some Ulysses wandering beyond the world we inhabit, who, as if in the place of the ocean, has used sleep, and sees neither the rising nor the setting sun.

units.la: Ruff. DAPHNON ÆGIRO. LVI.
units.tr: Ruff. DAPHNON TO AEGIRUS. LVI.

units.la: Ficus tuæ in meum fundamentum radices extenderunt, sub ditione tua amplius esse detrectantes. & iurisdictione tua sublata mihi donant suos prouentus, ad meos enim labores sua sponte transfugerunt. & id legis est rusticis, & obedi moribus inveteratis, senecio. quod si moribus nostris vis contradicere, ut novum te existentem legislatorem, & recentem, exturbabimus, & extra limites nostros eiiciemus, ut alienum.
units.tr: Your figs have stretched their roots into my estate, refusing any longer to be under your control. With your jurisdiction removed, they now give me their produce, for they have of their own accord gone over to my labours. This is the law for country folk, and you must obey long-established customs, old man. But if you wish to oppose our customs, as though you were a new and recent lawgiver, we will drive you out and throw you beyond our boundaries as a foreigner.

units.la: Amat, BYRRHIA PHILONIDI. LVII.
units.tr: Amat, BYRRHIA TO PHILONIDES. LVII.

units.la: Si amas, ne accusa deformitatem amatoris, non enim potest non cæcutire amans anima. Nam pervicax est amantium inter se mutuo affectus. si non amas, quid fles, & ingemiscis, & molestiam infers tibi ipsi voluntariam? utrinque igitur peccas, modo quidem, ut amator non bonus; modo ut antagonista formidolosus.
units.tr: If you are in love, do not complain of the lover's ugliness, for a loving soul cannot help being blinded. Indeed, the affection between lovers is stubborn toward one another. If you are not in love, why do you weep and groan, and bring voluntary distress upon yourself? So either way you are at fault: in one case as a poor lover, in the other as a timid rival.

units.la: Eth. DAMASCVS ANTIGONO. LVII- I.
units.tr: Eth. DAMASCUS TO ANTIGONUS. LVII- I.

units.la: Si vitæ pignora Socrates non habuit, pædagogus tuo filio non adsumatur. Vitæ vero pignora, intelligantur esse liberi. quem enim natura docuit esse patrem, eundem etiam pædagogum filiorum debere esse, sit verisimile: reipsa discentem & generationis habitū, & paterni in liberos amoris anxietatem.
units.tr: If Socrates did not have the pledges of life, let no one be chosen as tutor for your son. But the pledges of life are to be understood as children. For it is likely that the one whom nature taught to be a father ought also to be the tutor of his sons, learning in practice both the character of parenthood and the anxious love of a father for his children.

units.la: Rust. CEPIA CORIANO. LIX.
units.tr: Rust. CEPIA TO CORIANUS. LIX.

units.la: Adiutor esto mihi sub meridiem, Coriane. Maceria namq; agrum intersepiam, malos enim viatores habemus, nec sufficiendo sum brutis simul animalibus atq; hominibus. Lepus vineas, eruca deperdit olera. De talpis vero quid dicam? horribile enim hoc est malum rusticis, & hostis cui resisti non potest. quare te mihi adiunge, & partem laboris in te suscipias. & ego rursus iisdem operibus compensabo. Sic enim formicæ quoq; per mutuas operas laborem conficiunt, & maxima etiam quæque aggrediuntur.
units.tr: Help me out after noon, Corianus. For I am walling in my field with a wall, since we have wicked passers-by, and I cannot cope with both the beasts and the men at once. The hare ruins the vines, the rocket destroys the vegetables. And what shall I say about the moles? For this is a dreadful pest to country folk, an enemy that cannot be resisted. So join yourself to me and take on a share of the labour, and I in turn will repay you with the same kind of work. For in this way even ants finish their labour through mutual service, and they tackle even the largest tasks.

units.la: Amat. ANTHE'A BRIONI. LX.
units.tr: Amat. ANTHEA TO BRION. LX.

units.la: Omnia fœmineo sexui subiecta sunt; Laidem amat Diogenes; Softratam Phrygius; Philosophiæ maiestas periit; venerandos mores abiecerunt, ætheriam mentem reliquerunt, altum istud studium ementiti sunt; omnia euanuére, quæcunque olim illis ad exercitium faciebant. Intempestum verò ludicrum videtur esse mihi, virum senem, cano capite reuerendum, superbientem venerabilitate, adolescentis meretriculæ amore captum. Ego verò Cachinnos, & risum continere nequeo, quandocunque sollicitor ab istiusmodi senecionibus. Multum enim olim damnarunt Venerem, &, quod amplius est, amantes insanire furorem voluntarium, dixerunt, appetitu intemperantis animæ amores esse definientes, omnia ferre, sapientis est, sperare verò nimis est quam prudentissimum, nam multa tempus & fortuna possunt,
units.tr: Everything is made subject to the female sex. Diogenes loves Lais; the Phrygian loves Sostrata. The dignity of philosophy has perished; they have cast off their venerable manners, abandoned their heavenly minds, and pretended to that lofty pursuit; everything has vanished that once served their practice. It seems to me a most unseasonable joke that an old man, reverend for his grey head, proud of his dignity, should be captured by love for a young courtesan. As for me, I cannot keep from laughing whenever I am troubled by such old gentlemen. For the philosophers of old condemned Venus much, and, what is more, they said that lovers are mad with a self-chosen frenzy, defining love as the appetite of an intemperate soul; to bear everything is the mark of a wise man, but to hope is too much even for the most prudent, for time and fortune can do much.

units.la: Eth. SOSTRATVS LYSISTRATO. LXI.
units.tr: Eth. SOSTRATUS TO LYSISTRATUS. LXI.

units.la: Posteaquam pluribus & mirandis monitis sæpè, Penelopæ quidem telam visus sum detexere, agedum tandem, age, & fabulosam narrationem incipiamus, tuum enim forte captum dicta penetrabunt. In nouellis arbustis cicada sedens æstatis tempore, cecinit; & suam ipsius Harmoniam sentiens, eâ est oblectata. Formica verò messoribus aderat, & circa arcam est versata, & in terræ sinus abscondidit sua cibaria, vt quæ formica prudentior existeret cicadâ. Transiuit igitur à Boreali parte Sol, abiit autumnal, & hyems defcenditin terram. mare vérò tranquillitatis suæ fidem fregit. nautæ portus, vt in quibus salui forent, sunt amplexi, & rusticus fe ad suum recepit focum, ac formica in imis terræ visceribus exiis, quæ laborauerat, pabulum habebat sufficiens. supplex verò cicada à formica petiit, vt partem sibi daret repositorum. hæc verò melodam ablegauit à suis foribus, irrisam valdè ob pigritiam: eis; in memoriam reuocauit æstiuos cantus. Quapropter illi cessit cantus in famem: huic verò labor in luxum & opimitatem. Quadratin te fabula, Lysistrate. piger enim febricitante estinfelicior, duplo tantum comedens, quantum diligens. apage igitur pigritiam, optime, confpurcasti enim naturæ dona, dum vires eiusmodi roburque corporis, laborum exercitio neglecto, incultum præteris.
units.tr: Since I have often, with many striking admonitions, seemed to unravel Penelope's web, come now, come, let us begin a fabulous story, for perhaps what has been said will penetrate your ear. In the young shrubs a cicada, sitting in summer, sang; and feeling its own harmony, it took delight in it. But an ant was present with the reapers, and it ran about the threshing-floor and hid its food in the hollows of the earth, so that the ant might prove wiser than the cicada. Then the sun passed over from the northern part and departed into autumn, and winter came down upon the earth. The sea broke the faith of its calm; the sailors embraced the harbours, as places in which they might be safe, and the countryman returned to his own hearth. The ant, in the deepest recesses of the earth, had sufficient food from what it had laboured to gather. But the cicada, as a suppliant, asked the ant to give it a share of the stored provisions. The ant, however, sent the singer away from its doors, mocking it heartily for its idleness, and reminded it of its summer songs. Thus the song turned to hunger for the one, and the labour turned to luxury and plenty for the other. This story fits you, Lysistratus. For the idler is more unhappy when feverish, eating twice as much as the diligent man. Away, then, with idleness, my good fellow, for you have defiled the gifts of nature, while, neglecting the exercise of labour, you let the strength and vigour of your body go uncultivated.

units.la: Ruff. Tertigon Porphyrioni. LXII.
units.tr: Ruff. Tertigon to Porphyrio. LXII.

units.la: Felix vir est Corydon, & vt videtur, fortunæ amicus. Vites vuis grauantur, pyri curuantur, ac decerpi volunt, oleæ pronutantin terram, & multitudine fructuum ramos cogunt. prata, spissa græmine area florentibus similis sulcis. & muliercula post omnia exhilarat coniugem. Tot enim habet pueros, vt Danaum & Ægyptum fœcunditate vincat, alius enim est subrumus; alius lactare destitit; alij verò repunt nondum rectâ inambulantes: ali- qui balbutiunt, & dentes mutant: alij ad florem veniunt, & iam sunt adulti. arundinum in modum, quæ dispares collocantur in sistula, ætatum illi ordo conmine venationis dolos suos pertexit peffimus. sed neq; Lepus apud nos versatur, neque dorcas errat, neq; bubali, neque cerui, neq; aliquid aliud eorum quæ ad venationem sint utilia. Metu enim carcerū laqueorumq;, quibus capiuntur, arcentur hinc lepores[?]: dorcades autem & bubalides, vicinorum leonum. & quid tandem tibi millegenera ferarum recenscam, cum quibus simul etiam nos cfurimus? quod enim nulli homines hic sunt nobis, quod nullæ feræ feris malo est. Quoniā itaq; tibi cognatio intercedit, & nceeffitudo[?] cum iniurioso isto, Ciffybie[?], fac quod est optimum, & tui sermones cū reddant modcftiorem[?]. Nam scito illum canibus lacerandum, fi posthac nostros agros frequentarit. Iam verò canis fœmina cum filiis custodit mihi agllum[?] humana pinguedine expleri gcftiens[?].
units.tr: Corydon is a fortunate man and, it seems, a favourite of fortune. The vines are weighed down with grapes, the pear trees bend and beg to be picked, the olive trees nod towards the ground, and their branches are forced down by the sheer number of their fruit. The meadows are thick with grass, and the threshing floor is like a field of flowering furrows. And his little wife cheers her husband above all. For she has so many children that she would outdo the fertility of the Danaids and of Egypt: one is still a suckling, another has stopped nursing, others crawl and cannot yet walk upright, some babble and are losing their teeth, and others are coming into bloom and are already grown. They are arranged by age like reeds set unequally in a pipe. Yet the worst of hunters has woven his snares here. But no hare lives among us, no gazelle wanders, no buffalo or stag, nor anything else useful for hunting. For hares are kept away from here by fear of the pens and nooses in which they are caught, and gazelles and buffaloes by the neighbouring lions. And why should I recount to you the thousand kinds of wild beasts, with which we too are at war at the same time? For since there are no men here to be our enemies, no wild beast is a harm to another. Since, then, you have kinship and close ties with that wrongdoer, Cissybius, do what is best, and let your words make him more restrained. For know that he will be torn apart by dogs if he henceforth frequents our fields. Indeed, a bitch with her puppies is already guarding my little field, eager to be filled with human fat.

units.la: Amat. PITHO HIPPOLYTO. LXVI.
units.tr: Amat. Pitho to Hippolytus. LXVI.

units.la: Formam, non morum grauitatem amplectuntur potius amantes. Nam temperantiam non promittunt amores. sed pulchritudine corporis, oculum intemperantem inescant.quare fi propter mores Rhodocleam amas, non voluptatibus dominanturamores. Etenim ratione philosopha tclum[?] venereum non tangitur.
units.tr: Lovers embrace beauty of form rather than gravity of character. For love does not promise temperance; with bodily beauty it lures the intemperate eye. So if you love Rhodoclea for her character, love does not rule over your pleasures. For a philosopher's reasoning is not touched by the venereal dart.

units.la: Eth. ERATOSTHENES ÆSCHINI. LXVII.
units.tr: Eth. Eratosthenes to Aeschines. LXVII.

units.la: Iuramenta deuoras velut holera, & fi dentes complofcrisin numeratorem habere putas. adhaec expoltulantibus de hac re tecum, obloquutis, Lin-gua iui aui,mentem tuam atam gero: non sciens infrenè linguam, maiorem peccati subituram castigationé. Quæ enim sermone peccamus, re vera luemus. Moderatam igitur seruato linguam, caueosque vt non nisi cum veritate iures: nam cum leuis res videatur esse iuramentum: omni tamen onere grauius est. vnde Tantalus etiam punitus est, quoniam in rebus diuinis linguæ suæ non poterat moderari.
units.tr: You gobble up oaths like vegetables, and you think your teeth are a counting-house. When people remonstrate with you about this matter, you answer them with the line, "My tongue has sworn; the mind I carry is unsworn." Not knowing how to bridle your tongue, you will suffer a heavier punishment for sin. For what we sin with speech we shall in truth pay for. Therefore keep your tongue in check, and take care to swear only with truth. For though an oath seems a light matter, it is weightier than any burden. Hence Tantalus too was punished, because he could not restrain his tongue in divine matters.

units.la: Ruff. Sevtlio Coriano. LXVIII.
units.tr: Ruffus to Sextilius Coriano. LXVIII.

units.la: Cepi demum peffimam vulpeculam, & captam diuersis vinculis custodio fceleftiffimam, educamque in publicum, Coriane rusticis omnibus conuocatis, ac de hoste triumphabo. & publice ea poenas accipiet, pro multis malis vnum subitura supplicium.
