units.tr: At last I have caught the most wicked little fox. Bound in various chains, I am keeping the most criminal creature under guard, and I will lead her out into public, Corianus, once all the country people have been called together, and triumph over my enemy. Publicly she will receive her punishment, and she will suffer one execution to atone for her many crimes.

units.la: Amat. Calliope Laidi. LXIX.
units.tr: Amatoria. Calliope on Lais. LXIX.

units.la: Crobylo & cicada Gorgias ornatur, nondum pubescens. & ferocit propter formam, escamque doloris proponit nobis decorem. ego vero & fenectam,& morbum, & tristitiam tabulis inscribi-lans, ante ianuam amentis deponam, ea enim habebit aliquando suæ formæ decoriq; aduersaria.
units.tr: Gorgias adorns himself with a topknot and a cicada, though he is not yet grown up. He is proud of his looks and offers us the bait of pain as his charm. But I will have old age, sickness and sadness written on tablets and hang them by their thongs before the door, for one day she will be the enemy of her own beauty and grace.

units.la: Eth. Plato Axiocho. LXX.
units.tr: Eth. Plato Axiocho. LXX.

units.la: Habenis equos dirigimus, & nauigamus alias quidem velis extendentes nauim: alias anchoris frenantes quasi retinemus. sic gubernandum linguam, Axioche, alias quidem sermonibus exercen-do, alias autem silentio consopiendo.
units.tr: We steer horses with reins, and we sail, now stretching out the ship's sails, now checking and as it were holding it back with anchors. So too the tongue must be governed, Axiochus: now by exercising it in speech, now by lulling it into silence.

units.la: Ruff. RHODON CYPARISSO. LXXI.
units.tr: Ruff. Rhodon Cyparisso. LXXI.

units.la: Lucanos iterum obvenisse dicunt. ideo abiecta falce, hastam & stimulum fabricabo, & artem bel-licam exercebo. non enim nos ociari patitur Deus: mihi hyeme æstas est gelidior. nam quid bello fit horridius? vere adueniente fleui. quam comatus ager stat floribus, quam odoratus a myrtis agellus, quam ornata spissa ista platanus? virct[?] triticum, omnia mihi ad abundantiam festinant. sed malum nobis dant hostes. exoptabilior enim iis ensis est aratro.
units.tr: They say the Lucanians have come again. So I will put aside my sickle and fashion a spear and a goad, and practise the art of war. For God does not allow us to be idle: to me winter is warmer than summer. For what is more dreadful than war? When spring comes, I weep. How the field stands crowned with flowers, how fragrant the little farm is with myrtles, how thick and adorned that plane tree is! The wheat grows green, everything hastens to abundance for me. But our enemies bring us harm; for the sword is more welcome to them than the plough.

units.la: Amat. SOPATER TELESILLÆ. LXXII.
units.tr: Amat. SOPATER TELESILLÆ. LXXII.

units.la: Nisi venereis voluptatibus invenustam satietatem miscuisset natura, seruiret iam sexus masculus feminino, Telesilla. Non igitur superbias, mercatricula. Veneris mihi fax iam emortua est. neque dolores immortales amorum tela faciunt.
units.tr: If nature had not mixed unlovely satiety into the pleasures of Venus, Telesilla, the male sex would already be enslaved to the female. So do not be proud, little trader. The torch of Venus has already gone out for me, and the immortal pains of love are no longer made by the arrows of desire.

units.la: Eth. PROCLVS ARCHIMEDI. LXXIII.
units.tr: Ethical. PROCLUS TO ARCHIMEDES. LXXIII.

units.la: Polypos dicunt in capturæ penuria, tricas suas deuorare, membra sua nimirum miserrima, tanquam opsonium recuera[?] apparatum. Eduntigitur infelices membrorum suorum partes tenuissimas, & ostenduntur comedones esse propriæ carnis. Vt vero Xanthippe non omnibus habere polypi mentem videaris, saltem sane ego illud esse creado certissimum. Tractas enim nimis inhumaniter tuum patrem, neque naturam veritus, neq; poenam, quemadmodum barathrum timeri solet metuens. Sed si quidem refipicas, immemorem præteritorum malorum experieris Pronemesin : si vero in furiosa ista aurifame ineuitabili nempe malo perseveraveris, æqualem Lancem Deus tibi trutinat & pueros habebis paternæ malitiæ imagines & simulacra verissima. Sic enim & viperini partus maternam impietatem excipiunt, prægnantem & alumnam aluum disrumpendo.
units.tr: They say that when polyps lack prey they devour their own tentacles, their own most wretched limbs, as if these were a prepared relish. So the unhappy creatures eat the finest parts of their own limbs, and they are shown to be eaters of their own flesh. But so that you, Xanthippe, may not seem to have the mind of a polyp, at least I am quite certain you do not. For you treat your father far too inhumanly, neither respecting nature nor fearing punishment, as one who dreads the abyss is wont to fear. But if you indeed turn back, you will find that Retribution does not forget past evils. If, however, you persist in that frenzied hunger for gold, an evil that cannot be escaped, God will weigh out for you an equal balance, and you will have sons who are the images and very true likenesses of your paternal malice. For in this way also the offspring of vipers avenge their mother's impiety, by bursting the womb that is pregnant with them and nourishes them.

units.la: Rust. ELAPHO DORCONI. LXXIV.
units.tr: Rustic. ELAPHUS TO DORCON. LXXIV.

units.la: Fœcundus est ad fructus producendos, fimus pecudum. quare da mihi tuarum pecudum stercus. & contra recipies tu quoque precium beneficentiæ pyra, atque olera. sic tuum munus gratiis splendidioribus remunerabor.
units.tr: Animal dung is fertile for producing fruits. Therefore give me the dung of your cattle, and in return you too will receive the price of your kindness, pears and vegetables. Thus I shall repay your gift with more splendid thanks.

units.la: Amat. ARISTOXENVS POLYXENÆ. LXXV.
units.tr: Amatory. ARISTOXENUS TO POLYXENA. LXXV.

units.la: Meretriciis voluptatibus nihil instabilius est. infida sunt osculalabiarum tuarum. amor enim qui radices non egit, statim marcescit. ego temperantiam istam quæ videtur vulgò invenusta, eligam potius. stabilitatem enim præfert, & dote emam nuptias. Nam fidem emere meretriciam, difficillimum est.
units.tr: Nothing is more unstable than the pleasures of harlots. The kisses of your lips are untrustworthy. For love that has not taken root withers at once. I would rather choose that temperance which is commonly thought unlovely. For it prefers stability, and I will buy a marriage with a dowry. For to buy a harlot's fidelity is most difficult.

units.la: Eth. DIOGENES SOTIONI. LXXVI.
units.tr: Ethical. DIOGENES TO SOTION. LXXVI.

units.la: Parua hæc gloria tale quid videtur esse sapientibus, quale quod videmus in somniis. & fictis fabulis inanior est, & peior: instabilis; levis; ludus sonis reciprocis Echus & ventis vanior. Hæc eadem & cùm abest, molestè nos habet. & cùm accedit, ampliorem tristitiam facit. Etenim non multo post improba in cupitos suos deprehenditur : & ante esse transcurrit ad non esse. ne te concutiant fortunæ flatus: quæ ludit homines prout vult. Vanitates enim vanitatum sunt res hominum.
units.tr: This small glory seems to the wise to be of the same kind as what we see in dreams. It is emptier and worse than fictional tales: unstable, light, a plaything of echoing sounds, and more vain than the wind. This same glory, when it is absent, troubles us, and when it comes, it brings greater sadness. For not long afterwards it is caught out, and it passes from being to not being. Do not let the blasts of fortune shake you, for she toys with men as she pleases. For the affairs of men are vanities of vanities.

units.la: Rust. BVCOLION MYRONIDÆ. LXXVII
units.tr: Rustic. BUCOLION TO MYRONIDES. LXXVII.

units.la: Mazę tuum nepotem reddunt petulantem, Myronides. rubro panno bucceta terruit. & vitulum amabilem istum præcipitauit: Æquales autem eius ex calamitate fecerunt ludum. ne præbeas puero duos chænices vlterius. Pueri enim & cum turgent à cibo, sunt immodesti, & cum luxuriantur adhuc immodestiores.
units.tr: Honey-cakes make your grandson petulant, Myronides. A red cloth frightened him with a bogey, and he threw down that dear little calf; and his companions made sport of his misfortune. Do not give the boy two more dates. For boys are immoderate when they are stuffed with food, and even more immoderate when they indulge in luxury.

units.la: Amat. PERICLES CALLIOPÆ. LXXVIII.
units.tr: Amatory. PERICLES TO CALLIOPE. LXXVIII.

units.la: Virgineis potiri voluptatibus nimis & supra modum est arduum. ego vero pigror hanc animā. & quid faciam? Pacificationem enim, cum ferit, non admittit amor. Ipsa controuersiam hanc inter me & amorem discepta, ac da mihi calculum humanitatis. nam fascinant amores, amare quidem concedentes, petiri vero auferentes.
units.tr: To possess virginal pleasures is exceedingly and beyond measure difficult. But I am sluggish in this matter. And what shall I do? For love, when it strikes, does not admit of reconciliation. Settle this controversy between me and love yourself, and give me your vote of humanity. For loves bewitch: they allow us to love, but they snatch away the power to be loved.

units.la: Eth. ISOCRATES DIONYSIO. LXXIX.
units.tr: Ethical. ISOCRATES TO DIONYSIUS. LXXIX.

units.la: Præcursores, & lictores, & præcones, & sedium altissimarum adeptio, philosophiam obscurant, & imprimis pollent ad separandam semouendamq; virtutem. non mutaueris cum fortuna naturam. adhuc habes bulgam pelliceam. mortalis enim ab initio factus es. quid igitur inanem hanc gloriolam in tali luteo vtre inflalti? ad magnam redactus es amentiam miser, & à naturæ cognitione distractus, ita alta fortunæ culmina desistere te à pristina rerum contemplatione coegerunt, & utab ista moderata insania recederes, præpararunt. Olim quod erat altum,tibi erat humile,nunc humile, & quòd terram tantum non radit fortunæ fummus gradus est. Quapropter desiste à falsa felicitate & fugitiuam fortunam fug{?}c.Nam cum præuideris inftabilem,desubito ingruentem mutationem non ægrè feres.
units.tr: Forerunners, lictors, heralds, and the attainment of the loftiest seats obscure philosophy, and are especially powerful in separating and removing virtue. You have not changed your nature along with your fortune; you still have a fleshy bladder-skin. For you were mortal from the beginning. Why then do you puff up this empty little glory in such a clay bottle? Wretched man, you have been driven into great madness and drawn away from the knowledge of nature; the high summits of fortune, which have prepared you to abandon your former contemplation of things and withdraw from that moderate folly, have compelled you to desist. Once what was high was low for you; now what is low, and what barely grazes the earth, is the highest step of fortune. Therefore desist from false happiness and flee fortune, which is fleeting. For when you foresee an unstable change that suddenly bears down on you, you will not bear it grievously.

units.la: Rusticis nihil est miferabilius. premimur etiam à ventis,infelices. Deperdit nos Auster. spicas mihi cuanidas fecit. vitem læsit, & acinos corrupit. nec possum,eum qui me triftatin ius protrahere.quare falcem & hamam abiiciam,clypeum & galeam, & ensem sumpturus.ac miles fiam,& arte mutata fortunam experiar.
units.tr: Nothing is more wretched than country folk. We are oppressed even by the winds, unhappy that we are. The south wind ruins us. It has made my ears of corn into chaff, has harmed the vine and spoiled the grapes. Nor can I drag to court him who has made me sad. Therefore I will cast away my sickle and hook, my shield and helmet, and sword, and I will become a soldier, and by changing my art I will try my fortune.

units.la: Si quidem inter homines auro quid fit preciofius,doce; & maioribus donis emam voluptatem. quod fi non,leuiori fruar precio tuis Gratiis. neq; enim Danaes habes formam ; aut adeo ipsa es fanctior, neque ego sum Iouc{?} ditior, qui auro emam virginitatem.
units.tr: If indeed anything is more precious than gold among men, tell me, and I will buy pleasure with larger gifts. But if not, I will enjoy your Graces at a lighter price. For you do not have the beauty of Danae, nor are you so much holier, nor am I so much richer than Jove, who would buy virginity with gold.

units.la: Fth. SOCRATES ALCIBIADI. LXXXII.
units.tr: Ethical. SOCRATES TO ALCIBIADES. LXXXII.

units.la: Poefcos etiam lusus, pleni sunt sapientiæ. Cerã{?} Ulyffis socios obturaffe dicit aures Meletis filius, postquam nauigio aduecti fuissent ad intemperantes Sirenes. Lacertis vero filium vinculis se constrinxisse, quasi carcere quodam incuitabili, significat philosophiae secreta. Sirenas enim puto poesin singere informes ac turpes voluptates. & admiror nimium in modum Homerum, commiscentem rebus veritatem, & cyceona nectare suaviorem auditibus nostris instillantem, non secus ac revera notham aquam vino alicui generosissimo miscoret. sic enim neque fabulis fallemur, neque ininitain-[?] comprehensibiliq; entium comprehensione mentem inebriabimus. quare per ceram quidem ignorantiam; per vinculum philosophiam intellexit. inde solum Vlyssem, tam suavia, supra ipsos quoq; cycnos audiuisse carmina fingit, & vinculis perrupisse viam. In malorum enim perspicuitate, constitit virtus philosopha: in voluptatum vero fuga, philosophiae é certamine comparatum tropæum. Quoniam itaque, Antimache, Vlyssis errorem hæc vita exprimit, ac in mare turbarum miser homo innatat, & circumstant nos Sirenorum[?] cantuum voces, ventorum instar modo hinc modo alia nobis non bona intentant, Penelopeæ coniugem imitabimur, firmum istud virtutum & diuinum philosophiæ vinculum prætendentes.
units.tr: The playful things of poets too are full of wisdom. The son of Meletus says that Ulysses' companions stopped their ears with wax, after they had been carried by ship to the intemperate Sirens. And he signifies by the fact that the son bound himself with chains to the mast, as if in some inescapable prison, the secrets of philosophy. For I think the poem feigns the Sirens to be shapeless and base pleasures. And I greatly admire Homer, who mixes truth with things and instils into our hearing the sweeter-than-cyceon nectar, just as one would mix false water with a very fine wine. For in this way we are neither deceived by fables, nor do we intoxicate the mind with incomprehensible and inapprehensible grasp of beings. Therefore by the wax he understood ignorance, and by the chain philosophy. Hence he feigns that Ulysses alone heard songs so sweet, even above the swans themselves, and broke through the way with his bonds. For virtue, as a philosophical thing, stands firm in the clear sight of evils, and in the flight from pleasures a trophy is won from the contest of philosophy. Since therefore, Antimachus, this life presents the wandering of Ulysses, and wretched man swims in a sea of troubles, and the voices of the Sirens' songs surround us, and like the winds they threaten us now from this side, now from that with things not good, we will imitate Penelope's husband, holding out that firm bond of virtues and the divine bond of philosophy.

units.la: Rubr. ANTHINUS AMPELINO, LXXXIII.
units.tr: Rubr. Anthinus to Ampelinus, 83.

units.la: Appropinquat jam vindemia, & musto ebriosa sunt acina. circumspicias igitur qua potes optimé in via publica, & cretensem tibi canem adhibeas comitem. viatorum namque manus continentes non sunt, sed ad rusticis sudoribus iniuriam inferendam paratissimæ.
units.tr: The vintage is now at hand, and the grapes are growing drunk on the must. Look about you, then, and take the safest route along the public road, and keep a Cretan dog as your companion. For travellers' hands are not restrained; they are only too ready to inflict harm on the sweat of the countryfolk.

units.la: Amat. CHRYSIPPA SOSIPATRO. LXXXIV.
units.tr: Love. Chrysippa to Sosipater. 84.

units.la: Amatoriis retibus nónne captus es, Sofipater, qui Anthusam ames? ingenuorum oculorum fignum est, adolescentulam amare decoram, ne ingemisce victus pulcritudine. maius enim oblecta mentum inde capies. Amatoriæ lacrimæ, dulces exiftunt. nam voluptate sunt commissæ, quæ dolorem alias creant. & exhilarant Amores, cum trifta uerint. multiplicibus enim affectibus veneris cestus est insculptus.
units.tr: Have you not been caught in the nets of love, Sosipater, since you love Anthusa? It is a sign of a noble mind to love a lovely young girl, so do not groan, conquered by her beauty. For you will get greater delight from it. Tears of love turn out sweet, since they are mixed with pleasure, which otherwise produces pain. And loves cheer us when we are sad, for the girdle of Venus is embroidered with many kinds of feeling.

units.la: Eth. PLATO DIONYSIO. LXXXV.
units.tr: Ethical. Plato to Dionysius. 85.

units.la: Si mœrorem vis vincere, circui sepulchra. & passionis inuenies remedium, & maximas hominum fortunas vlterius cinerem videbis esse nihil.
units.tr: If you wish to overcome grief, go round the tombs. There you will find a remedy for suffering, and you will further see that the greatest fortunes of men are, in the end, nothing but ash.

units.la: IN proœmio dialogi. pag.1. lin.21 Μαλὶν ἐγὼ Συμεὼν[?]) Malim ego, Συμεὼν. moneat me illa, quae precedunt proxime; καὶ πρὸς τὸ ἑξῆς[?] Dicitur enim hic dialogus coram collegio philosophorum aliquot, quasi in theatro, & vt a metaphora non discedat, addit author πρὸς ἐξῆς[?] epistola prima & ut circa-da: τερπλίζεσ γῦνὸ μελαῶ̈ς βῆμα[?] alio interprete ad locum hunc non est opus, nec melior esse posset. Βῆμα appellat pulpitum, ἥν Συμπλίλη̈ quo loco erat altus in orchestra quinque pedes, forma mensa, sive altaris, unde Bacchi ea ara. Suidas in voce Σκηνὴ &c. ἐςιμὴ̈ ὀρχήςραν Σωμὸς Διονύσῳ, ὡς καλεῖ[?] θυμέλην. Iulii Pollucis lib. XVIII. cap. XLVII. Thymelici autem erant musici (cenici, qui in organis & lyris, & citharis praecinebant. Et dicti Thymelici, quod olim in orchestra stantes cantabant super pulpitum, quod Thymele vocabatur & cap. XLIV. Orchestra autem pulpitus erat scenae, vbi saltator agere poterat, aut duo inter se disputare. Ibi enim poetae comoedi & tragoedi ad certamen concurrebant &c. Facit hoc quod in eadem metaphora etiam postea perseueret, Naemilla.
units.tr: In the preface to the dialogue, page 1, line 21. Μαλὶν ἐγὼ Συμεὼν [Symeon]: I would rather read "Symeon." Let the words immediately preceding guide me. And "in the following," πρὸς ἐξῆς: the dialogue is said to be held before a college of several philosophers, as if in a theatre, and so that the author does not depart from the metaphor, he adds the first epistle and "as around" [ut circa-da]. The word τερπλίζεσ γῦνὸ μελαῶ̈ς βῆμα [garbled] needs no other translator for this passage, nor could a better be found. He calls the βῆμα [platform] the pulpit, which in the orchestra was a raised place five feet high, shaped like a table or altar, whence the altar of Bacchus. See Suidas under the word "Scene," etc. Julius Pollux, book 18, chapter 47: the thymelici were musicians (singers) who sang to the organ, lyre and cithara, and they were called thymelici because they formerly stood in the orchestra and sang upon the platform, which was called the thymele. Chapter 44: the orchestra was the stage-floor of the scene, where a dancer could perform or two could dispute with each other, for there comic and tragic poets competed, etc. This is why he afterwards keeps up the same metaphor, Naemilla.

units.la: ἐιδ᾽ς τι καὶ τὴν ᾠδὴν ἔξω φυσίμλω ἐυθμῶν, ἐωσχείτε φιλ[?] λοίμως μοι γὰρ λεγωδύμεναι est enim ea vox e theatro, ve-niam perentium muficorum[?]. Simile de Nerone canente apud Graecos in theatro. cap. xxiii. Sueton. Iudices autem priusquam inciperet, reverentissimè allo-quebatur, omnia se facienda fecisse, sed euentum in manu esse fortunæ, illos vt sapientes & doctos viros fortuita debere excludere &c.
units.tr: "And that I may sing the song outside the rhythms" [ἐιδ᾽ς τι καὶ τὴν ᾠδὴν ἔξω φυσίμλω ἐυθμῶν]: this word is from the theatre, the pardon sought by performing musicians. A similar case concerns Nero singing among the Greeks in the theatre, chapter 23 (Suetonius). Before he began, he very respectfully addressed the judges, saying that he had done everything that was to be done, but that the outcome lay in the hand of fortune, and that they, as wise and learned men, ought to exclude chance, etc.

units.la: lin.26. ᾳ ... ) lege, ... Ζεὺς.
units.tr: Line 26: read ... Zeus [Ζεὺς].

units.la: pag.2 lin.23. ἀ ... ἀπαγγεῖλαι ... ἀπάγγελλ[?]ν.
units.tr: Page 2, line 23: read ἀπαγγεῖλαι ... ἀπαγγέλλειν [apangeilai ... apangellein].

units.la: pag.4 lin.6. τῷ Κυρλωαῖω) videtur esse hemistichium Callimachi Cyrenei, Μηδ᾽ ἐν ἀγυιᾷ ἔχοιμι φίλῳ καλὸν-
units.tr: Page 4, line 6: τῷ Κυρηναίῳ: this seems to be a half-line of Callimachus of Cyrene, "Nor should I have a fine thing in the street for a friend" [Μηδ᾽ ἐν ἀγυιᾷ ἔχοιμι φίλῳ καλὸν-].

units.la: lin.22. scriptum est ἀνάγκη μὲ λέγων. pro, ἀνάγκη μέ-τέχον.
units.tr: Line 22: it is written "ἀνάγκη μὲ λέγων" [necessity compels me to say] instead of "ἀνάγκη μέ-τέχον."

units.la: pag.5.lin.1. ὅτι) Distinguendum, ὅ, τι.
units.tr: Page 5, line 1: "ὅτι" [that] should be punctuated as ὅ, τι [what].

units.la: pag.5.lin.25. ἑτέρα τὰ κόμας) Diffendo, ἑτέρα δὲ κό-μας ἀετῷ ... ἀπὸ ἀλλοι Galea. vel certè, ἑτερ' ἄλλα.
units.tr: Page 5, line 25: "ἑτέρα τὰ κόμας": I would read "ἑτέρα δὲ κόμας" with the eagle ... or at least "ἑτερ' ἄλλα" [other things].

units.la: pag.6 lin.22. τὸ χείρε πάχων εὐθὺς τοῖς κάλοις *ἀφελ-κομένων, τὸν κύρ[?]ον) Corruptus locus, ita reftitui poteft. τὴς ἐργώσ ... ἐαὐτὸ ... ἀλλαχώ, τὰ χείρε... ἀχείνεσι μὴ τοῖς καλοῖς ἀφελκόμενοι τὸν κύρ(ον. vel ἐνιαῖ, εἰ μὴ εὐθὺς τοῖς καλοῖς.
units.tr: Page 6, line 22: a corrupt passage, which can be restored thus: "τὴς ἐργώσ ... ἐαὐτὸ ... ἀλλαχώ, τὰ χείρε ... ἀχείνεσι μὴ τοῖς καλοῖς ἀφελκόμενοι τὸν κύρ(ον." Or perhaps "ἐνιαῖ, εἰ μὴ εὐθὺς τοῖς καλοῖς" [unless immediately by the fine ones].

units.la: pag.7.lin.23. ὅπ[?] ... ποίνικος ... φῦλα) verba inclusa signe hoc ( ) sunt superflua.
units.tr: Page 7, line 23: the words enclosed in this sign ( ) are superfluous.

units.la: lin.28.* ἐπειδὴ ... ) Nihil hic deest, nihil corruptum, si fallem reponatur, ἐπεὶ ἂν δ᾽ ἐκ.
units.tr: Line 28: "ἐπειδὴ ..." Nothing is missing here and nothing is corrupt, if one reads for "ἐπειδὴ" the form "ἐπεὶ ἂν δ᾽ ἐκ" [but if from].

units.la: pag.8.lin.1 ἐξυνῶν) ἐστιν) Scribe totum locum ita: ἐπεὶ ἂν δ᾽ ἐκ ἃ ἐξ κ ὕλες ἐστιν οἱ τούτης. Philes ἀλλὰ λύκων ᾿Αλλ᾽ ἐστὶν οἱ.
units.tr: Page 8, line 1: "ἐξυνῶν ... ἐστιν": write the whole passage thus: "ἐπεὶ ἂν δ᾽ ἐκ ἃ ἐξ κ ὕλες ἐστιν οἱ τούτης," and "ἀλλὰ λύκων" [but of wolves] "᾿Αλλ᾽ ἐστὶν οἱ."

units.la: pag.9.lin.3. ἀχρει ... Graeca phrasis indi-cat,
units.tr: Page 9, line 3: "ἀχρει ..." The Greek idiom shows what is meant.

units.la: cat legendum esse, ἀχοικότερος ἐπότε παῖς μὴν λῶ ἡλικίαν, ἀχοικότερος ὃ ἔννυν.
units.tr: It should be read: "ἀχοικότερος ἐπότε παῖς μὴν λῶ ἡλικίαν, ἀχοικότερος ὃ ἔννυν" [more homely...].

units.la: lin.5. καὶ λέγ' ὁρῶν μοι] Malo, καὶ ἂν ὁρῶν μοι ἐψιλό-κομα. ἐψιλύχομαι, vertex.sta fæpè alibi loquitur absolutè.
units.tr: Line 5: "καὶ λέγ' ὁρῶν μοι": I prefer "καὶ ἂν ὁρῶν μοι," "ἐψιλό-κομα" [I shave my head]; "ἐψιλύχομαι" [I am bald at the crown]: the author elsewhere often uses this word absolutely.

units.la: lin.20. προσεπιλέ[?]ξις] Dispungo, προς ὅπ τὴν ξις. Sic versus est hac particula, epistola 60. καὶ προς τὰς ἐρώτας μαίαν τεσεῖν αὐάρεζον ἔφασκον.
units.tr: Line 20: "προσεπιλέξις": I delete it, so that "προς ὅπ τὴν ξις" stands; thus in epistle 60 the verse has this particle: "καὶ προς τὰς ἐρώτας μαίαν τεσεῖν αὐάρεζον ἔφασκον" [and to the questions...].

units.la: lin.25. ἀλλ' ἔταν] Hemistichium est Homeri ἰλιαδ. B', pag.11.lin.15. ad ἀ ἐι ἀ προςοπελεῖρ] Per primam vocalem ἀ προςοπελεῖρειν.
units.tr: Line 25: "ἀλλ' ἔταν": this is a half-line of Homer, Iliad B. Page 11, line 15: for "ἀ ἐι ἀ προςοπελεῖρ," read by the first vowel "ἀ προςοπελεῖρειν."

units.la: pag.12.lin.13. τῇ φύσει ... ] Distinguendum, ... ὁ (supple ζῶον.
units.tr: Page 12, line 13: "τῇ φύσει ...": punctuate "...ὁ" and supply ζῶον [animal].

units.la: pag.15.lin.17. καὶ παῖδα ... ] Lege, ... quod vocabulum reperies apud Suidam, ... hic vocat, quem alibi ... enim, ... idem est quod μαγὸς. Pollux lib.11. onomasticon: οἱ μαγοὶ, καὶ τιτθοὶ καλεῖ, καὶ τιθία, μάλιστα δὲ ... vide etiam Hesychium.
units.tr: Page 15, line 17: "καὶ παῖδα ...": read "...," a word you will find in Suidas, "...," which he calls in another place "...," for it is the same as μαγὸς [magos]. Pollux, book 11 of the Onomasticon: "οἱ μαγοὶ, καὶ τιτθοὶ καλεῖ, καὶ τιθία, μάλιστα δὲ ..." See also Hesychius.

units.la: lin.19. τοῖς λογῶς] λαγώς, leporibus.
units.tr: Line 19: "τοῖς λογῶς" should be "λαγώς" [hares].

units.la: n 24. καθάπερ ἔφησεν ὁ Ἀβδηρείτης] Democritum intelligit, quem verisimile est aliquid de Animalibus edisse, præsertim cum in iis tam diligens ille studium posuerit ut patet ex longa illa elegantiq, epistola Hippocratis ad Demagetum.
units.tr: Line 24: "καθάπερ ἔφησεν ὁ Ἀβδηρείτης" [as the Abderite said]: he means Democritus, who probably wrote something on animals, especially since he applied such diligent study to them, as is plain from the long and elegant letter of Hippocrates to Demagetus.

units.la: pag.16.lin.11. ὥραν Διρες] Scribendum, non ὥραν, sed ὥρα Διρες.
units.tr: Page 16, line 11: "ὥραν Διρες": one should write not "ὥραν" but "ὥρα Διρες."

units.la: lin.21. ἑαυτὸν μηχάνοι] Lego, ὑπηχημένοι. unde ηχίζε τέτλε Hesiodo erratum contrarium fuerat in hoc Cleanthus verse: ἐν σῷ γὰρ ὄλλος ἰσομὲν ὄχω μίμημα λαχόντες. ἤχω enim pro ὄχω posuerant.
units.tr: Line 21: "ἑαυτὸν μηχάνοι": I read "ὑπηχημένοι." Whence the opposite error had occurred in Hesiod, and in this verse of Cleanthes: "ἐν σῷ γὰρ ὄλλος ἰσομὲν ὄχω μίμημα λαχόντες" [for we, having received the imitation...]. For they had put "ἤχω" for "ὄχω."

units.la: lin. 23. ἐξαίρεσιν ἔ[?]ειν] Malo, ἐπεσι.
units.tr: Line 23: "ἐξαίρεσιν ἔ[?]ειν": I prefer "ἐπεσι."

units.la: pag. 17. lin. 9. ὥσπερ ὀμήρῳ] Hemistichium Homeri μῦθος τ' ἀνδρῶσι μελήσει[?].
units.tr: Page 17, line 9: "ὥσπερ ὀμήρῳ": a half-line of Homer, "μῦθος τ' ἀνδρῶσι μελήσει" [speech will be a care to men].

units.la: pag. 18. lin. 14. ἴσως δὲ Ἀρτεμίδωρος ὑπὸ πᾶν Θεωρίας] Supra quidem problem. 19. de cicada femina, cur sit muta verbo huic feremmis utitur. καὶ τὶς ἐνθένδε μοι ἀκούει τετίλιων λόγος εἰσὶ Ἀ[?]. hoc tamen loco, ... reponendum est.
units.tr: Page 18, line 14: "ἴσως δὲ Ἀρτεμίδωρος ὑπὸ πᾶν Θεωρίας": above, in problem 19, concerning the female cicada, he uses the word for why it is mute: "καὶ τὶς ἐνθένδε μοι ἀκούει τετίλιων λόγος" [and from here a tale of the cicadas reaches me]. Yet in this place ... must be restored.

units.la: lin. 15. ὅτι ἐν Ἀχαρδὲν ... ] Nescio an melius foret, ὅτι τὰς ... χαράδρων ὑπὸ πολεύει νόμος. licet vocabulum ist ... ὑπερπολεύειν vix apud alium reperias.
units.tr: Line 15: "ὅτι ἐν Ἀχαρδὲν ...": I do not know whether it would be better to read "ὅτι τὰς ... χαράδρων ὑπὸ πολεύει νόμος" [because the law of the ravines...], although the word "ὑπερπολεύειν" is scarcely found in any other author.

units.la: lin. 25. ὀφθαλμὸς μύει] Expunge punctum. est enim dualis, ut vocant, numeri, ὀφθαλμῶ.
units.tr: Line 25: "ὀφθαλμὸς μύει": delete the point. For it is of the dual number, as they call it: "ὀφθαλμῶ" [of the two eyes].

units.la: pag. 19. lin. 23 καὶ ὄμβρον] Muta, καὶ ὄμβρων ἀπειλεῖν ἐνδημίαν.
units.tr: Page 19, line 23: "καὶ ὄμβρον": change to "καὶ ὄμβρων ἀπειλεῖν ἐνδημίαν" [and to threaten the showers of the season].

units.la: pag. 20. lin. 5. Πλυμίς ... ] Puto, ἀληθίς ... ex plurimis commixta, quam tamen vocem nondum reperi apud alios.
units.tr: Page 20, line 5: "Πλυμίς ...": I think it should be "ἀληθίς ..." mixed from many, though I have not yet found this word in other authors.

units.la: pag. 21. lin. 1. ὦ φίλος] φιλότης. typographicum mendum est.
units.tr: Page 21, line 1: "ὦ φίλος": it should be "φιλότης" [friendship]; it is a typographical error.

units.la: ead. τί τῶ] Inferendum arbitror particulam τί[?] ἢ τῶ ποτὲ πεπαράσχυ[?].
units.tr: Ibid., "τί τῶ": I think the particle "τί ἢ τῶ ποτὲ πεπαράσχυ" should be inserted.

units.la: lin. 14. καὶ ἐπιμύλη ἔχει] Abest aliquid, quod addo. ἐνθένδε δὴ καὶ ἐπιμύλην ἔχει τὸ ὀσφρησιν. ut dicat mel Atticum graniorum esse odoris, propterea, quod, quae abundat Attica, pascatur thymo apis eius opifex. quemadmodum Ponticum mel amarum est, ab synthii causa, quod in Ponto crebrum est. quod de fardo idem tradit Isidorus lib. xx. cap. 11. fardum amarum est ablynthij caufa, cuius copia eius regionis apes nutriuntur. lin. 26.
units.tr: Line 14: "καὶ ἐπιμύλη ἔχει": something is missing, which I add: "ἐνθένδε δὴ καὶ ἐπιμύλην ἔχει τὸ ὀσφρησιν," so that he says Attic honey has the smell of grain, because the bee, its maker, feeds on the thyme that abounds in Attica; just as Pontic honey is bitter, from the wormwood (absinthium), because it is abundant in Pontus. Isidore, book 20, chapter 11, says the same about the bitter honey: it is bitter because of absinthium, the plant of which is abundant in that region where the bees feed. Line 26.

units.la: lin.26.οἷα' τινες μέλιτ[?]] Lucretius:
units.tr: Line 26: "οἷα' τινες μέλιτ" [such as some honey]. Lucretius:

units.la: Florifetis utapes in saltibus omnia libant: Omnia nos itidem depascimur aurea dicta, Aurea perpetua semper dignissima vita,
units.tr: Like bees that sip from every flower in the flowery meadows, so we also graze on all the golden sayings, golden and ever most worthy of a lasting life.

units.la: pag.22.lin.5.ὁ Σωτίων[?]] Est ille Sotion, cuius fragmentum edidit [?] περὶ ὑδάτων [?] de fontibus, aquis & lacubus Henr. Stephanus, cum Aristotelis aliquot & Theophrasti opusculis.
units.tr: Page 22, line 5: "ὁ Σωτίων" [Sotion]. This is that Sotion, whose fragment On Waters, concerning fountains, waters and lakes, Henri Estienne published together with some small works of Aristotle and Theophrastus.

units.la: IN HISTORIARVM PERIOCHARVM EX PHOTIO.
units.tr: ON THE SUMMARIES OF HISTORIES FROM PHOTIUS

units.la: Ex libro primo.
units.tr: From the first book.

units.la: sol.24.lin.5.ὁ τερσαγιον[?]] Ioannes Langus, apud Nicephorum, lib.18.cap. VII. τερσαγιον vertit ter sanctum numen. de eo totū librum scripsit Iohannes Damascenus.
units.tr: Page 24, line 5, ὁ τερσαγιον[?]: John Langus, in Nicephorus, book 18, chapter 7, rendered tersagion [τερσαγιον] as "thrice-holy divinity" (ter sanctum numen). John Damascene wrote an entire book about it.

units.la: lin.7.ὁ φοίλησαι χένοι[?]] Langus ibidem ita: tyranni, impij tui temporibus non extabunt. videtur legisse ἀγένοις non γένοι.
units.tr: Line 7, ὁ φοίλησαι χένοι[?]: Langus there renders it: "your tyrants, your impious ones, will not survive in your times." He appears to have read ἀγένοις [agenois] rather than γένοι [genoi].

units.la: lin 10.ὁ Σίρμιον πολιορκήσας[?]] Sententia suadet scribendum esse, πολιορκήσεις.
units.tr: Line 10, ὁ Σίρμιον πολιορκήσας[?]: The sense suggests that it should be written πολιορκήσεις [poliorkēseis].

units.la: pag.25.lin.16.ἡ ἀσπολικῶ ἐῶν[?]] Ἀσπολικῶ ἐῶν vocat, utrinsq; canonis libros, tā veteres quam nouos.
units.tr: Page 25, line 16, ἡ ἀσπολικῶ ἐῶν[?]: He calls both collections of books of the canon, the old as well as the new, by the name ἀσπολικῶ ἐῶν [aspolikō eōn].

units.la: Ex libro secundo.
units.tr: From the second book.

units.la: pag.26.lin.12.τῷ ἀχειροποιήτῳ] Eandem ἀχειροποίητον, etiam infra mox nominat, & lib. III. seditione militis contra Priscum. videtur autem imago fuisse caelitus alicunde quod hodie de Maria Laurentana simulacro dicunt, delata: quam ex hoc loco constat fuisse summae religionis.
units.tr: Page 26, line 12, τῷ ἀχειροποιήτῳ: He names the same thing ἀχειροποίητον [acheiropoiēton], "not made by hands," again shortly below, and in book 3, at the sedition of the soldiers against Priscus. It seems to have been an image sent down from heaven from somewhere, like what people today say of the image of Mary at Loreto (Laurentana). From this passage it is clear that it was held in the highest reverence.

units.la: lin.21.κυαρ-ξπαρθῶν ζεως[?]] Non opinor esse à Parthis compositam vocē, sed à partibus. itaq; scribendum effet, κυαρ-ξπαρθ[?] litteram leniore. Quae vero fuerit illa legio, ipse autor subiicit.
units.tr: Line 21, κυαρ-ξπαρθῶν ζεως[?]: I do not think the word was formed from Parthi (Parthians), but from partes (parts). So it should be written with the softer letter. The author himself adds below which legion that was.

units.la: pag.28.lin.14.Σαπηρος ἡ σραιωτα] Saper hic dicitur, qui aliis Sapor nomen est Persicum lib.1. catalestorum Scaligeri,tit.2.veteris poeta carmen legitur,de eliciendis manibus Pompeii,
units.tr: Page 28, line 14, Σαπηρος ἡ σραιωτα: Here he is called Saper, whom others name Sapor, a Persian name. In Scaliger's Catalecta, book 1, title 2, there is read a verse of an old poet about drawing out the fates from the entrails of Pompey:

units.la: Fata per humanas solitus pernoscere fibrasImpius infanda relligionis aper.
units.tr: "The impious boar, accustomed to learn the fates from human entrails, of unspeakable religion."

units.la: Legendum est, Impius infanda relligione Saper. id est, persa.sed mutationem horū inter se nominum videbis infra sapius.
units.tr: It should be read "Impius infandae religione Saper," that is, the Persian. But you will often see the interchange of these names with one another below.

units.la: Ex libro tertio.
units.tr: From the third book.

units.la: lin.23. ἐκ ἀπέβη τῆς ἵππου] (contra tamen Xantho, Nicephorus, lib. xviii. cap. xi. ex interpretatione Langi: Ipse quoque Priscus in eo exercitus tumultu ingulatus fuisset,nisi equo conscenso Euslum fugisset.at qui equo conscenso,qui nō ex equo descenderat?
units.tr: Line 23, ἐκ ἀπέβη τῆς ἵππου: (Against Xanthus, however, Nicephorus, book 18, chapter 11, in Langus's translation:) "Priscus himself too would have been slaughtered in that tumult of the army, unless, having mounted a horse, he had fled from Euslus." But how could one who had mounted a horse not have dismounted from it?

units.la: lin.28.διὸ φεύγειν ἡ] Corrige,διὸ φεύγει ἡ. ἐς mox, ἐν Κω: ἐ σαν'ίνη,cum subdito puncto.
units.tr: Line 28, διὸ φεύγειν ἡ: Correct to διὸ φεύγει ἡ [dio pheugei ē]. Next, in Κω [Kō], as ἐ σαν'ίνη, with a dot added beneath.

units.la: pag.29.lin.18.Διαοῖλα δλω] Ἐναγριυς & Nicephorus Sittam nominatur, vbi de eius morte agit. Emedandū igitur diuisis litteris.ςΣιτα, vel etiàςιᾶ. nō duplicato charactere.
units.tr: Page 29, line 18, Διαοῖλα δλω: Nicephorus names him Sitta, where he treats of his death. The text should therefore be emended by dividing the letters, to Σιτα [Sita], or perhaps Σιτα [Sita] with a single rather than doubled character.

units.la: lin. 21.ἡ Σηλάξοι] Σηλάξοι, Sclaui. eosdem deinde semper Σηλαξλωὶς videbis dici.
units.tr: Line 21, ἡ Σηλάξοι: Σηλάξοι [Sēlaxoi] means the Sclavenes (Slavs). You will see them afterwards always called Σηλαξλωὶς [Sēlaxlōis].

units.la: lin. 25. ἀπναίον Νισκος] Et casus particula huius,est nomen vrbis,est autorum consensus,postulant vt rescri-batur, Πλησίον Νισίβιδος.
units.tr: Line 25, ἀπναίον Νισκος: The case-ending of this is the name of a city, and the agreement of the authors requires that it be written "near Nisibis" (Πλησίον Νισίβιδος [Plēsion Nisibidos]).

units.la: lin.27.πίπτει γὰρ Cecidit enim.id est, occisus est. ita enim vtitur hoc verbo epist. xxxii. de Dario: ςὶν ἐν τῇ πολέμῳ ποτῇ θρασαμένος ἀπέλωνός Δάρειον. at Niceophorus lib.18.cap.18.Persarum dux vna cum equo in terram deiectus,interiisset,nisi ex satellitibus qui-dam dam eum in equum, quem secum ducebat, fublatū è prælio fubduxiffet.non occisum esse dicit.
units.tr: Line 27, πίπτει γὰρ: "For he fell," that is, he was killed. For he uses this verb in this way in letter 32, about Darius: having boldly struck down Darius in the battle [...]. But Nicephorus, book 18, chapter 18, says: "The Persian leader, thrown to the ground together with his horse, would have perished, had not one of his attendants lifted him onto the horse he was leading with him and carried him away from the fight." He does not say that he was killed.

units.la: lin. 28. ὁ᾽ τ᾽ ... [?] φραώτης alii auto-res scribunt, inter quos Philostratus.
units.tr: Line 28, ὁ᾽ τ᾽ ... [?] φραώτης: Other authors write it so, among them Philostratus.

units.la: pag. 30. lin. 13. Δομεντ[?]ίολος δ᾽[?] Κομεντίολος δ᾽ ἐ. infra vero etiam τζύρπλον dicitur, quod Nicephoro, si Lango fides, τύρπλον ἐστί.
units.tr: Page 30, line 13, Δομεντ[?]ίολος δ᾽[?]: Κομεντίολος δ᾽ ἐ [Komentiolos d' e...]. Further below it is also called τζύρπλον [tzyrplon], which in Nicephorus, if Langus is to be trusted, is τύρπλον [tyrplon].

units.la: lin. 14. χαὶ Συμβάτιον] Inconstantia scriptorum. Συμβάτιος hic nominatur, qui tribus ante verfibus Σαββάτιος. Malo, ego vtrobig, legi, Συμβάσιον & Συμβάσιον.
units.tr: Line 14, χαὶ Συμβάτιον: The writers are inconsistent. Here he is named Symbation, while three verses earlier he is Sabbatios. I would prefer to read it as Symbasion in both places.

units.la: Ex libro quarto.
units.tr: From the fourth book.

units.la: pag. 31 lin. 8. ὅπως τε ἔαυ Βίνδου] Lege Βινδοῦ. Semper enim Βινδόνες.
units.tr: Page 31, line 8, ὅπως τε ἔαυ Βίνδου: Read Βινδοῦ [Bindou], since it is always Βίνδονες [Bindones].

units.la: lin. 15. χαταμαχίζει ἡ βασιλεὺς] Nimis nonè posse vi-dè legere, χαταμοιχίζει, vt stuprū intulerint regina, nisi viderem obstare auctoritatem Nicephori, qui coniugē cū filio ingulatam dicit, ipsum Hermisdam excecatum.
units.tr: Line 15, χαταμαχίζει ἡ βασιλεὺς: I might be tempted to read χαταμοιχίζει [katamoichizei], so that the queen was guilty of adultery, were it not that the authority of Nicephorus stands in the way. He says that the wife was slain along with her son, and Hermisdas himself was blinded.

units.la: lin. 14. ὃν ἐςἠνούτο πέρι βασιλείας] ὃν ἐςἠνούτο πέρι βασιλείας. quem Persæ regem constituerant.
units.tr: Line 14, ὃν ἐςἠνούτο πέρι βασιλείας: Whom the Persians had appointed king.

units.la: lin. 17. ὃτι ὁ Κιρκίνιον] Scribitur hoc libello aliquando Κιρκίνιον, aliquando Κιρκώνιον, femel, sed male, & vt opinor, vitio typographico, Κιρκώνιον. Nicephoro semper Κιρκήνιον.
units.tr: Line 17, ὃτι ὁ Κιρκίνιον: In this little book it is written sometimes Κιρκίνιον [Kirkinion], sometimes Κιρκώνιον [Kirkōnion]; once, however, and wrongly, I think through a typographical error, Κιρκώνιον. In Nicephorus it is always Κιρκήνιον [Kirkēnion].

units.la: pag. 32. lin. 8. ἡ ἀεὶ τ᾽ τ᾽ Σίτλα δὲ ἀ πυρὸς] Nicephorus, non éxuftum, sed in crucem actum dicit. vt & Euagrius lib. vi. cap. xviii. deinde à Martyropolitanis lapidibus obrutus, postea ab eisdem in crucem actus. nihilominus tamen etiam vri potuit: & eius rei exempla possent dari.
units.tr: Page 32, line 8, ἡ ἀεὶ τ᾽ τ᾽ Σίτλα δὲ ἀ πυρὸς: Nicephorus says that he was not burned but put to the cross, as also Evagrius, book 6, chapter 18: first he was stoned by the men of Martyropolis, and afterwards crucified by the same men. Nevertheless he could also have been burned, and examples of that could be given.

units.la: Ex libro quinto.
units.tr: From the fifth book.

units.la: pag. ead. lin. 18. ἀεὶ τ᾽ ὀκαὶ ἀγὶ αἰδεῖος] Vera lectio, ἐκ δ᾽ ἀ[?]ιος.
units.tr: Page ead., line 18, ἀεὶ τ᾽ ὀκαὶ ἀγὶ αἰδεῖος: The true reading is ἐκ δ᾽ ἀ[?]ιος [ek d' a...ios].

units.la: pag.33.lin.25. Πρόκυς᾽ χαλκηδόνος ] Nicephorus Prae-bu nominat episcopū Chalcedonensem, lib.xviii. c.xxvii. cum nos quoq; hoc loco sequemur, πρὸς τ̄ χαλκηδόνος [?].
units.tr: Page 33, line 25, Πρόκυς᾽ χαλκηδόνος: Nicephorus names the bishop of Chalcedon, book 18, chapter 27. We too shall follow him here, reading πρὸς τῆς Χαλκηδόνος [pros tēs Chalkēdonos].

units.la: pag.ead.lin.27. * ἐν ἡ φάσματος ] Arbitror in exemplari, unde hęc descripta sunt fuisse ἐν ὑν, vel tale quid, unde factum deinde quod hic vides, ἡ. Legendum autē, ἡ τ̄ σωτ[?] ἀπὸ ἐν ὕπνῳ φάσματος. Maria virgine apparuisse Chofroi per insomnium, narrat Niceph. lib. xviii. cap. xxvii.
units.tr: Page ead., line 27, * ἐν ἡ φάσματος: I suppose that in the copy from which these were transcribed it was ἐν ὑν [en hyn] or something like that, from which arose what you see here, ἡ. One should read, however, ἡ τῆς σωτ[?] ἀπὸ ἐν ὕπνῳ φάσματος. That the Virgin Mary appeared to Chosroes in a dream is related by Nicephorus, book 18, chapter 27.

units.la: Ex libro sexto.
units.tr: From book six.

units.la: pag.34.lin.22. Σιγλιδόνος ] statim posterum scribitur huius urbis nomē, at supra libro primo, Σιγλιδῶν legitur.
units.tr: p. 34, line 22. Siglidonos [Σιγλιδόνος]: Immediately afterwards the name of this city is written, but above, in book one, it is read as Siglidon [Σιγλιδῶν].

units.la: Ex libro septimo.
units.tr: From book seven.

units.la: pag.36.lin.1 ἀεὶ τῷ μαυρεσίων] Punctum ponendum est ante ἀεὶ. sed aberrantem distinctionem aliquando, lector ipse poterit animadvertere.
units.tr: p. 36, line 1. aei tō mauresiōn [ἀεὶ τῷ μαυρεσίων]: A full stop should be placed before aei. But the reader himself will be able to notice the misplaced punctuation at times.

units.la: lin.8. ἡ τῆς Αραβ. ὁ ἔθνος ] Agarenos intelligit, qui deinde etiam Saraceni dicti.
units.tr: line 8. hē tēs Arab. ho ethnos [ἡ τῆς Αραβ. ὁ ἔθνος]: He means the Agarenes, who were afterwards also called Saracens.

units.la: lin.9. τῆς Κόλχ] Et ea gens est barbara suspe&ta mibi tamen hęc vox. Nicephorus cap. xxx. Sogor nationis, cum suo principe Tucoch, à Chagano sublatas esse triginta myriadas. Quare si nō est falsa Nicephori lectio, Sogor ille vocat, τῆς Ἀγαρ.ἐξ pro τῆς κόλχ [?] hoc loco scribendum τύρος.
units.tr: line 9. tēs Kolch [τῆς Κόλχ]: That people is barbarian, but this word seems suspect to me. Nicephorus, chapter 30: the Sogor nation, with their prince Tucoch, were destroyed by the Chagan, thirty myriads. Therefore, if the reading of Nicephorus is not false, that Sogor is meant, and instead of tēs Kolch here one should write tyros [τύρος].

units.la: lin.10. ἐπανασ[?]ρ ἀπὸ Ρῶ] Nisi quis in his talibus historias inter se dissenter conserat, multa certe nobis ille monstra dabit. sic hīc & illos locos nemo verterit, in hoc libello, nisi cum ingenti quadam τερατολογία. Sunt enim hic que distracta sunt, ac ita porro committenda: ἀλλὰ ἢ ἐπανασ[?]ρ ἀπὸ Τυρῷ μανελῶν. vide Nicephorum lib. xviii. cap.xxx
units.tr: line 10. epanas... apo Rhō [ἐπανασ[?]ρ ἀπὸ Ρῶ]: Unless someone compares histories that disagree with one another on such matters, that author will certainly give us many monsters. Thus no one would translate these passages, in this little book, without a great deal of teratologia [τερατολογία]. For what has been torn apart is here, and must be joined together thus: alla hē epanas... apo Tyrō manelōn [ἀλλὰ ἢ ἐπανασ[?]ρ ἀπὸ Τυρῷ μανελῶν]. See Nicephorus, book eighteen, chapter thirty.

units.la: lin.13. ἀ[?]ρ Νεκε] Idem Nicephorus eodem capite Mucritas hanc gentem nominat, si retle habet Langis versio. Sed reliqua, Οὐαρ[?]ὰ χ[?]υνί aliter apud eundem auto-rem reperias, Οὐὶς νιμιρυμ & Κυνί.
units.tr: line 13. a... Neke [ἀ[?]ρ Νεκε]: The same Nicephorus, in the same chapter, names this people the Mucritae, if Lange's version is correct. But you will find the remaining words, Ouar...chouni, differently in the same author: Ouis nimirum and Kuni [Οὐὶς νιμιρυμ & Κυνί].

units.la: lin.21. eo ordine legenda sunt, sublato puncto post χυ-νί. [Greek: ἐδὰν ἡ ὡς σεωλλὰ[?] ...] [Greek: ...] [?]
units.tr: line 21. They are to be read in that order, with the full stop after chu-ni removed. [ἐδὰν ἡ ὡς σεωλλὰ[?] ...] [...] [?]

units.la: lin.28. ὅπως τε ἡν Δξ... ] Affecto huic loco ita forte medeberis. ὅπως [?] Σπχύνδος [?] Πεἰσχυς-αλεἰς. nec video quid impediat.
units.tr: line 28. hopōs te ēn Dx... [ὅπως τε ἡν Δξ...]: Perhaps you may heal this afflicted passage thus: hopōs [?] Spchyndos [?] Peischys-aleis [ὅπως [?] Σπχύνδος [?] Πεἰσχυς-αλεἰς]. I do not see what prevents it.

units.la: pag.37. lin.2. ὅτι ἡ ἐνεύ[?] ... ] Disturbatus est horum verborum ordo, ac ita, veluti Sorex, ipsa suo se produnt indicio. Locum totum ita constituendum dico: ὅτι τὸ [?] ... ἐτει τῆς Ɛαστλείας [?] vix est ut portentum hoc in aliud tempus consiciat Nicephorus. Otto certè Frifingensis, non malus autor, aperte decimum nonum Imperii eius annum notat. Annale v. cap. vii.
units.tr: p. 37, line 2. hoti hē eneu[?] ... [ὅτι ἡ ἐνεύ[?] ... ]: The order of these words has been disturbed, and so, like a shrew, they betray themselves by their own sign. I say the whole passage should be constituted thus: hoti to [?] ... etei tēs Eastleias [ὅτι τὸ [?] ... ἐτει τῆς Ɛαστλείας]. It is hardly likely that Nicephorus refers this portent to another time. Otto of Freising, certainly not a bad author, clearly marks its nineteenth year of his reign. Annals, book five, chapter seven.

units.la: At Maurilius cum à persecutione beatissimi papæ Gregorii non cessaret, xix. imperii sui anno videt in somnis virum Monachico habitu, gladium in manu habentem, ad se terri-biliter venire, ac eum moriturum pronunciare. nisi quod in eo erret, quod in somnis apparuisse narrat, contra relationem aliorum.
units.tr: But Maurilius, since he did not cease from the persecution of the most blessed Pope Gregory, in the nineteenth year of his reign saw in a dream a man in monastic habit, holding a sword in his hand, coming terribly toward him, and declaring that he would die. Except that he errs in this: he says it appeared in a dream, contrary to the account of others.

units.la: lin.5. [Greek: ὡς ἀναξ... ] [Greek: ἀφ' ἀναγείων].
units.tr: line 5. [ὡς ἀναξ...] [ἀφ' ἀναγείων]: as lord... [ὡς ἀναξ...]; from the ... [ἀφ' ἀναγείων].

units.la: lin.8. [Greek: ἀφ' ἡ συμβάν[?]ς λοιμὸς] Apage hanc pestem. Non enim peste, sed fame laborarunt exercitus, quod apparet ex sequentibus, & Ottone Frifingensi, citato loco: Porrò exercitus à Mauritio missus, cum ob eius auaritiam laborarent fame, in seditionem versi, Focam imperatorem creant. Et hoc ergo est, quod è fame certius, quam fibris pecudum prædixit iste Herodianus. Notum vero est λοιμὸν esse pestem, λιμὸν famem. quare lubricus eo magis lapsus est.
units.tr: line 8. [ἀφ' ἡ συμβάν[?]ς λοιμὸς]: Away with this plague! For the armies did not suffer from plague but from famine, as is clear from what follows and from Otto of Freising, in the passage cited: "Moreover, the army sent by Maurice, since on account of his avarice they were suffering from famine, turned to sedition and created Phocas emperor." And so this is what this Herodianus foretold from famine, more surely than from the entrails of beasts. It is well known that loimon means plague and limon famine. Therefore he slipped all the more.

units.la: pag. 38. lin. 3. Σαρμάτωνος.[?] Dinido, quae coalita, δ᾽ Αρμάτωνος. Theophylactus ipse infra suis verbis, legatione V. Romanorum ad barbaros: ὁ βασιλεὺς προσκαλεσάμενος τὸν Αρμάτωνα πρέσβιν χειροτονεῖ.
units.tr: p. 38, line 3. Sarmatonos [Σαρμάτωνος]? Reading the joined letters, d'Armatonos [δ᾽ Αρμάτωνος]. Theophylact himself below, in his words on the fifth embassy of the Romans to the barbarians: "The emperor, summoning Armaton, appoints him ambassador" [ὁ βασιλεὺς προσκαλεσάμενος τὸν Αρμάτωνα πρέσβιν χειροτονεῖ].

units.la: lin.10. Αναρχίδ᾽ τ᾽ Κνιδί᾽ς[?] Lege, Αγαθαρχίδς[?]. &c.
units.tr: line 10. Anarchid' t' Knidi's [Αναρχίδ᾽ τ᾽ Κνιδί᾽ς]: Read Agatharchidas [Αγαθαρχίδς], etc.

units.la: Reliqua enim desiderantur, disiectain-ter chartas Commeli-nianas.
units.tr: For the rest is missing, scattered among the Commelinian sheets.

units.la: FINIS
units.tr: THE END
